1999-002-F1.quotation: But growth in E-commerce is certain, and even traditional retailers sense they cannot ignore the Internet for long. This year, some of their customers might just decide to stay home and click on that little shopping cart icon. Speed and convenience are the obvious lures -- no more waiting in the check-out line or on hold for a customer service agent to take your catalogue order (though back orders can be a big problem in cyberspace, too).
1999-002-F1.synopsis: Argues that e-commerce's speed and convenience will inevitably pull customers away from physical stores.
1999-002-F1.article_context: Opens the editorial's case for why traditional retailers can no longer ignore the Internet.
1999-002-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it states the e-commerce-inevitability claim in confident, declarative terms — worth comparing to how confidently later 1999 pieces make the same prediction, and to how it actually played out.

1999-002-F2.quotation: It turns out that many customers will research products on line, then phone in their orders or even visit the store. Fears about sending a credit card number over the Internet may be a factor. But a lot of consumers obviously think that talking to a sales clerk is an indispensable part of the hassle. At least for now, most of them prefer a live human to an electronic mouse.
1999-002-F2.primary_subject: Consumers researching online but buying offline
1999-002-F2.synopsis: Notes that many consumers research products online but still complete purchases by phone or in person, preferring human contact.
1999-002-F2.article_context: Complicates the editorial's opening claim by showing e-commerce adoption is partial, not total, in practice.
1999-002-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because it's an early, concrete instance of 'research online, buy offline' behavior — a consumer pattern that recurs across decades of retail discourse and complicates any simple e-commerce-inevitability narrative.

1999-008-F1.quotation: These prices reflect huge amounts of money. Amazon.com is valued at around $26 billion, about the same as CBS and nearly three times as much as Federated Department Stores, the largest department store chain. Yahoo, the Internet search engine that went public almost three years ago, is valued at about $39 billion, nearly 100 times its valuation when it went public and more than Boeing or Anheuser-Busch.
1999-008-F1.primary_subject: Internet company valuations vs. old-economy peers
1999-008-F1.synopsis: Compares Amazon's and Yahoo's market valuations to CBS, Boeing, Anheuser-Busch, and Federated Department Stores.
1999-008-F1.article_context: Opens the article's evidentiary case for calling Internet valuations extraordinary.
1999-008-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it shows financial scale used as rhetorical evidence, on its own, that the Internet represents something unprecedented — before the article ever states that claim outright.

1999-008-F2.quotation: Retail activity would increasingly be dominated by Internet sales, to an extent hard to imagine. Federal Express would be an immediate beneficiary, assuming that Star Trek technology -- ''Beam me up, Scotty'' -- will not be perfected for packages.
1999-008-F2.synopsis: Predicts Internet sales will dominate retail, limited mainly by physical shipping capacity.
1999-008-F2.article_context: Opens the article's speculative "what would the economy look like" section.
1999-008-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because the Star Trek aside shows the author using humor to soften an otherwise sweeping economic prediction — a register worth tracking across the wider 1999 corpus.

1999-008-F3.quotation: Deflation would be likely in the new Internet economy. It is much easier to compare prices on the Internet, a fact that will tend to force prices -- and profit margins -- down on items that are easily comparable. One of the wonders of the performance of Amazon.com is that it specializes in just such products. A book from one store is no different than a book from another.
1999-008-F3.synopsis: Argues online price transparency will compress margins on standardized goods like books.
1999-008-F3.article_context: Continues the speculative section with the deflation half of the argument.
1999-008-F3.analytical_significance: Selected because it's the clearest statement in the corpus of price transparency as a distinct economic consequence of the Internet, separate from the more common "Internet as new market" framing.

1999-008-F4.quotation: Some stores no doubt will continue to prosper. Lettuce does not age well, so food stores are an obvious candidate. For clothes, where fit is important, many will prefer to shop where they can try on before buying. No one will want to wait for mail delivery of a new car battery.
1999-008-F4.synopsis: Names food, clothing, and urgent-purchase categories as resistant to Internet displacement.
1999-008-F4.article_context: Qualifies the speculative section before the article returns to its central prediction.
1999-008-F4.analytical_significance: Selected because it demonstrates argumentative balance — Norris doesn't present Internet-driven disruption as total, which nuances the "revolution" framing carried elsewhere in the same article.

1999-008-F5.quotation:
The most likely outcome is that the Internet will grow to be a much larger economic force than it now is, but that the stocks of Internet companies will nonetheless prove to be horrid investments for those who buy at current prices. Those who are buying do not really expect such an economy. They are just betting that this mania will not end soon.

There is a precedent. In the 1920's, the great speculative stock was Radio Corporation of America, which took six years to rise 100-fold, twice the time Yahoo required. As the bulls forecast, R.C.A. became a dominant player in an industry that revolutionized American life. But those who bought the stock in 1929 still lost nearly all the money they invested.
1999-008-F5.primary_subject: Historical analogy to RCA (1920s stock mania)
1999-008-F5.synopsis: Compares the Internet stock boom to the 1920s RCA boom to predict most Internet stocks will fail as investments.
1999-008-F5.article_context: Closes the article by justifying its prediction with a historical precedent.
1999-008-F5.analytical_significance: Selected because it exemplifies how a specific historical analogy (RCA, 1929) is used to naturalize a prediction about an ostensibly unprecedented new technology — a rhetorical pattern worth tracking wherever an End of History claim recurs across the corpus.

1999-009-F1.quotation: There are some who will tell you that 1999 will be remembered as the year of Clinton, Starr and Lewinsky. Wrong. This remarkable year will be remembered a decade from now as the year of the Amazon -- the cyber-river and the real river, Ama zon.com and Amazon.country, also known as Brazil.
1999-009-F1.primary_subject: Amazon.com and Amazon (Brazil) as dual symbols of 1999
1999-009-F1.synopsis: Declares that 1999 will be remembered for "the Amazon" in its double sense — the company and the country/river.
1999-009-F1.article_context: Opens the column with the central wordplay that structures its globalization argument.
1999-009-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it's the article's opening rhetorical hook — establishing the Amazon/Amazon double meaning the whole column's globalization argument depends on.

1999-009-F2.quotation: But while the buyers of Ama zon.com have the general trend right, whether Amazon.com is actually worth $148 a share before it's ever made a dime of profit depends on how you see the future. The Amazon.com bulls believe that there is a huge race going on right now for everyone's credit card. The race is between a number of major on-line retailers -- AOL, Amazon, Yahoo, Excite, etc. The assumption is that all of these sites will eventually become full-service on-line shopping centers that will sell everything, and that you will give your credit card number to one or two of them -- where you will do most of your shopping -- but to fewer than five of them. Therefore, if Amazon.com is one of those winning sites, its profits will be enormous. It will be an on-line shopping mall for the world.
1999-009-F2.primary_subject: The bull case for Amazon.com's valuation
1999-009-F2.synopsis: Explains the bullish theory that a handful of online retailers will consolidate consumer spending, justifying today's high valuations.
1999-009-F2.article_context: Sets up the "bull" side of the valuation debate before Friedman states his own skeptical position.
1999-009-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because it lays out the winner-take-most logic used to justify dot-com valuations — a reasoning pattern worth tracking against how it was judged after the 2000-01 crash.

1999-009-F3.quotation: The Amazon.com bears, and I'm one, believe that the problem with on-line retailing is that the barriers to entry are so low -- with $100,000 I could start a rival Amazon.com tomorrow -- that there will always be one too many competitors making sure that Amazon's profit margins never get as big as people project. Amazon.com offers 30 percent off almost every hardcover. So Barnes andnoble.com matches that, and then Buy.com comes along and offers best sellers at 50 percent off. Buy.com's founder told USA Today he has no intention of ever making money selling books, but just wants to build up volume to sell ads.
1999-009-F3.primary_subject: The bear case — low barriers to entry erode margins
1999-009-F3.synopsis: Argues that because online retail has almost no barriers to entry, competitors like Barnesandnoble.com and Buy.com will keep undercutting Amazon's margins indefinitely.
1999-009-F3.article_context: States Friedman's own skeptical position, directly countering the bull case in the previous fragment.
1999-009-F3.analytical_significance: Selected because Friedman codes low barriers to entry as itself a hierarchy-flattening force — market structure, not politics, is doing the leveling here, a distinctive version of End of Politics worth comparing to more state/regulation-focused versions elsewhere in the corpus.

1999-009-F4.quotation:
Those two rivers are flip sides of the same coin, and the coin is globalization. The incredible run-up in the stock price of Amazon.com and the incredible run-down in the stock markets of Amazon.country, i.e., Brazil, are both reflections of investors trying to figure out what companies and countries will be worth in this new era of globalization.
“Brazil knows that if it doesn't do what the global herd demands, the herd will just move to Thailand.country or Mexico.country.”
“What Amazon.com and Ama zon.country are telling us is that the next phase of globalization is going to be a real bear. It's going to squeeze the profit margins of every company that does business over the Internet, which will be great for consumers and a terror for producers. And it's going to squeeze the politics of developing countries even tighter, which is going to be tough on their citizens and a terror for their politicians. Yesterday's 228-point drop in the Dow, because of the economic turmoil in Brazil, is just a small reminder that life on the real Amazon still matters, and it can, and will, affect life on the banks of Amazon.com.
1999-009-F4.primary_subject: Amazon.com and Brazil as one globalization force
1999-009-F4.synopsis: Argues that Amazon.com's stock surge and Brazil's market collapse are both products of the same borderless global-investment logic.
1999-009-F4.article_context: Closes the column by fusing the two "Amazons" into a single argument about globalization's reach.
1999-009-F4.analytical_significance: Selected because it's the clearest statement in the corpus of "the internet economy" and "the geopolitical economy" being treated as literally one borderless force — an explicit End of Geography claim built entirely on a pun.

1999-016-F1a.quotation: I write instead to inform potential investors that I have come up with the ultimate Internet business. I guarantee tremendous revenue growth. I guarantee ''eyeballs.'' I guarantee that my first-year losses will be a scant 5 percent of revenue -- it's a lock. (Compare that with Amazon's 21 percent margin!)
1999-016-F1a.primary_subject: Mock-guarantee of losses and eyeball metrics
1999-016-F1a.synopsis: Promises investors guaranteed revenue growth and "eyeballs" while guaranteeing first-year losses of only 5 percent, explicitly compared to Amazon's 21 percent margin.
1999-016-F1a.article_context: Opens the essay's mock investor pitch immediately after the setup paragraphs establish real dot-com valuation logic as the target of parody.
1999-016-F1a.analytical_significance: Selected because it shows the satire adopting real Wall Street valuation vocabulary (eyeballs, margins) verbatim, making the parody legible as a direct citation of actual analyst language rather than invented absurdity.

1999-016-F1b.quotation: Like most recent Internet issues, I don't foresee any profits on the horizon, but my daily traffic will be tremendous. I am sure that advertising revenue will go through the roof (someday).
1999-016-F1b.primary_subject: No-profit business model normalized as routine
1999-016-F1b.synopsis: Declares no foreseeable profits but tremendous daily traffic, predicting advertising revenue will eventually "go through the roof."
1999-016-F1b.article_context: Continues the pitch mid-essay, reinforcing the parody's premise that traffic and vague future revenue substitute for profit.
1999-016-F1b.analytical_significance: Selected because it isolates the deferred-profit logic ("someday") as the load-bearing absurdity, distinct from the eyeball/margin joke that precedes it.

1999-016-F1c.quotation: My idea is this: a site that sells $100 bills for $95. The losses are manageable -- and think of the revenue! I will build up a loyal following, a subscriber base of, no doubt, millions of ''unique'' site visitors. I will limit the offer only by restricting the orders to one (1) hundred-dollar bill per visit -- no automated visits allowed. Each purchaser will have a unique log-in name, and I am certain that I will be able to show that visitors return to the site. If I can get one million registered users to log on every day, my revenue will skyrocket to $665 million per week.
1999-016-F1c.synopsis: Describes a fictional Web site that sells $100 bills for $95, projecting revenue of $665 million per week from one million daily registered users.
1999-016-F1c.article_context: Delivers the essay's central comic image and its most concrete absurdist arithmetic, forming the joke's climax before the closing football-team punchline.
1999-016-F1c.analytical_significance: Selected because the $100-for-$95 conceit is the essay's clearest reductio ad absurdum of dot-com unit economics, making it the single passage that most directly satirizes unprecedented-era investment logic.

1999-016-F2.quotation:
We've all read stories about ''businesses'' without profit (or even the near-term prospect of profit) that have market capitalizations in the billions. Wall Street analysts value these companies based on revenue growth, volume and more exotic measures heretofore unheard of: ''eyeball counts,'' ''traffic,'' ''click-through rates'' and the like. Most investors nervously justify the companies' huge losses as ''investments'' in creating a brand name; the theory is that once Web sites' owners build a loyal customer base, they will -- no one says when or how -- find a way to turn a profit.
“Yet somehow, whenever I suggest to otherwise intelligent individuals that the Internet frenzy is the biggest speculative bubble in our lifetimes, they laugh at me. Even the recent plunge in Internet stock prices is, they insist, merely a slight correction, nothing to worry about.”
“I write instead to inform potential investors that I have come up with the ultimate Internet business. I guarantee tremendous revenue growth. I guarantee ''eyeballs.'' I guarantee that my first-year losses will be a scant 5 percent of revenue -- it's a lock. (Compare that with Amazon's 21 percent margin!)”
“Like most recent Internet issues, I don't foresee any profits on the horizon, but my daily traffic will be tremendous. I am sure that advertising revenue will go through the roof (someday).
1999-016-F2.primary_subject: Diagnosing Internet-stock valuation logic as unmoored from profit
1999-016-F2.synopsis: Argues that investors justify profitless "eyeball"-based valuations as brand-building, dismissing bubble warnings as alarmism.
1999-016-F2.article_context: States the essay's real argument directly, in the passage the myth was coded against.
1999-016-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because it's an explicit 'reasoned null' case for the Unprecedented claim — the author names the biggest-speculative-bubble framing specifically to endorse it as diagnosis, refuting any claim that the dot-com economy is without precedent.

1999-017-F1.quotation: While the morning coffee was still brewing, we spent our time battling for the free line every time one popped out of someone's modem. We no longer turned on the television before skiing to check conditions, and no one trusted the thermometers outside. Instead there were weather Web sites to visit  and voice mail and E-mail to check.
1999-017-F1.primary_subject: Competing for phone lines to check weather sites and messages
1999-017-F1.synopsis: Describes friends competing each morning for a free phone line to check weather websites, voicemail, and email before skiing.
1999-017-F1.article_context: Opens the piece with a vignette establishing how connectivity had already displaced older morning rituals like checking a thermometer.
1999-017-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it captures connectivity as a mundane morning ritual rather than a dramatic transformation — a small, concrete instance of everyday adoption rather than a sweeping claim.

1999-017-F2.quotation: A year ago, if someone in our group had had to take a conference call, that person would have had to skip a few hours of skiing to wait for the call at home. But this trip no one thought twice about bringing a phone along on the slopes.
1999-017-F2.primary_subject: Mobile phones eliminating the need to choose between work and skiing
1999-017-F2.synopsis: Contrasts this year's casual mobile-phone-on-the-slopes behavior with last year's need to stay home for a work call.
1999-017-F2.article_context: Closes the anecdote with the explicit before/after comparison that makes the connectivity claim concrete.
1999-017-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because the explicit one-year before/after framing makes the pace of connectivity's normalization the actual evidence for the myth, not just the fact of connectivity itself.

1999-019-F1.quotation: U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers joked the other day that he had a new idea for solving the problem of Brazil's collapsing currency, the real. He suggested the Brazilians rename their currency -- ''real.com.'' Judging from U.S. stock markets, it would double in value every 90 days.
1999-019-F1.primary_subject: Summers's joke about renaming Brazil's currency "real.com"
1999-019-F1.synopsis: Opens with Larry Summers's joke that Brazil's currency would double in value if renamed "real.com," mocking dot-com stock inflation.
1999-019-F1.article_context: Opens the column with a joke that sets up its argument about the gap between Internet-stock exuberance and developing-world economic reality.
1999-019-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because the joke itself performs the argument — that appending ".com" to anything was treated as a source of value, a rhetorical habit Friedman is about to critique more seriously.

1999-019-F2.quotation:
There is a train that is leaving and we should have known this and done our homework. But now you should slow the train a bit and give us a chance to jump on.''
“As the Deutsche Bank economist Ken Courtis observed: ''The developing world has decided to catch the train just as it's being dematerialized and turned into a virtual experience.'' That's not an easy train to catch.
1999-019-F2.synopsis: Quotes a developing-world official pleading for globalization to slow down, and an economist noting the "train" is dematerializing into something even harder to catch.
1999-019-F2.article_context: Introduces the train metaphor that structures the rest of the column's argument about inevitability and pace.
1999-019-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because it's the article's central metaphor for treating globalization's pace as something to be caught or missed rather than governed — the inevitability framing in its most concrete image.

1999-019-F3.quotation: What's worse, no one can slow the train down, because the world economy today is just like that Internet: everybody is connected but nobody is in charge.
1999-019-F3.synopsis: States directly that no one can slow global economic change because, like the Internet itself, it has no central authority.
1999-019-F3.article_context: Delivers the column's sharpest one-line statement of ungovernability, following directly from the train metaphor.
1999-019-F3.analytical_significance: Selected because it's the most compact statement in the corpus of the Internet's decentralized structure being used as a direct analogy for the ungovernability of the global economy itself.

1999-019-F4a.quotation:
And that's what is scary about this year's Davos: Just when the developing world is coming to really grasp that it has no choice but to get itself ready to climb aboard this train, Bill Gates is predicting that the train is going to get faster -- not slower -- as the developing world moves toward Internet-based commerce, communication and learning systems.
“But people are missing the most important point about the Internet stock boom, said Mr. Gates. Whether or not it's a bubble, it is attracting enormous amounts of new venture capital to every imaginable Internet-related company, and this influx of cash is going to drive ''the pace of Internet innovation even faster.''
1999-019-F4a.primary_subject: Gates's prediction of accelerating Internet-driven change
1999-019-F4a.synopsis: Reports Bill Gates predicting that the pace of Internet innovation will keep accelerating because venture capital is flooding in regardless of whether stocks are in a bubble.
1999-019-F4a.article_context: Introduces Friedman's turn from Davos-elite bubble talk to the accelerating-future claim that will next be reframed as frightening for developing countries.
1999-019-F4a.analytical_significance: Selected because it isolates the acceleration claim itself, in Gates's own words, before Friedman attaches the developing-world dread reaction to it in the following passage.

1999-019-F4b.quotation:
For the global business leaders here, nothing could be more exciting. But for the other invisible party -- the leaders of developing countries -- nothing could be more depressing than the thought that the world will be getting faster. There was a time when the head of state of a developing country -- such as Thailand or  Mexico -- wouldn't want to miss Davos and the chance to show off for the big multinationals. It was almost as if by simply coming here, you were automatically part of the global economy.”
“''I understand we need to get prepared for this globalization and that is partly our responsibility. There is a train that is leaving and we should have known this and done our homework. But now you should slow the train a bit and give us a chance to jump on.''”
1999-019-F4b.synopsis: Contrasts global business leaders' excitement about a faster world with developing-country leaders' fear of it, then quotes an editor asking for the "train" to be slowed so his country can "jump on."
1999-019-F4b.article_context: Follows immediately after the Gates acceleration prediction, splitting its reception into elite excitement versus developing-world dread.
1999-019-F4b.analytical_significance: Selected because it demonstrates the paired register directly: the identical acceleration claim reads sublime for Davos elites and demonic for developing-world leaders, split explicitly by who is speaking.

1999-019-F4c.quotation: "As the Deutsche Bank economist Ken Courtis observed: ''The developing world has decided to catch the train just as it's being dematerialized and turned into a virtual experience.'' That's not an easy train to catch.
1999-019-F4c.primary_subject: Dematerialization of the train metaphor into virtual experience
1999-019-F4c.synopsis: Quotes a Deutsche Bank economist saying the developing world is trying to "catch the train" just as it is being "dematerialized and turned into a virtual experience."
1999-019-F4c.article_context: Closes the article by extending the train metaphor into full dematerialization, the essay's final and most abstract image.
1999-019-F4c.analytical_significance: Selected because the dematerialized-train image is the article's closing rhetorical escalation, turning a concrete acceleration claim into a literal transcendence-of-matter figure at the very end of the piece.

1999-020-F1.quotation: ''Bubble'' is a pejorative term for an investment whose price rises and rises, and then collapses. It is widely agreed that just such a thing happened to Japanese stock and real estate prices in the late 1980's, and that Japan has yet to recover.
1999-020-F1.primary_subject: Defining "bubble" via the Japanese asset-price precedent
1999-020-F1.synopsis: Defines "bubble" as a pejorative term for a price that rises then collapses, citing Japan's 1980s stock and real estate crash as the clearest agreed-upon example.
1999-020-F1.article_context: Opens the column by defining its key term before applying it to the current Internet-stock debate.
1999-020-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it's a clean, citable definition of "bubble" for cross-referencing against every other bubble-definition fragment in the corpus.

1999-020-F2.quotation:
Bubble talk is back.

From Davos, where Microsoft's Bill Gates was expressing bewilderment as to why people would pay so much for Internet stocks, to Washington, where Alan Greenspan, the Federal Reserve chairman, questioned overall stock prices but said some Internet companies might be good investments even at current prices, people are talking about investment bubbles that might burst.
1999-020-F2.primary_subject: Gates and Greenspan both questioning Internet stock prices
1999-020-F2.synopsis: Notes that both Bill Gates and Fed chairman Alan Greenspan were publicly questioning Internet stock valuations at the same moment.
1999-020-F2.article_context: Establishes that bubble skepticism was coming from top insiders, not just outside critics, before the column complicates that skepticism.
1999-020-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because it shows bubble skepticism being voiced by the very figures (Gates, Greenspan) most invested in the technology's or economy's success — undercutting any reading of bubble-talk as merely outsider pessimism.

1999-020-F3a.quotation: That argument, however, does not give sufficient weight to the role of psychology in investing. ''There is nothing,'' Mr. Kindleberger has written, ''so disturbing to one's well-being and judgment as to see a friend get rich.'' In any period of speculative excess, those who urge caution are discredited well before the bubble bursts. Many thought Yahoo, the Internet company, was overpriced a year ago. Now it is about 10 times as high as it was then.
1999-020-F3a.primary_subject: Envy and discredited caution as bubble psychology
1999-020-F3a.synopsis: Argues that envy of others getting rich, plus the discrediting of cautious voices, drives speculative excess, citing Yahoo's tenfold rise despite being called overpriced a year earlier.
1999-020-F3a.article_context: Follows the dismissal of the rational-markets counterargument, pivoting the column toward its own psychological explanation of bubbles.
1999-020-F3a.analytical_significance: Selected because it names the specific psychological mechanism (envy, discrediting of skeptics) the column uses to explain bubble persistence, distinct from the historical anecdotes that follow it.

1999-020-F3b.quotation: In 1720 Sir Isaac Newton, a very smart person, invested in the South Sea Company, whose dreams of profiting from exploration made it into a classic bubble. Realizing prices had gone crazy, he sold at a profit, explaining, ''I can calculate the motions of heavenly bodies, but not the madness of people.'' But prices kept rising, and Newton bought again, at the top. He suffered huge losses.
1999-020-F3b.primary_subject: Newton's losses in the South Sea Company bubble
1999-020-F3b.synopsis: Recounts Isaac Newton selling South Sea Company stock at a profit, then buying back in at the top and suffering huge losses, quoting his line about calculating heavenly motions but not human madness.
1999-020-F3b.article_context: Introduces the 1720 South Sea Company as a historical analogy immediately after the psychology argument, before the article turns to contemporary economists' views.
1999-020-F3b.analytical_significance: Selected because the Newton anecdote is the corpus's clearest deep-historical (pre-1929) analogy for dot-com speculation, worth cross-referencing against the more common RCA/1929 comparison used elsewhere in the corpus.

1999-020-F3c.quotation: Peter L. Bernstein, an economic historian and consultant to money managers, is one who thinks that the Internet stocks are in a bubble, but that while the stock market as a whole is overvalued it is well short of one. What's the difference? ''A bubble is totally out of touch with reality, where the greater-fool theory is the dominant driving force, where you are totally confident that somebody will be willing to pay higher prices no matter what you pay,'' he said.
1999-020-F3c.primary_subject: Bernstein's definition of a true bubble
1999-020-F3c.synopsis: Quotes economic historian Peter Bernstein distinguishing a genuine bubble, driven entirely by the "greater-fool theory," from an overvalued but not-yet-bubble market.
1999-020-F3c.article_context: Follows the Newton anecdote by returning to present-day expert testimony, supplying the analytic definition the rest of the column tests against.
1999-020-F3c.analytical_significance: Selected because Bernstein's definition supplies the article's operative criterion for what counts as a bubble, functioning as the piece's analytic anchor rather than another illustrative anecdote.

1999-023-F1.quotation: On the other hand, many of these same experts speculate that in a matter of years there may be other products offering access to the Internet for consumers. It may soon be possible to pick up a telephone, turn on a television or flip on a hand-held device to get on the Internet, without using Windows at all. But that is not the real world yet. Right now, the Justice Department is right to demand that Microsoft not use its current monopoly to restrict consumer choices.
1999-023-F1.primary_subject: Future alternatives to Windows don't excuse present monopoly conduct
1999-023-F1.synopsis: Concedes that future non-Windows ways to access the Internet may emerge, but argues that doesn't excuse Microsoft's present-day monopoly restrictions.
1999-023-F1.article_context: Closes the editorial's argument by acknowledging the "market will fix itself" counterargument before rejecting it as premature.
1999-023-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it's an explicit instance of the codebook's own rule that arguing FOR regulation is the myth inverted, not carried — the editorial names a possible future of dispersed competition specifically to argue current regulation is still necessary.

1999-023-F2.quotation: The original focus of the Microsoft trial was on whether the company illegally combined its own Internet Explorer browser with its basic Windows software in order to muscle aside the rival browser made by Netscape. It has expanded into a larger Government argument that Microsoft engaged in predatory conduct with rivals. Microsoft argues that it is not a monopoly because of the fiercely competitive and fast-changing environment in computers. Yesterday Microsoft repeated its line that special deals with Intuit and other companies are no different from various exclusive licensing arrangements throughout the industry.
1999-023-F2.primary_subject: The Microsoft antitrust trial's browser-bundling allegations
1999-023-F2.synopsis: Summarizes the trial's core allegation — that Microsoft illegally bundled Internet Explorer with Windows to undercut Netscape — and Microsoft's defense that its deals with Intuit are industry-standard.
1999-023-F2.article_context: Provides the factual and legal background the editorial's argument rests on.
1999-023-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because it names the browser-bundling mechanism precisely, giving concrete grounding to what "monopoly power" meant in this specific 1999 antitrust dispute.

1999-027-F1.quotation: This would force Web site operators either to put up age verification barriers or delete potentially sensitive materials from Web pages in an effort to avoid possible prosecution. It could also deter adult Internet users from obtaining access to all kinds of non-pornographic material because they may not want to lose their anonymity by entering an identification or credit card number into the computer.
1999-027-F1.primary_subject: Chilling effects of age-verification requirements on legitimate speech
1999-027-F1.synopsis: Argues that a proposed age-verification requirement would deter adult users from accessing legitimate non-pornographic material for fear of losing anonymity.
1999-027-F1.article_context: States the editorial's central objection to the proposed legislation.
1999-027-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it's a clear early articulation of the anonymity-chilling-effect argument against content-verification laws — a free-speech framing worth tracking against similar arguments in the 2025 AI/deepfake-era corpus.

1999-029-F1.quotation: There, a single Iowa family, headed by Lyle Bowlin, is re-creating Amazon.com in a spare bedroom. I tell you this not because they're an immediate threat to Amazon.com, but to underscore just how easy it is to compete against Amazon.com, and why therefore I'm dubious that Amazon and many other Internet retailers will ever generate the huge profits that their stock prices suggest.
1999-029-F1.primary_subject: Introducing Lyle Bowlin's spare-bedroom Amazon competitor
1999-029-F1.synopsis: Introduces Lyle Bowlin, who recreated Amazon.com's business from his spare bedroom, as proof of how easy it is to compete with the company.
1999-029-F1.article_context: Opens the column's central case study before developing the low-barriers-to-entry argument.
1999-029-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it's the article's thesis in miniature — a single household competing with a billion-dollar company is offered as evidence that corporate hierarchy in e-commerce is dissolving.

1999-029-F2.quotation: When the Internet and Amazon.com came along, said Mr. Bowlin, ''I realized that in my spare time I could create a virtual independent bookstore.''
1999-029-F2.primary_subject: Bowlin's realization that the Internet enabled a one-person bookstore
1999-029-F2.synopsis: Quotes Bowlin describing his realization that the Internet let him build an independent virtual bookstore in his spare time.
1999-029-F2.article_context: Continues the Bowlin narrative with his own account of the idea's origin.
1999-029-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because it's Bowlin's own words framing the Internet as a hierarchy-flattening enabler, in his own voice rather than Friedman's narration.

1999-029-F3.quotation: So first he set up a commercial Web site -- www.positively-you.com. Then he contacted the very same book wholesalers that Amazon.com uses and discovered something interesting -- that to get virtually the same volume discounts that Amazon.com gets, all he needed to do was order five copies of any particular book.
1999-029-F3.primary_subject: Bowlin accessing the same wholesale discounts as Amazon
1999-029-F3.synopsis: Describes how Bowlin discovered he could access nearly the same wholesale book discounts as Amazon by ordering just five copies at a time.
1999-029-F3.article_context: Provides the specific mechanism that makes Bowlin's low-barrier competition possible.
1999-029-F3.analytical_significance: Selected because it's the article's key factual claim — that the scale advantages assumed to protect Amazon's margins are smaller than they appear — the actual evidentiary basis for the hierarchy-flattening argument, not just anecdote.

1999-029-F4.quotation:
He pays an Internet service provider, ACES, $30 a month to house his very colorful Web site, and $30 a month to Americart to enable people to charge books on their credit cards over a secure server line. He pays his bank $50 a month to manage the credit card transactions, and has $40 a month printing costs, largely for his own monthly book newsletter.

''I have no employees,'' says Mr. Bowlin. ''My daughter does the accounting, I maintain the Web site and my wife does the shipping. Altogether, I only need to generate $150 a month in profits to cover all my expenses, and the rest is cream.''
1999-029-F4.primary_subject: The full cost breakdown of Bowlin's one-family operation
1999-029-F4.synopsis: Itemizes Bowlin's monthly costs (hosting, payment processing, banking, printing) and notes his business runs entirely on unpaid family labor.
1999-029-F4.article_context: Grounds the article's argument in exact dollar figures, making the low-barrier claim concrete rather than impressionistic.
1999-029-F4.analytical_significance: Selected because the specific dollar figures ($30, $30, $50, $40) are doing the rhetorical work of the whole argument — precision itself functions as proof that scale matters less than assumed.

1999-029-F5.quotation: Mr. Bowlin just spread the word among his neighbors, colleagues and friends that not only could he offer them everything Amazon.com did, but he could do it cheaper and make a profit from day one. He now has customers from 23 states and Canada. It is funny to go to his Web site and see it offering ''Millions Of Books At Great Prices,'' knowing that it is all being done out of his spare bedroom -- as a hobby!
1999-029-F5.synopsis: Notes Bowlin has customers in 23 states and Canada despite marketing only by word of mouth, run entirely as a hobby.
1999-029-F5.article_context: Extends the case study by showing the business's real geographic reach, not just its low cost.
1999-029-F5.analytical_significance: Selected because geographic reach without paid marketing is offered as further proof that the Internet, not capital or scale, is doing the work of market access — reinforcing the hierarchy-flattening claim.

1999-029-F6.quotation: So the next time your broker tells you that this or that Internet retailing stock is actually worth some crazy multiples, just think for a moment about how many Lyle Bowlins there already are out there, and how many more there will be, to eat away at the profit margins of whatever Internet retailer you can imagine. It only costs them $150 a month and they can do it as a hobby!
1999-029-F6.primary_subject: Generalizing Bowlin into a warning about Internet stock valuations
1999-029-F6.synopsis: Warns investors to remember how many "Lyle Bowlins" exist when evaluating whether high Internet retail stock valuations are justified.
1999-029-F6.article_context: Pivots from the single case study to its intended investment-advice conclusion.
1999-029-F6.analytical_significance: Selected because this is where the anecdote is explicitly converted into investment advice — the clearest statement of the article's practical thesis, not just its narrative color.

1999-029-F7.quotation: Or think about it like this: For about the cost of one share of Amazon.com, you can be Amazon.com.
1999-029-F7.synopsis: Closes with a one-line formulation: a single share of Amazon.com costs roughly as much as building a competing business.
1999-029-F7.article_context: Delivers the column's memorable closing line, condensing the whole argument into one sentence.
1999-029-F7.analytical_significance: Selected because it's the article's most quotable line and the tightest possible formulation of the "anyone can be Amazon" hierarchy-flattening claim — a strong biography-voice candidate.

1999-029-F8.quotation: Testifying before Congress Tuesday, Alan Greenspan wouldn't exactly come out and say that there was a little irrational exuberance behind some of the Internet stocks, but he said these share prices had reached levels that gave him ''concerns.''
1999-029-F8.primary_subject: Greenspan's cautious congressional testimony on Internet stocks
1999-029-F8.synopsis: Reports that Greenspan stopped short of calling Internet stocks irrationally exuberant but admitted their prices gave him "concerns."
1999-029-F8.article_context: Closes the column with a brief coda connecting the Bowlin case to top-level regulatory caution about the same stocks.
1999-029-F8.analytical_significance: Selected because it pairs Friedman's grassroots evidence (Bowlin) with elite institutional caution (Greenspan) arriving at the same skeptical conclusion via entirely different routes.

1999-032-F1.quotation: ''There has never been a commercial technology like this in the history of the world, whereby from the minute you adopt it, it forces you to think and act globally,'' argues Robert Hormats of Goldman, Sachs.
1999-032-F1.primary_subject: Hormats on the Internet's unprecedented global reach
1999-032-F1.synopsis: Quotes Goldman Sachs's Robert Hormats calling the Internet a commercial technology with no historical precedent, since it forces global thinking from day one of adoption.
1999-032-F1.article_context: Provides expert testimony for the column's claim that the Internet is historically unprecedented.
1999-032-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it's a banker, not a technologist, making the unprecedented-technology claim — evidence the framing had spread beyond Silicon Valley boosterism into mainstream finance.

1999-032-F2.quotation:
Mr. Bowlin's experience underscores another point: If you think globalization is overrated, you're also wrong. You ain't seen nothin' yet. As Lyle Bowlin can tell you, the minute you start to do business on the Web, you now have to think globally. You have to think about your customers as global, your competitors as global, your readers as global, your suppliers as global and your partners as global.

''There has never been a commercial technology like this in the history of the world, whereby from the minute you adopt it, it forces you to think and act globally,'' argues Robert Hormats of Goldman, Sachs.
“Another group was small-business people around the world -- particularly craft makers -- who were interested in competing against the big boys from their spare bedrooms at home, just like Mr. Bowlin, and wanted to know how to get started.
1999-032-F2.primary_subject: Bowlin's experience as proof globalization reaches everyone
1999-032-F2.synopsis: Argues that Bowlin's experience shows even a spare-bedroom business must now think about customers, competitors, and suppliers as global.
1999-032-F2.article_context: Extends the Bowlin case study into a broader claim about globalization reaching small businesses.
1999-032-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because it generalizes the Bowlin anecdote from a single quirky example into a claim about globalization's reach into ordinary small businesses and craft makers.

1999-032-F3a.quotation: I recently wrote a column about Lyle Bowlin, who, for about $150 a month, had managed to put together a Web site that could compete with Amazon.com for selling books. Mr. Bowlin was underselling Ama zon.com (and making a profit!) while running the whole operation out of a spare bedroom in his home in Cedar Falls, Iowa. Well, the column elicited the usual range of skeptical responses from experts, who argued that Mr. Bowlin's operation was just a fluke, or that he wasn't calculating his costs properly, or that Amazon.com would soon crush him and all other would-be little-guy competitors.
1999-032-F3a.primary_subject: Skeptical experts dismissing Bowlin's small operation
1999-032-F3a.synopsis: Recaps a prior column about Lyle Bowlin's low-cost, profitable Amazon-competing bookselling site and the skeptical experts who called it a fluke doomed to be crushed by Amazon.
1999-032-F3a.article_context: Opens the follow-up column by restating the original claim and the skepticism it drew, setting up the rebuttal that follows.
1999-032-F3a.analytical_significance: Selected because it stages the skeptical counter-position Friedman is about to refute with reader-response evidence, establishing the argumentative stakes before the data arrives.

1999-032-F3b.quotation: Well, to all of you I say: YOU'RE WRONG.
1999-032-F3b.synopsis: Declares the skeptical experts wrong in a single blunt sentence: "YOU'RE WRONG."
1999-032-F3b.article_context: Functions as the column's rhetorical pivot, a one-line turn from recapping skepticism to asserting the counter-claim.
1999-032-F3b.analytical_significance: Selected because this single declarative sentence is the article's argumentative hinge, marking the shift from setup to counter-evidence in the most compressed form possible.

1999-032-F3c.quotation: You think the Internet is overrated. It's underrated. Here's the E-mail I got from Mr. Bowlin two days after the column ran, both in The Times and on line on www.nytimes.com:
1999-032-F3c.synopsis: Asserts that the Internet is underrated rather than overrated, introducing Bowlin's email as forthcoming proof.
1999-032-F3c.article_context: Bridges the rebuttal to the evidence, previewing the reader-response data about to be quoted.
1999-032-F3c.analytical_significance: Selected because it states the column's thesis in its most compact form before the data supporting it is introduced, making explicit the claim the hit-count evidence is meant to prove.

1999-032-F3d.quotation:
''Dear Tom, I thought I would just fill you in on the impact the column has had. We had over 142,000 hits between 11 P.M. Thursday night [when the column first appeared on the Web] and 2 P.M. Friday afternoon from 40 different countries, before the software that tracks hits gave up and crashed. I have personally responded to over 1,400 E-mails.''
“''There is a whole group of people out there,'' says Mr. Bowlin, ''who like the idea of the 'little guy' competing against Amazon.com. People see Amazon.com as this big impersonal thing. Whereas they like the idea of dealing with a person they know actually exists. Even though their contact with me is over the Web, and it is through E-mail, they know when they contact me the answer is coming from a real person, with a real name. I'm a real person, not a virtual person. If someone sends me an order and forgets something or makes a mistake, I will send them a message and say, 'Didn't you mean this?' ''”
“Another group was small-business people around the world -- particularly craft makers -- who were interested in competing against the big boys from their spare bedrooms at home, just like Mr. Bowlin, and wanted to know how to get started.
1999-032-F3d.primary_subject: Reader response and personal-touch preference over Amazon
1999-032-F3d.synopsis: Quotes Bowlin's email reporting 142,000 hits and 1,400 personal email replies, and readers explaining they prefer buying from a "real person" over the impersonal "big" Amazon.com.
1999-032-F3d.article_context: Supplies the concrete evidentiary payload of the column, delivered right after the thesis statement and before Friedman's own interpretive gloss about the "backyard barbecue."
1999-032-F3d.analytical_significance: Selected because this is the article's actual evidence for hierarchy flattening — a viral personal response undercutting a corporate giant — making it the passage that most directly carries the Death of hierarchy claim.

1999-034-F1.quotation:
E*bucks.com

The Internet spin-off of Starbucks. Web buyers can order any size, flavor, caffeinated or decaffeinated, fatte or nonfatte, latte, cappuccino, mochaccino or frappaccino and have it delivered anywhere in the world next day. The company promises ''that same burned, bitterly strong addictive flavor that has put a Starbucks on every block.'' E*bucks.com is a partnership with Fedex, developer of the patented Foamvelope for all E-ccino product deliveries. Javascript only.
1999-034-F1.primary_subject: E*bucks.com — a fictional Starbucks Internet spin-off
1999-034-F1.synopsis: Parodies a Starbucks Internet spin-off delivering coffee drinks worldwide via a fictional "Foamvelope" partnership with FedEx.
1999-034-F1.article_context: Opens the satirical list of fake dot-com pitches.
1999-034-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it's the opening joke establishing the essay's premise — that appending ".com" to literally any absurd idea reads as a viable pitch in 1999.

1999-034-F2.quotation:
felloffatruck.com

The most popular seller of pirated editions on the Web, felloffatruck.com offers a wide array of popular books at unbelievably low prices that can be obtained only through the company's strict avoidance of paying royalties to writers. A complete set of the works of Barbara Taylor Bradford (with the author's forged signature in every volume) goes for $2.17. The company also sells bootleg copies of top 10 CD's and videos at equally unbeatable prices. For example, Hootie (unfortunately without the Blowfish) costs 38 cents a disk, while the tape of ''Armaggedon'' (with neither the ending nor Bruce Willis's performance) goes for $1.02.
1999-034-F2.synopsis: Parodies a site selling pirated books and bootleg CDs/videos at absurdly low prices, made possible by not paying royalties.
1999-034-F2.article_context: Continues the satirical list with a joke about piracy and copyright disregard.
1999-034-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because the joke specifically targets royalty avoidance — an early satirical anticipation of the piracy and copyright anxieties that would dominate the following decade.

1999-034-F3.quotation:
e.floss.net

The only on-line dental hygiene site. Pentium V required. High-intensity kilobyte-impression frequencies are E-mailed 14 million times per second. The user sits as close to the screen as possible, mouth wide open, and is virtually flossed in as little as one hour, depending on modem speed. Tartar ctrl.
1999-034-F3.primary_subject: e.floss.net — a fictional online dental hygiene site
1999-034-F3.synopsis: Parodies an "online dental hygiene" site that virtually flosses users' teeth via high-intensity data transmission.
1999-034-F3.article_context: Continues the satirical list with a joke about applying Internet framing to physically impossible services.
1999-034-F3.analytical_significance: Selected because it's the clearest example of the essay's core joke mechanic — taking "virtual" service framing completely literally, to absurd effect.

1999-034-F4.quotation:
sherp@.com

Man, you're gonna carry that weight! The first Internet, global positioned courier/moving system. Web users are outfitted with a digital paging system (optionally implanted). Whenever and wherever you are, a sherpa will be dispatched to schlep all grocery bags, luggage, packages, parcels, even garbage to its destination. Every sherp@.com sherpa is surgically calibrated with G.P.S. chip and digital g-force/baropedometer. User accounts are updated every 10 feet and/ or 10 seconds. Golf caddying, children's backpacks, watercooler replacement, large appetizer platters, weekend newspaper editions, anything inconveniently weighty can be billed. No tipping.
1999-034-F4.primary_subject: sherp@.com — a fictional GPS-dispatched human courier service
1999-034-F4.synopsis: Parodies a service dispatching human "sherpas" via GPS to carry any burdensome item on demand.
1999-034-F4.article_context: Continues the satirical list, mocking gig-style on-demand labor platforms before they existed.
1999-034-F4.analytical_significance: Selected because it anticipates on-demand gig-economy labor platforms roughly a decade before they existed commercially, played entirely for laughs rather than as a genuine prediction.

1999-034-F5.quotation:
@hh!closure.com

Nothing is worthless in today's cyberworld of possibilities. Whether it's an old blue sock, a weathered left glove or a salt shaker without a top, @hh!closure.com will search the on-line world for the right potential mate. If you have a periscope, we'll help you find the submarine that happens to be missing one. @hh!closure.com is the only, and lonely, Internet merchandise value reclaiming service.
1999-034-F5.synopsis: Parodies a matching service for finding the "mate" to any random broken or single household object.
1999-034-F5.article_context: Continues the satirical list with a joke about the Internet's promise to make anything findable, however trivial.
1999-034-F5.analytical_significance: Selected because it takes the "Internet finds anything" promise to its most trivial possible extreme, satirizing the scale of ambition attached to mundane problems.

1999-034-F6.quotation:
Ovitz.com

Unlimited transactional representation by the world's superest agent. A team of 8,000 highly trained Portland-based support technicians field all potential sales/purchase orders and refer them by category/pricepoint to specialists around the world to ''cut the best deal.'' Buying a canary or selling a chipped Derbyshire tureen, fixing the eaves or hiring an illegally immigrated cleaning woman, Ovitz.com will put your interests ahead of theirs, for 10 percent of the closing price with an irrevocable option on all future trades, and a fixed percentage of incremental material gains in perpetuity.
1999-034-F6.primary_subject: Ovitz.com — a fictional universal negotiating-agent service
1999-034-F6.synopsis: Parodies a service offering Hollywood-agent-style negotiation for literally any transaction, at a steep permanent commission.
1999-034-F6.article_context: Continues the satirical list, mocking the era's fee-heavy intermediary business models.
1999-034-F6.analytical_significance: Selected because the joke specifically targets intermediary fee structures — a satirical jab at how many dot-com business models were really about extracting a cut, not creating value.

1999-034-F7.quotation:
toomanyboxes.com

Has today's cyberworld of home shopping created too much garbage for you? At toomanyboxes.com, we work with U.P.S., Fedex and the Postal Service to track precisely how many packages your home is receiving. Biweekly, or daily if necessary, toomanyboxes.com will send you a really big box, big enough to handle all the bubble wrap, corrugated cardboard and plastic foam chippies you've accumulated from on-line shopping. When you're ready, just E-mail us and we'll send over a licensed technician to burn everything on your lawn. Don't have a lawn? Don't worry! The staff at toomanyboxes.com can contain a fire indoors. Prefer recycling? No problem! Toomanyboxes.com will take all of your packing material away and burn it in a field somewhere else, or ship it to Virginia. All for the same price! Don't let the convenient life style of cybershopping force you out of your home. ''C'mon! Clean house!''
1999-034-F7.primary_subject: toomanyboxes.com — a fictional shipping-waste disposal service
1999-034-F7.synopsis: Parodies a service that collects and burns the cardboard and packaging waste generated by online shopping.
1999-034-F7.article_context: Closes the satirical list with a joke connecting online shopping's convenience to its environmental cost.
1999-034-F7.analytical_significance: Selected because it's the only entry in the list that gestures at a real externality (packaging waste) rather than pure absurdity, closing the satire on a faintly serious note.

1999-035-F1a.quotation: Take a walk through the residence halls of any college in the country and you'll find students seated at their desks, eyes transfixed on their computer monitors. What are they doing with their top-of-the-line PC's and high-speed T-1 Internet connections?
1999-035-F1a.primary_subject: Dorm students transfixed by computer monitors
1999-035-F1a.synopsis: Describes students in dorm rooms seated at desks, eyes fixed on their computer monitors, and rhetorically asks what they are actually doing with their high-speed connections.
1999-035-F1a.article_context: Opens the essay's central observational section immediately after the introductory claim questioning the wisdom of campus computer mandates.
1999-035-F1a.analytical_significance: Selected because it is the essay's opening image and rhetorical question, framing the entire inventory of distraction that follows as an answer to it.

1999-035-F1b.quotation: They are playing Tomb Raider instead of going to chemistry class, tweaking the configurations of their machines instead of writing the paper due tomorrow, collecting mostly useless information from the WorldWide Web instead of doing a math problem set -- a host of other activity that has little or nothing to do with traditional academic work.
1999-035-F1b.synopsis: Lists specific academic tasks (chemistry class, a paper, a math problem set) being displaced by playing Tomb Raider, tweaking machine settings, and browsing the Web.
1999-035-F1b.article_context: Follows the opening image with the essay's most itemized, side-by-side contrast between specific schoolwork and specific non-academic computer use.
1999-035-F1b.analytical_significance: Selected because its explicit one-to-one substitutions (game instead of class, browsing instead of problem set) make the displacement claim concrete rather than impressionistic.

1999-035-F1c.quotation: I have friends who have spent whole weekends doing nothing but playing Quake or Warcraft or other interactive computer games. One friend sometimes spends entire evenings -- six to eight hours -- scouring the Web for images and modifying them just to have a new background on his computer desktop.
1999-035-F1c.synopsis: Describes friends spending whole weekends playing Quake or Warcraft, and one friend spending six to eight hours scouring the Web just to find a new desktop background image.
1999-035-F1c.article_context: Extends the inventory of distraction with more extreme personal examples (whole weekends, six-to-eight-hour sessions) than the general claim just made.
1999-035-F1c.analytical_significance: Selected because the extremity of the specific hours cited (whole weekends, six to eight hours for a background image) escalates the essay's evidence beyond the general claim into anecdote-level detail.

1999-035-F1d.quotation: And many others I know have amassed overwhelming collections of music on their computers. It's the searching and finding that they seem to enjoy: some of them have more music files on their computers than they could play in months.
1999-035-F1d.primary_subject: Music file hoarding as its own activity
1999-035-F1d.synopsis: Notes that other students have amassed more music files on their computers than they could listen to in months, suggesting the searching and collecting itself is the appeal.
1999-035-F1d.article_context: Adds a third category of non-academic use (music hoarding) to the gaming and browsing examples already given.
1999-035-F1d.analytical_significance: Selected because it identifies collecting/searching itself, rather than consumption, as the activity's appeal — a distinct psychological observation from the gaming examples surrounding it.

1999-035-F1e.quotation: Several people who live in my hall routinely stay awake all night chatting with dormmates on line. Why walk 10 feet down the hall to have a conversation when you can chat on the computer -- even if it takes three times as long?
1999-035-F1e.synopsis: Describes dormmates staying awake all night chatting online with people down the hall, asking why anyone would type instead of walking ten feet to talk in person.
1999-035-F1e.article_context: Adds the essay's fourth specific example (online chat) to the list of non-academic dorm computer uses, emphasizing its inefficiency compared to in-person contact.
1999-035-F1e.analytical_significance: Selected because it is the essay's clearest example of technology substituting for, rather than enabling, human contact, foreshadowing later corpus material on digital displacement of face-to-face interaction.

1999-035-F1f.quotation: You might expect that personal computers in dorm rooms would be used for nonacademic purposes, but the problem is not confined to residence halls. The other day I walked into the library's reference department, and five or six students were grouped around a computer -- not conducting research, but playing Tetris. Every time I walk past the library's so-called research computers, it seems that at least half are being used to play games, chat or surf the Internet aimlessly.
1999-035-F1f.primary_subject: Distraction extending beyond dorms into the library
1999-035-F1f.synopsis: Reports that library reference-department computers are also used for Tetris rather than research, with roughly half of "research computers" observed being used for games, chat, or aimless surfing.
1999-035-F1f.article_context: Widens the essay's claim beyond dorm rooms to the library, generalizing the distraction problem to the whole campus before the essay's concluding argument.
1999-035-F1f.analytical_significance: Selected because extending the observation to library "research computers" specifically undercuts the premise that campus computing serves academic work, strengthening the essay's closing argument.

1999-035-F1g.quotation: Colleges and universities should be wary of placing such an emphasis on the use of computers and the Internet. The Web may be useful for finding simple facts, but serious research still means a trip to the library.
1999-035-F1g.primary_subject: Warning against overreliance on computers for research
1999-035-F1g.synopsis: Argues colleges should be wary of emphasizing computers and the Internet, since the Web is useful only for simple facts while serious research still requires the library.
1999-035-F1g.article_context: States the essay's normative conclusion, following directly from the library anecdote and preceding the closing argument about students' natural tendency to procrastinate.
1999-035-F1g.analytical_significance: Selected because it is the essay's explicit policy recommendation, converting the preceding anecdotal evidence into a direct argument against tech-heavy campus mandates.

1999-035-F2.quotation:
For most students, having a computer in the dorm is more of a distraction than a learning tool. Other than computer science or mathematics majors, few students need more than a word processing program and access to E-mail in their rooms.

It is true, of course, that students have always procrastinated and wasted time. But when students spend four, five, even ten hours a day on computers and the Internet, a more troubling picture emerges -- a picture all the more disturbing because colleges themselves have helped create the problem.
1999-035-F2.primary_subject: Computers as distraction rather than learning tool
1999-035-F2.synopsis: Argues that most students need little more than word processing and email, and that dorm computers mainly enable more elaborate procrastination.
1999-035-F2.article_context: Closes the essay by generalizing the opening observations into its explicit thesis statement.
1999-035-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because it's the essay's explicit thesis sentence — useful for any argument about early skepticism toward educational-technology claims, offered here by a student rather than an administrator or critic.

1999-037-F1.quotation: Here's the sad part. He might be right. Just check out the chat boards these days. They're filled with people who are day trading and speculating and trying to pump up stocks for a quick and easy gain. And to me, they suggest what is truly significant about Dow 10,000. It is not merely that this is the latest, greatest milestone in this astonishing bull market. It is that, unlike 1987 when the Dow Jones average hit 2,000, or even 1995, when it breached the 5,000 barrier, the stock market in 1999 has become a different kind of place, populated by a different kind of investor.
1999-037-F1.primary_subject: Chat-board day traders as a new kind of investor
1999-037-F1.synopsis: Observes that online chat boards are full of day traders speculating and pumping stocks, arguing this makes 1999's market fundamentally different from earlier Dow milestones.
1999-037-F1.article_context: Opens the column's central claim by pointing to online trading culture as the source of a qualitative market shift.
1999-037-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it locates the "new era" claim specifically in investor behavior (chat-board day trading) rather than in the technology itself — a claim about culture, not just infrastructure.

1999-037-F2.quotation:
It is that, unlike 1987 when the Dow Jones average hit 2,000, or even 1995, when it breached the 5,000 barrier, the stock market in 1999 has become a different kind of place, populated by a different kind of investor.

At the heart of this change is the Internet.
1999-037-F2.primary_subject: The Internet as the cause of a "different kind of" stock market
1999-037-F2.synopsis: States directly that the Internet is at the heart of what makes the 1999 stock market a fundamentally different kind of place.
1999-037-F2.article_context: States the column's core "new era" thesis explicitly, in the passage coded as carrying the myth.
1999-037-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because the demonic register here — the "new era" framed as troubling rather than exciting — distinguishes it from most other New Era claims in the 1999 corpus, worth cross-referencing against the more celebratory versions elsewhere.

1999-037-F3.quotation: Without question, the new medium has ''empowered'' investors -- offering them tools that have put them on a more equal footing with the smart money boys on Wall Street. The proliferation of cheap on-line trading has made it easy for investors to make their own instantaneous buy-and-sell decisions, instead of having to rely on brokers. And on, and on.
1999-037-F3.synopsis: Argues that cheap online trading has put ordinary investors on a more equal footing with Wall Street professionals.
1999-037-F3.article_context: Closes the column by naming the specific mechanism (cheap online trading) behind the democratization claim, in a slightly weary, "and on, and on" tone.
1999-037-F3.analytical_significance: Selected because the closing "and on, and on" tag signals Nocera's own skepticism toward the empowerment claim even as he reports it — a paired register achieved through tone rather than explicit argument.

1999-047-F1.quotation: In offering to settle, Microsoft has put forth a document suggesting that it would consider changes in its restrictive contracts with Internet companies and computer makers, including possible limits on its ability to customize the opening screen of Windows. But before accepting such promises, the Justice Department would have to be satisfied that Microsoft had truly changed its ways. The best mechanism to guarantee this might be an agreement on new rules for pricing and other incentives to insure freedom of choice by the company's rivals and consumers. If a set of adequate ground rules cannot be agreed upon, the company may find itself faced with demands for an outright breakup.
1999-047-F1.synopsis: Argues the Justice Department must verify Microsoft has genuinely changed before accepting its settlement promises, or risk having to pursue a breakup.
1999-047-F1.article_context: States the editorial's central conditional argument about the proposed settlement.
1999-047-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it names a specific remedy (breakup) as the fallback if a negotiated settlement fails — a concrete stake for what "settling" the case would mean.

1999-047-F2.quotation: Any resolution of the antitrust suit, whether negotiated or ordered by the courts, would have to remedy the problems defined cogently by the Justice Department. Microsoft has been clearly shown to exercise monopoly power in operating-systems software for personal computers in ways that coerce competitors and clients, depriving consumers of choices. The initial focus of the suit was the contention that Microsoft, by tying its operating system to its Internet Explorer browser, was muscling aside the rival browser made by Netscape. During the trial, the prosecution expanded its attack to include charges of strong-arm tactics against computer makers, software rivals and others.
1999-047-F2.synopsis: Summarizes the Justice Department's core finding — that Microsoft used its Windows monopoly to disadvantage Netscape and other rivals — as the baseline any settlement must address.
1999-047-F2.article_context: Provides the legal and factual grounding beneath the editorial's settlement argument.
1999-047-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because it states the trial's core factual finding in one compact sentence — useful as a baseline reference for the whole Microsoft antitrust subplot in the corpus.

1999-047-F3.quotation: After a decidedly uneven presentation of its case in court, Microsoft has come forward with a proposal to settle the antitrust suit it has been challenging since last year. The word from the Justice Department and some of the 19 state attorneys general prosecuting the case is that Microsoft's initial offer does not address their concerns about what they regard as anticompetitive conduct by the company. But the department and the attorneys general are right to pursue a possible settlement with Microsoft. A negotiated agreement, if done right, would be preferable to years of litigation, appeals and uncertainty for businesses and consumers in the fast-changing computer and software industry.
1999-047-F3.primary_subject: Endorsing continued settlement negotiation over prolonged litigation
1999-047-F3.synopsis: Argues a negotiated settlement, if done right, would be preferable for businesses and consumers than years of continued litigation.
1999-047-F3.article_context: Closes the editorial by endorsing the settlement process itself, while insisting on real substance.
1999-047-F3.analytical_significance: Selected because it shows the editorial board favoring negotiated regulation over adversarial litigation — a specific institutional preference worth tracking across the corpus's other antitrust pieces.

1999-050-F1.quotation: An important factor in this merger wave is the popularity of Internet stocks, which have risen to extraordinarily high prices. That has made it difficult for established companies to afford to buy Internet firms, but it has made it easy for Internet companies that have high-priced stock to expand by buying other companies for stock. Both Yahoo and Amazon.com have done deals to expand their Internet offerings, while America Online, a company now valued by the market at about the same amount as I.B.M., took over Netscape.
1999-050-F1.primary_subject: High Internet stock prices fueling stock-based acquisitions
1999-050-F1.synopsis: Explains that high-priced Internet stocks let companies like Yahoo, Amazon, and AOL acquire others using stock rather than cash.
1999-050-F1.article_context: Opens the editorial by explaining the financial mechanism driving the merger wave.
1999-050-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it explains the mechanical financial cause of the merger wave (inflated stock as acquisition currency) rather than treating consolidation as simply inevitable.

1999-050-F2.quotation:
But while antitrust regulators need to keep a close watch, most of these deals reflect a vibrant state of competition, not an effort to end it.

The deals also reflect a state of confusion among the people running the companies involved. They can see that developing technologies are changing the world they will compete in, but they cannot see clearly which technologies will prevail. Some very successful companies fear they could become the 21st century's equivalent of buggy-whip manufacturers.
“Some of the deals may prove to have been brilliant steps that positioned companies as leaders in a technology destined to become dominant.”
“Others no doubt will have been bad for everyone except the investment bankers who pocketed fees for arranging them. The fact that companies are pursuing such deals is a positive one, however, reflecting both the uncertainty and the excitement of the technological progress now being made.
1999-050-F2.primary_subject: Merger wave as confusion and competition, not monopoly
1999-050-F2.synopsis: Argues the merger wave reflects genuine competitive uncertainty — companies fearing technological obsolescence — rather than a coordinated effort to suppress competition.
1999-050-F2.article_context: States the editorial's central judgment, balancing continued antitrust vigilance against a generally positive reading of the merger wave.
1999-050-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because the "buggy-whip manufacturers" image is a vivid, self-deprecating admission of uncertainty from within corporate America itself, not an outside critique.

1999-058-F1.quotation:
But precisely because the Internet is such a neutral, free, open and unregulated technology it means that we are all connected, but no one is in charge. The Internet is democracy, but with no constitution.
“The Internet changes that by giving people unlimited choices and unlimited power to make them.
1999-058-F1.synopsis: Describes the Internet as a democracy with no constitution — universal connection without any governing authority.
1999-058-F1.article_context: States the column's central metaphor before developing its implications for parenting and judgment.
1999-058-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because "democracy with no constitution" is a compact, quotable formulation of both the promise and danger the column goes on to develop.

1999-058-F2a.quotation:
But precisely because the Internet is such a neutral, free, open and unregulated technology it means that we are all connected, but no one is in charge. The Internet is democracy, but with no constitution. It is Orwellian in the way it can connect us all, but with no Big Brother watching over us all. And therefore personal judgment and responsibility are critical when using this technology. The only filter is the one you bring in your own head or your own heart, and since kids often lack the judgment microchip, it is even more critical that parents and educators provide it.
“But the Internet empowers people in ways that were not possible with television or newspapers. With these broadcast-type media there was a producer or an editor making decisions for the audience -- deciding what they should see or hear. That simplified things, and it also deprived the audience of the full range of choices.''
1999-058-F2a.synopsis: Argues that because the Internet is neutral, free, open, and unregulated, everyone is connected but no one is in charge, calling it "democracy, but with no constitution" and comparing it to an Orwellian world with no Big Brother.
1999-058-F2a.article_context: States the column's central structural claim about the Internet's ungoverned nature, positioned after the AOL/N.R.A. comparison and before Friedman turns to Steve Case's response.
1999-058-F2a.analytical_significance: Selected because "democracy, but with no constitution" is the article's clearest carried claim that the Internet dissolves institutional governance, the load-bearing sentence for its End of Politics content.

1999-058-F2b.quotation:
The Internet changes that by giving people unlimited choices and unlimited power to make them.”
“''When they have more choices,'' Mr. Case argued, ''they have more responsibility to show good judgment. We can't unilaterally impose that judgment, and we shouldn't try. But we can try to offer certain tools like technological filters, and educate parents about them and encourage them to take some responsibility here. The same attention that parents should pay to what their kids watch on television, or how they use the telephone, has to be paid with the Internet, only more so, because this is an interactive technology with no editor. Instead of us trying to be the all-powerful censor, we are trying to encourage parents to take control of the dashboard. Technology can be a useful tool, but it can't be a replacement for caring, involved parents.''
1999-058-F2b.primary_subject: Case's account of unlimited choice requiring parental responsibility
1999-058-F2b.synopsis: Quotes AOL CEO Steve Case arguing that the Internet gives people unlimited choices and power, which shifts responsibility for good judgment onto parents rather than a censor or editor.
1999-058-F2b.article_context: Follows the governance-obsolescence claim by introducing Case's own reasoning about why no single actor can or should police the medium.
1999-058-F2b.analytical_significance: Selected because it shows an industry actor (Case) himself affirming the no-editor premise while proposing parental responsibility as the practical substitute, extending rather than repeating the prior sub-fragment's structural claim.

1999-058-F2c.quotation: To put it another way, if we are all connected and no one is in charge in cyberspace, then cultivating citizens in the schoolyard or the backyard becomes that much more important. The more the Internet makes us all broadcasters, all researchers, all consumers and, alas, all potential bomb makers, the more critical it is that our teachers, parents and communities are still making us all citizens.
1999-058-F2c.primary_subject: Civic education as the substitute for institutional control
1999-058-F2c.synopsis: Concludes that because no one is in charge in cyberspace, cultivating good citizens through schools and families becomes more critical as the Internet makes everyone a broadcaster, researcher, and potential bomb maker.
1999-058-F2c.article_context: Closes the column by drawing the practical conclusion from the no-one-in-charge premise, ending on the call for civic and parental education.
1999-058-F2c.analytical_significance: Selected because it is the column's closing move, relocating governance from institutions to civic/family upbringing — the practical resolution of the End of Politics claim rather than a restatement of it.

1999-060-F1.quotation:
The First Amendment, therefore, should shoulder none of the guilt in the Littleton killings. In truth, the First Amendment leaves considerable room for government to exert control, and the advent of the Internet neither broadens nor narrows government's options.”
“Nor, for that matter, is the Fourth Amendment protection against unreasonable searches and seizures among the culprits here. Those who launch murderous plots by posting their deranged plans on a Web site are exposing their schemes in a public space, one that government agencies may freely browse without a warrant despite the fanciful argument that all talk on the World Wide Web is as private as E-mail messages might be.
1999-060-F1.primary_subject: Rejecting the "Internet defeats government oversight" claim
