1999-060-F1.synopsis: Argues that posting plans on a public website doesn't create a Fourth Amendment shield — government agencies can freely browse such public postings, undercutting claims that the Internet makes oversight impossible.
1999-060-F1.article_context: Opens the essay by directly rejecting blame narratives connecting the Internet to the Littleton shooting.
1999-060-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it directly refutes a governance-obsolescence claim in the specific, urgent context of a post-Columbine free-speech panic — a deflated myth with real political stakes attached.

1999-060-F2.quotation:
The point to remember is that basic constitutional principles do not arise and disappear as each new technology comes on the scene.
“Early in the 20th century, the Supreme Court expressed doubt that free-speech principles had any application at all to motion pictures, and in 1981, Justice Byron White introduced his analysis of a law regulating outdoor billboard advertising by saying, ''We deal here with the law of billboards.''”
“Only in recent years has the Court recognized that new technology doesn't affect basic constitutional principles. The Court has found that technological details, however, can be relevant to certain applications of the law, especially because, in principle, speech may not be restricted any more than necessary.”
“For instance, the Supreme Court struck down provisions in 1997 of the Communications Decency Act because they blocked pornographic materials from being transmitted over the Internet, when technology already existed that allowed parents to selectively censor such materials.”
“Even though the Internet allows nearly anyone to obtain or transmit information instantaneously to and from anywhere on the planet, it does not deserve more -- or less -- free-speech protection than older media.”
“A Web page simulating, or even glorifying, violence and hatred is not outside the First Amendment's protection any more than are disgusting board games, magazines or political tracts. The same First Amendment that safeguards the right of Nazis to march through Skokie protects the right of an adult to put virtual machine guns aimed at lifelike human targets on his or her computer screen.”
“At the same time, Internet speech doesn't have more constitutional protection than speech disseminated in a more old-fashioned and limited manner. In particular, direct threats or other messages that by their very utterance cause harm receive no more protection on the Internet than anyplace else. Releasing a computer virus through E-mail deserves no greater immunity than crying ''Fire'' in a crowded theater.
1999-060-F2.synopsis: Argues at length that basic constitutional principles have never changed with new technology — from motion pictures to billboards to the Internet — and shouldn't now.
1999-060-F2.article_context: Delivers the essay's central legal argument, tracing First Amendment precedent from film and billboards to the Internet.
1999-060-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because it's Tribe's core thesis sentence-by-sentence — an explicit, sustained refutation of Internet exceptionalism from a leading constitutional scholar, and the article's single richest passage for the reasoned-refutation pattern in the corpus.

1999-074-F1.quotation: In its start-up year, the e-rate program created by Congress as part of the 1996 Telecommunications Act has helped tens of thousands of rural and low-income communities connect to the Internet. Given the growing needs, Federal Communications Commission chairman William Kennard has properly recommended that the program -- which subsidizes telecommunications services and Internet hook-ups for schools and libraries -- be financed at the maximum authorized level of $2.25 billion for the coming year. The commission is expected to vote on the plan this month.
1999-074-F1.synopsis: Reports that the e-rate program connected tens of thousands of rural and low-income communities to the Internet in its first year, and the FCC recommends full funding going forward.
1999-074-F1.article_context: Opens the editorial with the program's record of success before defending it against proposed cuts.
1999-074-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it establishes the program's concrete track record before the editorial pivots to defending it politically — evidence-first argumentation.

1999-074-F2.quotation: Despite strong support from schools and educators, the e-rate program has been politically vulnerable from the start. It is financed mostly by fees from long-distance phone companies as part of the bargain under the 1996 act. But the industry has complained loudly about the costs ever since. Under heavy pressure from lawmakers, the F.C.C. scaled down the program initially, awarding only $1.7 billion in the first 18 months, even though demand was much higher.
1999-074-F2.primary_subject: Political vulnerability of the e-rate program
1999-074-F2.synopsis: Explains that the e-rate program, funded by fees on long-distance phone companies, has faced industry complaints and was already scaled down once under political pressure.
1999-074-F2.article_context: Establishes the program's history of political vulnerability before the current funding fight.
1999-074-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because it shows the program's funding fight as a recurring pattern, not a one-time event — useful for tracking how infrastructure-access programs get politically contested over time.

1999-074-F3.quotation:
More than 32,000 applications requesting $2.4 billion in subsidies have been submitted for the coming year. But Republicans in Congress are pushing to restructure and reduce the program. Senator Conrad Burns introduced legislation this week that would cut the program to roughly $1.9 billion a year for five years, to be financed by part of the current 3 percent Federal excise tax on phone service instead of the current e-rate fees. The rest of the excise tax would be eliminated. After five years, the aid would be financed through annual appropriations, and would be capped at $500 million a year.

Their proposal would destabilize a program that works, and, worse, cut assistance even as telecommunications become increasingly important in education.
1999-074-F3.primary_subject: A Republican proposal to cut and restructure e-rate funding
1999-074-F3.synopsis: Details Senator Conrad Burns's proposal to cut e-rate funding roughly in half and shift its financing, which the editorial argues would destabilize a working program.
1999-074-F3.article_context: Closes the editorial with the specific legislative threat and the board's judgment against it.
1999-074-F3.analytical_significance: Selected because it names the specific legislator and mechanism behind the funding threat — concrete political detail rather than a general "some in Congress" framing.

1999-082-F1.quotation:
1. The Internet is becoming increasingly pervasive, unavoidable and indispensable."
"You have to make sure your kids are connected, because that is the future and it is important that everyone have access to the future, so we don't widen society's gaps with a digital divide as well. But as you get connected you have to understand this is an empowering medium. It gives you millions of new choices, but many will not be appropriate. So with empowerment must come greater responsibility.''
1999-082-F1.primary_subject: The Internet as pervasive, unavoidable, and indispensable
1999-082-F1.synopsis: States as a numbered premise that the Internet has become pervasive and unavoidable, and that children must be connected to avoid a "digital divide."
1999-082-F1.article_context: Opens the column's numbered-list argument with its foundational claim about inevitability.
1999-082-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it's explicitly numbered as premise "1" of the column's argument — the inevitability claim functions as the article's starting axiom, not its conclusion.

1999-082-F2.quotation: 2. There is a dawning realization that the Internet, as such a tool, is different from radio, television and newspapers in that it is a totally open, interactive technology -- but with no built-in editor, publisher, censor or even filters. With one mouse click you can wander into a Nazi beer hall or a pornographer's library, hack the NASA computers or roam the Sorbonne library, and no one is there to stop or direct you. You interact with the network naked. The only really effective filters are the values, knowledge and judgment that your kid brings to the Web in his or her own head and heart.
1999-082-F2.primary_subject: The Internet's total absence of institutional gatekeepers
1999-082-F2.synopsis: States as numbered premise "2" that the Internet has no built-in editor, censor, or filter, unlike radio, television, or newspapers.
1999-082-F2.article_context: Continues the numbered-list argument, setting up the column's parenting-judgment conclusion.
1999-082-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because "you interact with the network naked" is one of the corpus's most vivid images for the absence of institutional mediation online.

1999-082-F3.quotation:
1. The Internet is becoming increasingly pervasive, unavoidable and indispensable.
2. There is a dawning realization that the Internet, as such a tool, is different from radio, television and newspapers in that it is a totally open, interactive technology -- but with no built-in editor, publisher, censor or even filters. With one mouse click you can wander into a Nazi beer hall or a pornographer's library, hack the NASA computers or roam the Sorbonne library, and no one is there to stop or direct you.
1999-082-F3.synopsis: Restates both numbered premises — pervasiveness and the absence of gatekeepers — together as a single combined passage.
1999-082-F3.article_context: A condensed recap of the same two-part argument, coded separately for its borderlessness implication: unrestricted global reach (a Nazi beer hall, NASA, the Sorbonne, all one click away).
1999-082-F3.analytical_significance: Selected because the same two premises support three different myths depending on which implication is foregrounded (inevitability, democratization, borderlessness) — a clean example of one passage doing multiple mythological jobs at once.

1999-082-F4a.quotation:
Mr. Chambers declared that, though most people did not grasp it yet, the Internet was about to change ''everything'' about how people work, invest, learn, shop and communicate.
“A year and a half later I now appreciate Cisco's ad, and Mr. Chambers's prediction. The year 1999 will go down as the year that the Internet really began to penetrate the consciousness of Americans -- that the way they buy everything from cars to airline tickets, and the way they communicate, invest, work and learn, is being fundamentally transformed by the Web. But it has come on so fast that people are feeling overwhelmed by it. When I travel around America today, one of the most frequent foreign policy questions I get is about cyberspace.”
1999-082-F4a.synopsis: Recalls Cisco CEO John Chambers's earlier prediction that the Internet would change "everything" about how people work, invest, learn, shop and communicate, and declares 1999 the year that prediction visibly came true in American consciousness.
1999-082-F4a.article_context: Opens the column by recounting a personal anecdote (interviewing Chambers, receiving the Cisco ad kit) that sets up the column's central premise before it pivots to the parenting argument.
1999-082-F4a.analytical_significance: Selected because it names a specific, falsifiable 1998 prediction (Chambers's "everything") and marks 1999 as the year it was judged to have come true — a rare moment of explicit prediction-tracking within the corpus itself.

1999-082-F4b.quotation:
"That is, unless parents are building kids with sound fundamentals -- with the individual judgment, values and knowledge skills to handle this technology on their own -- Lord only knows what can happen. It can be like everyone letting his kids drive without a license, map or sense of purpose."
"2. There is a dawning realization that the Internet, as such a tool, is different from radio, television and newspapers in that it is a totally open, interactive technology "
Kindergarten becomes more important than college in the Internet age.
1999-082-F4b.primary_subject: Parental fundamentals as the answer to an unfiltered Internet
1999-082-F4b.synopsis: Argues that because the Internet is a totally open, filterless medium, children need old-fashioned fundamentals and internal judgment more than tech skills, ranking kindergarten-level grounding above college in importance.
1999-082-F4b.article_context: Delivers the column's concluding prescriptive claim, following the enumerated 'dangerous cocktail' of open network plus absent parenting.
1999-082-F4b.analytical_significance: Selected because it shows the New Era claim doing double duty as moral argument — the Internet's unprecedented openness is invoked not to celebrate transcendence but to justify a conservative, values-based parenting prescription, a paired register worth tracking against purely celebratory New Era claims elsewhere in the 1999 corpus.

1999-085-F1.quotation: It happened one day at lunch, when my friend Paul quietly revealed to me that, three years after investing his pension by himself, he had made a million dollars on America Online. A million! Even in the era of $4 cappuccinos (a deliciously frothy coffee drink I've recently discovered), that's a lot of money, not to mention a pretty good return for a dentist investing from home on a Wednesday afternoon.
1999-085-F1.primary_subject: A friend's AOL windfall as the essay's inciting incident
1999-085-F1.synopsis: Recounts learning that a friend turned his pension into a million dollars by investing in America Online.
1999-085-F1.article_context: Opens the personal essay with the anecdote that triggers the author's own reckless investing.
1999-085-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it's the essay's inciting incident — envy at a friend's windfall, not analysis, is what triggers the investing behavior the piece goes on to satirize in himself.

1999-085-F2.quotation: Before that day I had been vaguely aware that the market was strong. I read the papers every day. I knew that the Dow had passed 10,000 in the same way I understood that our trade deficit is large and the speed of light is fast. Those numbers had none of the relevance of Paul's 1,000,000. In those zeros I saw the incredulous eyes of my progeny, demanding to know how I had managed to sleepwalk through the greatest market we've ever known.
1999-085-F2.primary_subject: Abstract market numbers becoming personally real
1999-085-F2.synopsis: Describes how abstract market facts (Dow 10,000) meant nothing to him until a friend's personal windfall made the boom feel real and urgent.
1999-085-F2.article_context: Explains the psychological shift from detached awareness to active participation in the boom.
1999-085-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because it names precisely the psychological mechanism — a friend's specific dollar figure, not aggregate statistics — that converts market awareness into market participation.

1999-085-F3.quotation:
That was the day the ''greater fool'' theory found its greatest fool yet. My selection of that particular stock at that particular price was the product of blind faith, trivia and superstition: faith in the infinite expansion of a transcendent economy, trivial knowledge that Michael Dell is, like me, a thirtysomething son of an orthodontist and a superstitious notion that if this company had brought billions to my parallel-life soul mate, I too could expect a healthy return. There was no more science to this transaction than the time I put $50 down on 23 black in honor of my favorite Yankee.

Three weeks later, I could have bought a Dell computer with the money I'd lost
1999-085-F3.synopsis: Admits his stock pick was driven by blind faith, trivia, and superstition rather than analysis, and that he'd already lost money within three weeks.
1999-085-F3.article_context: Delivers the essay's central self-deprecating diagnosis, explicitly invoking the "greater fool" theory.
1999-085-F3.analytical_significance: Selected because it's the essay's explicit self-application of "greater fool theory" — a first-person confession rather than an outside critique of the same dynamic Norris and others describe analytically elsewhere in the corpus.

1999-085-F4.quotation: For those who scrutinize leading market indicators, my bid to ride the bull market cannot be good news. If my past is prologue, we've just arrived at the end of a trend. Which means this boom may end with nearly everyone a millionaire and me left holding the bag. Or maybe we can prolong the prosperity by bringing to the market the last few people more clueless than I am.
1999-085-F4.primary_subject: The author's own bad timing as a market-top signal
1999-085-F4.synopsis: Jokes that his own late, uninformed entry into stock buying is itself a contrarian indicator that the boom is near its end.
1999-085-F4.article_context: Extends the self-deprecating diagnosis into an explicit prediction about the market's trajectory.
1999-085-F4.analytical_significance: Selected because it turns personal comic anecdote into an implicit market-timing argument — the "dumb money arriving late" theory of bubble tops, made through self-mockery rather than economic analysis.

1999-085-F5.quotation: I  may be the only person who has ever invested in Dell Computer and lost money. Three weeks ago I purchased my very first stock, buying $3,000 worth of Dell that's worth $2,300 today. As of now, a darling stock of the delirious market has me $700 in the hole.
1999-085-F5.primary_subject: The concrete dollar loss on Dell stock
1999-085-F5.synopsis: States the specific dollar loss ($700) on his first-ever stock purchase, made just three weeks earlier.
1999-085-F5.article_context: Grounds the essay's comic self-deprecation in a specific, verifiable dollar figure.
1999-085-F5.analytical_significance: Selected because the precise, small-scale dollar figures ($3,000 to $2,300) contrast sharply with the millions discussed elsewhere in the corpus — a rare ordinary-investor's-eye view of the boom rather than an aggregate or elite one.

1999-085-F6.quotation: That lunch set in motion a process that began with a 10-day self-taught crash course in picking stocks and ended the morning the price for Dell Computer, a company regarded as the General Motors of the new economy, fell below $40 a share. Gazing into the monitor of my desktop computer, I bought a piece of the action.
1999-085-F6.primary_subject: A 10-day self-taught crash course in stock picking
1999-085-F6.synopsis: Describes teaching himself stock-picking in ten days before buying Dell, described as "the General Motors of the new economy."
1999-085-F6.article_context: Narrates the mechanics of the impulsive decision that followed the opening anecdote.
1999-085-F6.analytical_significance: Selected because calling Dell "the General Motors of the new economy" is a clean example of new-economy language borrowing old-economy legitimacy — a rhetorical move worth tracking against similar comparisons elsewhere in the 1999 corpus.

1999-085-F7.quotation: Remember what's at stake: the 14-year-old who smoked his first cigarette today could be the one chasing up the price of your biotech stock tomorrow. I say we get out there and help Charles Schwab recruit fresh troops of self-taught investors with more cash than brains. It might just be our last, best hope of getting Dell Computer back up to 39 3/8.
1999-085-F7.primary_subject: Recruiting more naive investors as the boom's fuel
1999-085-F7.synopsis: Jokes that the boom needs ever more naive, self-taught investors — recruited via Charles Schwab — to keep prices rising.
1999-085-F7.article_context: Closes the essay with its darkest joke, explicitly describing the boom as dependent on recruiting more "fools."
1999-085-F7.analytical_significance: Selected because it's the essay's closing punchline and its most explicit statement of the boom's dependence on continuously recruiting less-informed buyers — a comic version of the same structural critique Friedman makes analytically about barriers to entry.

1999-090-F1.quotation:
This seems like a lot of money for good advice about skin care, nutrition and sexually transmitted diseases, but the Internet is that way, effortlessly amplifying into electronic commerce an existing, yet unprofitable, trusting relationship with consumers. With millions of users only one click away from Drkoop.com's information and advertisements, the site promises to quickly become among the most influential sources of health information.
In pre-Internet days, Dr. Koop might have hoped to make a good living through public speaking and careful product endorsements. Now the Internet allows direct contact between the embodiment of the brand -- Dr. Koop -- and his audience, with the result that the doctor is not only in, but the doctor is rich, too. (And with more than $80 million to spend, one can only boggle at the expected grandeur of Dr. Koop's new corporate uniforms.)
1999-090-F1.primary_subject: The Internet letting Dr. Koop monetize trust directly
1999-090-F1.synopsis: Argues the Internet let Dr. Koop convert an existing trusted relationship with the public directly into personal wealth, without traditional institutional intermediaries.
1999-090-F1.article_context: Explains the specific mechanism (direct brand-to-audience contact) behind the Drkoop.com windfall.
1999-090-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it frames disintermediation (cutting out institutional gatekeepers between a trusted figure and the public) as the actual wealth-generating mechanism, not the Internet's information capacity itself.

1999-090-F2.quotation:
The two most important business terms of the late 1990's seem to be ''brand'' and ''Internet.'' The application  of either term seems to naturally generate success, while combining the two often appears to be a recipe for instant wealth.

Just ask any of the 14 Internet billionaires identified in a recent issue of Business 2.0 magazine, none of whom was a billionaire three years before. These new rules were followed this week in a pair of separate events -- the departure of Lou Dobbs, a CNN business anchorman, for a startup Internet company, and the initial public stock offering of Dr. C. Everett Koop's cleverly named Internet company, Drkoop.com.
1999-090-F2.primary_subject: "Brand" plus "Internet" as an automatic wealth formula
1999-090-F2.synopsis: Claims combining "brand" and "Internet" had become a near-automatic formula for instant wealth, citing 14 new Internet billionaires and CNN anchor Lou Dobbs's jump to a startup.
1999-090-F2.article_context: Opens the column by naming the era's two magic business words before the Dr. Koop case study illustrates them.
1999-090-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because "brand + Internet = wealth" is stated as a nearly mechanical formula — a compact articulation of the era's causal logic worth comparing against more skeptical formulations elsewhere in the corpus.

1999-091-F1.quotation: A company's Internet IQ, argues Don Listwin, Cisco's executive V.P., is the product of two measures: the degree to which its own internal operations -- and how it delivers products and services -- are now built around using the Internet, and the degree to which its external behavior exploits the global spread of the Internet.
1999-091-F1.synopsis: Defines Cisco executive Don Listwin's concept of "Internet IQ" as a combination of internal operations and external market behavior built around the Internet.
1999-091-F1.article_context: Opens the column by defining its central organizing concept before applying it.
1999-091-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it's a clean definitional fragment for a specific 1999 business-jargon concept ("Internet IQ") worth cross-referencing against other era-specific readiness metrics in the corpus.

1999-091-F2.quotation:
It's hard to predict exactly when desk clerks at Motel 6 will be telling you that, but thanks to the Internet it will be a lot sooner than you think. It took America Online nine years to sign up its first million members; AOL just added its latest million members in 42 days. Two years ago, the average AOL member was on line for 14 minutes a day; now it's 55. The U.S.-based Internet economy has gone from $0 to roughly $300 billion in revenues in five years.”
“Things are changing so quickly that Cisco Systems, which makes the black boxes that connect the Internet, has just come up with a model through which companies can measure themselves for how close they are to what Cisco believes is the ideal business model needed for success in the Internet economy.
1999-091-F2.primary_subject: AOL's accelerating growth rate as proof of the Internet's pace
1999-091-F2.synopsis: Cites AOL's growth accelerating from nine years to sign up its first million members to just 42 days for its latest million as proof of the Internet economy's pace.
1999-091-F2.article_context: Provides the concrete acceleration statistics that ground the column's "faster than you think" framing.
1999-091-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because the nine-years-to-42-days comparison is one of the corpus's most concrete, quotable acceleration statistics — precise numbers doing the rhetorical work an adjective like "fast" alone couldn't.

1999-091-F3.quotation:
(1) Does your management understand the opportunities, and destructive potential, of the Internet for its business? (2) Is your business strategy fully aligned with what the Internet now makes possible, or do you deal with the Internet as just another piece of technology to add on to your computers? (3) Do you use the Internet to anticipate customer behaviors and recognize market changes? (4) Does your company cultivate Internet skills for its workers and managers?
“(5) Can your company's technological infrastructure accommodate rapid change and customization without sacrificing scale and security? (6) Are Internet sales an important component of your overall revenues? (7) Can your company handle an Internet ecosystem in which you are intimately tied together over the Internet with multiple suppliers and multiple customers? (8) Is each one of your employees empowered to use Internet technology to build employee ecosystems within the company?  (9) Can you operate in warp-speed Internet time to get to market faster and establish first-mover positions?  (10) Do you have systems for measuring the impact of the Internet on your business and cost-cutting?”
“Yeah, it's probably just a gimmick, you say. Nothing to worry about. Right. The next thing you know someone will tell you that Motel 6 is offering every movie ever made in any language on its room TV's.
1999-091-F3.synopsis: Lists Cisco's ten-question checklist for measuring a company's Internet readiness, closing with a sarcastic aside toward skeptics who'd dismiss it as a gimmick.
1999-091-F3.article_context: Delivers the substance of the "Internet IQ" framework as an actionable checklist, closing the column with a rhetorical jab at doubters.
1999-091-F3.analytical_significance: Selected because the closing "it's probably just a gimmick, you say... Right" line preemptively dismisses skepticism rather than engaging it — a rhetorical tell worth noting when assessing how the column forecloses counterargument.

1999-092-F1.quotation:
''Where do you find history?'' I imagine asking the students of the future.

''On the Web,'' they answer.

''How do you get at it?''

''By surfing.''

''What method will you use to write your paper?''

''Access, download, hyperlink and printout.''
1999-092-F1.primary_subject: An imagined future exchange about how students will "find" history
1999-092-F1.synopsis: Imagines a future dialogue in which students describe finding history entirely through surfing, downloading, and hyperlinking.
1999-092-F1.article_context: Opens the essay with a speculative dialogue that frames its concern about historical research becoming purely digital.
1999-092-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because the imagined-dialogue device stages the essay's anxiety as a hypothetical future conversation rather than a direct claim, letting the students' own flattened language make the argument.

1999-092-F2.quotation: Instead of turning our backs on cyberspace, we need to take control of it -- to set standards, develop quality controls and direct traffic. Our students will learn to navigate the Internet successfully if we set up warning signals and teach them to obey: ''Proceed with caution. Danger lies ahead.''
1999-092-F2.primary_subject: Calling for standards and quality control rather than rejection
1999-092-F2.synopsis: Argues for actively setting standards and "warning signals" for Internet research rather than simply rejecting it.
1999-092-F2.article_context: States the essay's constructive proposal, positioned against both uncritical enthusiasm and outright rejection.
1999-092-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because it positions Darnton's argument as a middle path — neither techno-enthusiasm nor rejection — worth comparing against more binary takes elsewhere in the education-topic corpus.

1999-092-F3.quotation: Does the Internet help college students learn? Enthusiasts proclaim that it has made a world of information available to any freshman with a computer. Skeptics warn that cyberspace is so full of junk that research in it will never amount to anything more than garbage collecting.
1999-092-F3.primary_subject: Framing the enthusiast/skeptic debate over Internet research
1999-092-F3.synopsis: States the essay's central question by contrasting enthusiast and skeptic positions on whether the Internet helps or harms student research.
1999-092-F3.article_context: Frames the essay's central debate directly before Darnton stakes out his own qualified position.
1999-092-F3.analytical_significance: Selected because "garbage collecting" is a vivid, quotable phrase for the skeptic position, useful for tracking similarly dismissive framings of Internet research across the corpus.

1999-092-F4.quotation:
Of course, the Internet can open up bibliographical pathways and can even provide digitized versions of primary sources. But no digitized text can duplicate the original -- its handwriting or typography, its layout, its paper and all the paratextual clues to its meaning. We read the front page of a newspaper as if it were a map of yesterday's events. We gauge the importance of each article by the size of its headline, its position (lead story on the right, off-lead on the left, lighter fare below the fold) and by whatever photographs or sidebars may accompany it. If we merely read the article in isolation on a screen, we would miss the context that shapes its meaning.

Digitizers often dump texts onto the Internet without considering their quality as sources, and students often fail to read those texts critically. Instead, they scan them with search engines, locate key words, jump in at any point and cobble passages together by computerized cutting and pasting.
1999-092-F4.primary_subject: What digitization loses from primary sources
1999-092-F4.synopsis: Argues that digitized texts strip away the physical and contextual cues — layout, typography, paper — that give historical documents their meaning, encouraging shallow keyword-based reading.
1999-092-F4.article_context: Delivers the essay's core scholarly argument about what is lost in digitization, closing its central case.
1999-092-F4.analytical_significance: Selected because it's the essay's most substantive methodological claim — a historian's specific account of what digitization loses, not just a general anxiety about screens.

1999-097-F1.quotation:
The Internet Tax Freedom Act, passed last fall, imposes a three-year moratorium on cyber-specific taxes. By banning the infamous ''bit tax,'' which would tax every E-mail and downloaded image, the law helped the Internet marketplace flourish. Freedom from a thicket of 30,000 state and local taxing jurisdictions has provided predictability to the Web economy.

But we have yet to address the long-term tax consequences of the movement of trade on line. Last year, Americans bought $43 billion in goods and services over the Internet; next year the figure is expected to reach $250 billion. That's a lot of lost sales tax. Governments will have two choices: cut services or find this money elsewhere. When the moratorium expires in 2001, the Internet will become fair game. Retailers who can't or won't sell on line, from barbers to boutiques, will clamor for equal sales tax treatment.
1999-097-F1.primary_subject: The temporary Internet tax moratorium and its looming expiration
1999-097-F1.synopsis: Explains the three-year moratorium on Internet-specific taxes and projects online sales growing from $43 billion to $250 billion, representing substantial lost sales tax revenue.
1999-097-F1.article_context: Opens the essay by establishing the current tax-free status quo and its coming expiration date.
1999-097-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because the specific dollar projections ($43 billion to $250 billion) ground an otherwise abstract tax-policy debate in concrete, trackable figures.

1999-097-F2.quotation: Why can't we just extend the obligation to collect sales tax to Internet merchants? Thirty thousand taxing jurisdictions means millions of rules, not easily adapted to E-commerce. The big states are quiet because they themselves are high-tech leaders. Though the commission will make its recommendations next May in an election year, it shouldn't pull punches. If the panel doesn't develop fair tax rules for the new economy, 30,000 local authorities and their overseas counterparts will be waiting.
1999-097-F2.primary_subject: The practical complexity of taxing Internet commerce
1999-097-F2.synopsis: Argues that extending existing sales tax rules to Internet merchants is impractical given 30,000 separate taxing jurisdictions, urging a simplified new framework instead.
1999-097-F2.article_context: Closes the essay with its practical policy recommendation and a warning about the consequences of inaction.
1999-097-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because it names the specific structural obstacle (30,000 jurisdictions) that makes Internet taxation a genuine policy problem rather than simple political reluctance.

1999-101-F1.quotation: In the nine months since the Microsoft trial began, the Government has no doubt shown that Microsoft is a very big company with very bad manners. But it certainly hasn't proved that Microsoft has violated the antitrust laws by harming consumers. It's time for the antitrust division to give up yet another misguided effort to micromanage the fast-moving information-technology business.
1999-101-F1.primary_subject: The government's failure to prove consumer harm
1999-101-F1.synopsis: Argues that after nine months of trial, the government has shown Microsoft behaves badly but has not proven it harmed consumers, the actual legal standard.
1999-101-F1.article_context: Opens the essay's argument by distinguishing "bad manners" from proven antitrust violations.
1999-101-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it names the precise legal standard (consumer harm) the essay argues the government failed to meet — a sharper framing than generic pro-Microsoft sentiment.

1999-101-F2.quotation: Moreover, Windows is under attack from other directions. Linux use is growing rapidly. E-mail and Internet access can now be had through portable devices that don't rely on Windows. And there is a new generation of machines, like Sony's Playstation II, that do not use Windows, can do many operations at three times the speed of the fastest Intel chip and could easily be adapted to word processing or Internet browsing. In short, a lot of serious companies are investing serious money because they think they can displace Windows. Speaking from behind a pile of old Microsoft E-mails detailing its nefarious plans to rule the software world, the Government's lawyers still deny that this is possible.
1999-101-F2.primary_subject: Competitive threats to Windows from Linux and non-PC devices
1999-101-F2.synopsis: Lists Linux, portable non-Windows devices, and Sony's PlayStation II as emerging competitive threats undercutting claims of Microsoft's secure dominance.
1999-101-F2.article_context: Provides the essay's evidentiary case for why Microsoft's market position is more precarious than the antitrust case assumes.
1999-101-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because naming a game console (PlayStation II) as a Windows competitor is a distinctive, non-obvious argument for market contestability, broader than the usual browser-war framing.

1999-101-F3a.quotation: To maintain its ''monopoly,'' Microsoft spent a fortune to create an Internet browser good enough to go toe-to-toe with Netscape's Navigator. And then Microsoft gave the browser away -- bundling it with Windows 95 and Windows 98 -- even offering other companies incentives for distribution. The motive, the Government contends, was to deprive Netscape of enough customers to break out of the aforementioned ''applications barrier'' and lead the way to a world less dependent on Windows. While that may prove a convincing argument for some, it is hard to sell to most economists and legal specialists.
1999-101-F3a.synopsis: Summarizes the government's theory that Microsoft's free browser bundling was a deliberate strategy to starve Netscape of customers and preserve the Windows "applications barrier," then declares that theory hard to sell to most economists and legal specialists.
1999-101-F3a.article_context: Introduces the government's strongest strategic argument against Microsoft immediately before the column pivots to rebutting it point by point.
1999-101-F3a.analytical_significance: Selected because it stages the opposing argument in its strongest form before dismantling it, demonstrating a legal-op-ed rhetorical technique of steelmanning the government's case only to discount it as unpersuasive to experts.

1999-101-F3b.quotation: For one, Microsoft had solid commercial reasons to bundle a free browser with Windows. Adding features is Microsoft's tried-and-true formula for getting computer users to buy upgrades -- a formula about as anti-consumer as Gillette's decision to make a razor with three edges instead of two. That's why Windows 98 contains a dozen or so programs that do everything from create computer art to tidy up a messy hard drive.
1999-101-F3b.synopsis: Argues Microsoft had ordinary commercial reasons to bundle a free browser with Windows, comparing it to routine feature-adding practices like Gillette's multi-blade razors.
1999-101-F3b.article_context: Follows directly from the government's bundling theory to supply the column's central counter-explanation for that same conduct.
1999-101-F3b.analytical_significance: Selected because it directly rebuts the specific bundling allegation at the center of the Microsoft antitrust case, offering the corpus's clearest pro-Microsoft legal counter-argument grounded in ordinary-business-practice framing rather than technological exceptionalism.

1999-114-F1.quotation:
The Commerce Department has just reported that 67 percent of Americans still do not use the Internet. Even 38 percent of households with personal computers don't have an Internet connection.

Is this bad news? It certainly can look that way. African-American and Hispanic households are much less likely to have access to the WorldWide Web than white or Asian-American households. The big cities in the Northeast are significantly less connected than those in the West. The report concludes that the gap between the already-wired haves and the less-connected have-nots is turning a ''digital divide'' into a ''racial ravine.''
1999-114-F1.primary_subject: The Commerce Department's digital divide report
1999-114-F1.synopsis: Reports that 67% of Americans were not yet online in 1999, with the digital divide falling disproportionately along racial and regional lines.
1999-114-F1.article_context: Opens the essay by citing the government report and its "racial ravine" framing before complicating it.
1999-114-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it establishes the "digital divide" framing precisely so the essay can complicate it — a clean baseline citation for tracking how divide rhetoric was used and questioned.

1999-114-F2.quotation:
Few will argue with the report's concern about this gap, and with the call for expanded access to the Web in schools, libraries and other public places. (It may be time to throw in some new books, too.) But the document implies more. It suggests -- though it never quite says directly -- that everybody should be on the Web, just as nearly everybody is on the telephone network.

But does everybody want to be? Nonusers and occasional users have rational grounds for skepticism. A survey included in the report found that 40 percent of all respondents were ''very concerned'' about confidentiality on the Internet. People regularly give up Internet connections because of expense or disappointment -- ''temporary'' files accumulate on hard drives if not removed, innocuous search queries land the user at a pornographic link, malicious programs are outpacing anti-virus software, and so on.
1999-114-F2.primary_subject: Questioning whether universal Internet adoption is actually desired
1999-114-F2.synopsis: Argues that non-users may have rational reasons for staying offline, citing survey data that 40% of respondents were "very concerned" about online privacy.
1999-114-F2.article_context: Pivots the essay from accepting the divide's premise to questioning its underlying assumption that everyone should be online.
1999-114-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because it reframes non-adoption as a rational choice rather than a deficiency — a distinctive counter-narrative to the "everyone must get connected" assumption common elsewhere in the 1999 corpus.

1999-114-F3.quotation: Regular users of the Web should heed this and learn to appreciate the nonwired and occasional user, for several reasons. For example, these holdouts prod the computer industry into cutting profit margins and lowering prices for connections. If a personal Internet link really became as ubiquitous and as necessary as the telephone, the drive for new business would stop, and providers might seek growth in higher charges or more intrusive on-line advertising instead.
1999-114-F3.primary_subject: Non-users as a market discipline on Internet pricing
1999-114-F3.synopsis: Argues that Internet holdouts indirectly benefit connected users by pressuring providers to keep prices competitive.
1999-114-F3.article_context: Provides the essay's first concrete "benefit of holdouts" argument, an economic one.
1999-114-F3.analytical_significance: Selected because it's a counterintuitive economic argument — that non-adoption benefits adopters — running against the usual framing of non-users as simply behind.

1999-114-F4.quotation: Also, if everyone were on the Web, the rest of cultural life, although it would not evaporate, could certainly be impaired. Book sales have already slumped even though the economy has surged and on-line bookselling has exploded. Independent and small-chain bookstores are folding. Compressed on-line music formats may displace some higher-quality CD's. Internet holdouts help protect intellectual variety and choice in such areas.
1999-114-F4.primary_subject: Non-adoption as protection for cultural variety
1999-114-F4.synopsis: Argues that universal Internet adoption risks impairing offline cultural life, citing slumping book sales and closing independent bookstores.
1999-114-F4.article_context: Extends the "benefits of holdouts" argument from economics to cultural variety.
1999-114-F4.analytical_significance: Selected because it links Internet adoption directly to a specific, measurable cultural cost (bookstore closures) rather than a vague nostalgia for offline life.

1999-114-F5.quotation: But the biggest benefit from the Internet holdouts is not what they consume but what they save: energy. In ''Earth in the Balance,'' Al Gore celebrated the potential of a future national computer network to help spare the environment through telecommuting. Now we have wide access to the Internet, yet consumption of electricity continues to rise as electronic devices multiply. Some scientists, unconvinced that reserves are growing as reported, predict new petroleum shortages within a decade. If so, the Web's contribution to the energy load will compound them.
1999-114-F5.synopsis: Argues that despite Al Gore's prediction that computer networks would spare the environment through telecommuting, widespread Internet use has instead driven electricity consumption up, not down.
1999-114-F5.article_context: Delivers the essay's central refutation of a specific green-technology optimism claim, using it to introduce the energy argument.
1999-114-F5.analytical_significance: Selected because it directly names and refutes a specific optimistic prediction (Gore's telecommuting-saves-energy claim) with contrary evidence — a clean case of the myth being invoked specifically to be deflated.

1999-114-F6.quotation: Thanks to all that cruising, the servers and routers that harbor Web sites and distribute data -- and the factories that make the chips -- use energy prodigiously. Writing recently in Forbes, Peter Huber has estimated that it takes ''about 1 pound of coal to create, package, store and move 2 megabytes of data'' and that computer-related demand already consumes 13 percent of America's electricity.
1999-114-F6.primary_subject: The energy cost of Internet infrastructure
1999-114-F6.synopsis: Cites an estimate that it takes roughly one pound of coal to create, store, and move 2 megabytes of data, with computing already consuming 13% of America's electricity.
1999-114-F6.article_context: Provides the specific quantitative evidence for the energy-cost argument introduced in the previous fragment.
1999-114-F6.analytical_significance: Selected because the "1 pound of coal per 2 megabytes" statistic is a strikingly early, concrete articulation of digital infrastructure's physical energy cost — an argument usually associated with much later AI-era data-center discourse.

1999-114-F7.quotation: Internet enthusiasts should consider what would happen to their utility bills if most nonusers jumped onto the Internet just as new generations of chips arrive, running hotter than ever. During the summer, the extra heat would be pumped into city streets by air-conditioners, supercharging the local microclimate as well as contributing to global greenhouse gases; we would demand still more cooling, until cities and even regions faced the likelihood of blackouts.
1999-114-F7.primary_subject: Projecting blackout risk from universal adoption
1999-114-F7.synopsis: Projects that if all current non-users came online alongside hotter-running new chips, the resulting cooling demand could push cities toward blackouts.
1999-114-F7.article_context: Closes the essay with its starkest hypothetical consequence of achieving universal Internet adoption.
1999-114-F7.analytical_significance: Selected because it's a striking, specific worst-case prediction (blackouts from universal adoption) that reads as a direct historical precedent to 2025-era arguments about AI data centers straining the power grid — an unusually apt cross-era pairing candidate.

1999-123-F1.quotation:
More and more I find myself reacting to people with cell phones the same way I react to people smoking cigars at the dinner table next to me -- violently. I call it Y2K rage.

I can't wait for the day when they have soundproof, glass-enclosed cell-phone sections in restaurants. ''Cell phone or no cell phone?'' the maitre d' will ask. I also can't wait for the day that Motorola comes out with a device that enables you to jam all the cell phones around you as easily as opening your garage door. Zap -- no more dial tone. So sorry.
1999-123-F1.primary_subject: "Y2K rage" at public cell phone use
1999-123-F1.synopsis: Describes visceral irritation at public cell phone use, comparing it to secondhand cigar smoke, and jokes about wanting a cell-phone-jamming device.
1999-123-F1.article_context: Opens the column with a comic personal complaint that sets up its more serious argument about overconnectedness.
1999-123-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it opens on comic irritation before the column pivots to a more serious diagnosis — worth noting how register shifts within a single piece from joke to genuine social critique.

1999-123-F2.quotation:
This Israeli motorist with a cell phone in each ear, driving with his elbows, gets my vote as the poster boy for the social disease of the next millennium -- overconnectedness. This is the real Y2K virus for developed countries. It is the anxiety that is going to be produced when telecommunications combines with the ''Evernet'' -- the technology that will soon allow people to get on line from their watches, their cars, their toasters or their Walkmans -- so that everyone will be able to be connected all the time, everywhere.
“This virus of overconnectedness is spreading daily, and it has no known cure. I was recently in a restaurant with my daughter and found myself seated between two families, both of whose fathers were speaking loudly into cell phones, as if they were in their offices. I wanted to scream: ''Look, I'm on vacation. I'm trying to get away from my office. I don't want to be in your office. Turn off that phone!''”
“It is not surprising that overconnectedness is the disease of the Internet age. Because as the Internet and globalization shrink both time and distance, it's great for business, but it's becoming socially claustrophobic. Time and distance provide buffers and breathing space in our lives, and when you eliminate both you eliminate some very important cushions. The New Yorker carried a cartoon a few weeks ago of a man escorting his date back to her apartment door after dinner. She squeezes his hands and says, ''I'd love to ask you in, Howard, but they start trading in Hong Kong in ten minutes.''”
“A friend who works on Madison Avenue said to me that before cell phones and beepers, when someone called his office and he was out, his secretary would simply say, ''Alan is out.'' Now when someone calls and the secretary says he's out, the next thing the caller says is, ''Well, connect me to his cell phone or beep him.'' The presumption now is that he's always reachable -- that he's never out. Out is over. Now, you're always in. And when you're always in, you're always on. And when you're always on, you're just like a computer server. You can never stop and relax.”
“When was the last time you heard someone say, ''Well, let me sleep on that''? Good luck. A Wall Street exec I know tells me he used to love going to Japan, working all day and then hitting the great Tokyo restaurants at night. But now he works all day, and just when he's about to head for the sushi bars, the faxes, beeper messages and cell-phone calls start coming in from New York. ''I haven't been out to dinner in Tokyo in five years,'' he says. ''I end up working a 19-hour day now'' -- the full Tokyo day and the full New York day.”
“What happens when we're always connected is that the boundary between work and play disappears. Yes, working moms and dads can now be home more. That's good. But what it often means is that the workday just becomes 19 hours. I have a friend in a high-stress government legal job. He told me he often came home early, and on weekends, with his cell phone and tried to work at home to be with his teen-age daughter. Even though it meant that 20 minutes out of every two hours he was on his cell phone, he figured it was better than nothing. His daughter disagreed. She eventually got so upset with all the interruptions that she finally said to him, ''Dad, just stay at the office.''
1999-123-F2.primary_subject: "Overconnectedness" as the real millennial social disease
1999-123-F2.synopsis: Names "overconnectedness" as the true social disease of the coming millennium, tracing how cell phones erase the boundary between work and personal life until people are never truly "out."
1999-123-F2.article_context: Delivers the column's central diagnosis, moving through several anecdotes — a secretary's changed answer, a friend's 19-hour Tokyo workday, his own daughter's complaint — to build the case.
1999-123-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because it's one of the corpus's clearest demonic-register connectivity claims from 1999 — directly anticipating the same "always-on" anxiety that recurs as a dominant theme in the 2025 AI/wellbeing subcorpus, making it a strong cross-era comparison candidate.

1999-141-F1.quotation: TAIPEI, Taiwan -- So I was having lunch the other day with a group of Taiwanese news editors, and I asked them if I could take notes on my computer. As I opened up my laptop, I joked that I hoped they didn't mind that I was using an American Dell Inspiron and not a Taiwanese-made Acer computer. Without missing a beat, the Taiwanese editor on my left said, ''Oh, don't worry, your Dell was made here, too.'' The others laughed. I couldn't resist turning my Dell over and looking at the bottom. It said: ''Made in Taiwan.''
1999-141-F1.primary_subject: Discovering "Made in Taiwan" on an American laptop
1999-141-F1.synopsis: Recounts a Taipei lunch where Friedman learns his "American" Dell laptop was actually made in Taiwan, the joke that opens the column.
1999-141-F1.article_context: Opens the column with a personal anecdote that sets up its argument about hidden global supply chains.
1999-141-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because the personal anecdote — a journalist surprised by his own laptop's origin — makes an abstract supply-chain argument concrete and immediately legible.

1999-141-F2.quotation: It is one of those little known facts that PC's and laptops are made in a global supply chain, and Taiwan, and Taiwanese-owned firms in China and Asia, are the key link in that chain. They make the most important parts that go into Dell, Compaq, Acer, Hewlett-Packard and I.B.M. PC's, as well as into Cisco systems that keep the Internet flowing.
1999-141-F2.primary_subject: Taiwan as the hidden key link in PC manufacturing
1999-141-F2.synopsis: States that Taiwanese firms make the critical components inside Dell, Compaq, Acer, Hewlett-Packard, and I.B.M. computers.
1999-141-F2.article_context: Generalizes the opening anecdote into the column's factual thesis about Taiwan's supply-chain centrality.
1999-141-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because it names the specific brands whose products depend on Taiwanese manufacturing — concrete corporate detail rather than a general "globalization" claim.

1999-141-F3.quotation: Most U.S. computer firms have moved out of manufacturing. While they assemble computers in the U.S. from parts made in Taiwan, they are increasingly focused on software and Internet technologies. This has left Taiwanese firms as the world's largest supplier of 13 critical computer components. We're talking about cases, screens, microprocessors, hubs, modems, LAN cards, keyboards, monitors, scanners, motherboards, power supplies, CD-ROM's and graphics cards. Many are sole-sourced in Taiwan. Compaq alone will reportedly source $7 billion in PC components out of Taiwan this year.
1999-141-F3.primary_subject: The US-Taiwan division of labor in computing
1999-141-F3.synopsis: Describes how U.S. firms shifted toward software and Internet technology while Taiwan became the dominant supplier of 13 critical hardware components.
1999-141-F3.article_context: Deepens the supply-chain argument with a specific division-of-labor claim between U.S. and Taiwanese firms.
1999-141-F3.analytical_significance: Selected because it names a precise number (13 critical components) and a specific dollar figure (Compaq's $7 billion Taiwan sourcing) — quantified evidence for an otherwise abstract globalization claim.

1999-141-F4.quotation: Taiwan is great at taking other people's innovations, improving them and then manufacturing them cheaper. The problem is, cheaper labor markets around Asia are catching up to Taiwan in this game. Therefore, to keep its standard of living rising, Taiwan has to move up the computer food chain and start doing its own software and Internet innovation. But for now, Taiwan can't compete with U.S. firms in this area, because they have access to a huge, English-speaking market in North America, full of designers. Designing Internet and software products for that market has great risks but offers great rewards, so thousands of U.S. firms are involved. Taiwan needs its own huge Chinese-speaking market that would offer the same rewards and talent pool for the next generation of software and Internet technologies. It needs China.
1999-141-F4.primary_subject: Taiwan's need to move up the value chain via China
1999-141-F4.synopsis: Argues Taiwan must shift from cheap manufacturing toward its own software and Internet innovation, and that it needs China's market scale to do so.
1999-141-F4.article_context: Pivots the column from describing Taiwan's current role to its strategic challenge and proposed solution.
1999-141-F4.analytical_significance: Selected because it's the column's strategic thesis — Taiwan needing China specifically for market scale — foreshadowing the geopolitical entanglement between technology and cross-strait relations that recurs in the 2025 corpus.

1999-141-F5.quotation: ''Our democratic system gives us the ability to do anything we want [by way of innovation] -- the problem is that our market is too small,'' says Mr. Shih. ''So it doesn't encourage people to take innovative risks because the rewards are too small. We have to find a way to have a big market, so China is our hope. Many Taiwanese companies have software centers in China. We have hundreds now, but our plan is to have thousands. Our future technology development depends on leveraging the human resources in China. We need China for brains and we need it for the market -- to be able to justify the risks in developing Internet-enabling technologies and services.''
1999-141-F5.primary_subject: A Taiwanese executive on democracy, market size, and China
1999-141-F5.synopsis: Quotes a Taiwanese executive (Mr. Shih) arguing that Taiwan's democratic system enables innovation, but its small domestic market limits the payoff, making China's market and talent essential.
1999-141-F5.article_context: Closes the column with a direct quote that crystallizes the argument in a source's own words.
1999-141-F5.analytical_significance: Selected because it links democratic governance explicitly to market-scale limitations — a distinctive 1999 articulation of the tension between political system and market size that anticipates later US-China tech-competition framing.

1999-142-F1.quotation: Whether consumers will have a choice other than cable monopolies like AT&T and Time Warner will depend on the emergence of other high-speed technologies. Local telephone companies have begun to upgrade their service with a technology known as digital subscriber lines, or D.S.L., which could compete with cable. They may not have acted so quickly if it were not for the threat of AT&T and Time Warner. Satellite and wireless communications might also provide consumers with another way to tap into the Internet. America Online points out that these alternatives to cable are only in formative stages. But the interest of consumers is served by letting all these technologies develop and taking regulatory action only if they fail to provide adequate competition.
1999-142-F1.primary_subject: Waiting for DSL and other technologies before regulating
1999-142-F1.synopsis: Argues that consumer choice depends on emerging technologies like DSL and satellite competing with cable, and regulation should wait to see if they succeed.
1999-142-F1.article_context: States the editorial's cautious, wait-and-see policy conclusion.
1999-142-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it's an explicit instance of the codebook's rule that arguing for regulatory restraint is not the same as arguing regulation is obsolete — the editorial recommends watchful waiting, not deregulation as a principle.

1999-142-F2.quotation:
With each new technological advance, the Internet beckons as a rich and competitive playing field for business, communication and entertainment. One of the most promising recent innovations is high-speed Internet access through upgraded cable television lines. Before long, these lines are expected to offer a nearly limitless variety of television programs, movies, music, face-to-face telephones, commercial transactions and other interactive services.

But that lucrative prospect has produced a battle royal in cyberspace. It revolves around AT&T's acquisition of major cable systems as well as its big stake in Excite@Home, an Internet service provider that would give AT&T customers access to the World Wide Web. The fear is that by controlling both the cable and the avenue to the Internet, AT&T can dictate where users can go and what to buy.
1999-142-F2.primary_subject: The risk of AT&T controlling both cable and Internet access
1999-142-F2.synopsis: Explains the specific antitrust concern — that AT&T's control of both cable lines and Excite@Home could let it dictate consumers' Internet access and choices.
1999-142-F2.article_context: Provides the factual background and the core competitive fear underlying the editorial's caution.
1999-142-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because it names the specific structural mechanism (controlling both pipe and portal) behind the era's cable-Internet antitrust anxieties, a concern structurally similar to later net-neutrality debates.

1999-143-F1.quotation: Mr. DeLay asserts that since ''hate-mongers and pornographers'' can freely use the Internet, campaign fund-raisers ought to be able to do so as well. But he is deliberately distorting the effects of the Shays-Meehan bill in order to scare people.
1999-143-F1.primary_subject: DeLay's free-speech argument for unlimited campaign Internet spending
1999-143-F1.synopsis: Accuses Representative Tom DeLay of using a disingenuous "hate-mongers and pornographers use the Internet freely" argument to justify unlimited campaign spending online.
1999-143-F1.article_context: Opens the editorial by naming and rejecting DeLay's central rhetorical move.
1999-143-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it identifies a specific rhetorical tactic — invoking Internet free-speech norms to justify an unrelated campaign-finance loophole — worth tracking as a recurring move in how "the Internet is unregulated" gets weaponized politically.

1999-143-F2.quotation: All these alleged concerns of Mr. DeLay are actually a smokescreen to weaken existing laws and introduce new channels for use of unlimited campaign funds. His amendment, for example, would allow corporations and unions to make campaign expenditures for ads on the Internet, which existing law forbids. It would also allow state political parties to circumvent existing limits on what they can spend for Presidential or Congressional candidates, as long as they spent the money on the Internet. House members should see Mr. DeLay's bill for what it is, a ''killer amendment'' that would turn the clock back.
1999-143-F2.primary_subject: The amendment's actual mechanics and effect
1999-143-F2.synopsis: Details how DeLay's amendment would let corporations, unions, and state parties bypass existing campaign finance limits specifically through Internet ad spending.
1999-143-F2.article_context: Closes the editorial by explaining the amendment's concrete legal mechanics and delivering its verdict.
1999-143-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because it spells out the exact legal mechanism (an Internet-specific carve-out) by which a seemingly narrow technology provision could unravel broader campaign finance law.

1999-147-F1.quotation:
Perhaps the server is located on Mars, or is suffering the death of a thousand hackers. No matter. The quality of the notes isn't the point. Glitches will be de-glitched, and similar sites will follow as surely as advertisers follow a market. No doubt someone is about to register the Internet addresses Notes!.com and CollegeforDummies.com.

I.P.O.'s won't be far behind. And higher education may be as virtual as black lightning.
1999-147-F1.primary_subject: Predicting a wave of note-sharing dot-coms
1999-147-F1.synopsis: Sarcastically predicts a coming wave of note-sharing and lecture-download websites, IPOs and all, that would make higher education itself feel "virtual."
1999-147-F1.article_context: Uses biting sarcasm to project the note-sharing business model forward into a full commercial ecosystem before critiquing what it actually teaches.
1999-147-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because the sarcastic IPO prediction frames commercialized note-sharing as a paradigm shift the author views with dread, not enthusiasm — a demonic-register education take distinct from the more common markets-focused demonic claims.

1999-147-F2.quotation:
Education by Download misses one of the keys to learning. Education is a meeting of minds, a process through which the student educes, draws from within, a response to what a teacher teaches.
“Perhaps the server is located on Mars, or is suffering the death of a thousand hackers. No matter. The quality of the notes isn't the point. Glitches will be de-glitched, and similar sites will follow as surely as advertisers follow a market. No doubt someone is about to register the Internet addresses Notes!.com and CollegeforDummies.com.

I.P.O.'s won't be far behind. And higher education may be as virtual as black lightning.
1999-147-F2.primary_subject: "Education by Download" as a failure of real learning
1999-147-F2.synopsis: Argues that "Education by Download" fundamentally misunderstands learning, which requires an active meeting of minds rather than passive downloading.
1999-147-F2.article_context: States the essay's core pedagogical argument, combining the direct thesis with the sarcastic IPO passage that follows it.
1999-147-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because "Education by Download" is a sharp, quotable coinage for the essay's central critique — worth tracking as an early formulation of anxieties that recur around AI-assisted learning in the 2025 corpus.

1999-147-F3.quotation: The very act of taking notes -- not reading somebody else's notes, no matter how stellar -- is a way of engaging the material, wrestling with it, struggling to comprehend or to take issue, but in any case entering into the work. The point is to decide, while you're listening, what matters in the presentation.
1999-147-F3.synopsis: Argues that the physical act of taking one's own notes is itself a necessary form of cognitive engagement, not just a record-keeping task.
1999-147-F3.article_context: Closes the essay with its constructive pedagogical claim about what note-sharing sites actually remove from learning.
1999-147-F3.analytical_significance: Selected because it makes the essay's abstract pedagogical claim concrete and testable — note-taking as decision-making, not transcription — a claim worth comparing against 2025-era arguments about AI note-taking and cognitive offloading.

1999-149-F1.quotation:
There is a club here in Melbourne, the Kelvin Club, where they have a rule that really appeals to me: If you are at the bar and your cell phone goes off, you have to buy everyone in the bar a drink.

The reason they need such a rule here is that Australia has become one of the most wired countries in the world, with both the Internet and cell phones. America is first in PC's per capita; Australia is second. America is fourth in Internet usage; Australia is sixth (Iceland is first!). The Premier of the Australian state of Victoria, Jeff Kennett, campaigned so heavily on the Internet that he is now best known to voters by his domain name, Jeff.com.
1999-149-F1.primary_subject: Australia's unusually high rate of connectivity
1999-149-F1.synopsis: Opens with an anecdote about a Melbourne club's cell-phone-fine rule, then cites Australia as the world's second-most PC-connected country.
1999-149-F1.article_context: Opens the column with a light anecdote before establishing Australia's connectivity statistics as its subject.
1999-149-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because Australia's connectivity ranking is used as a factual hook, not a myth claim itself — the framing device the column's larger argument builds from.

1999-149-F2.quotation: The only problem, of course, is that being wired is always a two-way street. The Australian mining company Western Minerals took advantage of the stock market's obsession with ''.com'' companies by abandoning the mining business and relisting itself on the stock exchange as a sex products store -- Adultshop.com, offering sexy lingerie. Years ago, the Australian Government set up an ethnic TV station called Imparja, to give a cultural voice to remote, outback Aboriginal communities. However, the station developed a taste for American sitcoms, particularly ''Seinfeld.'' People from all over Australia -- including the Aborigines -- started watching it to soak up the worst of Americana rather than the best of the Aboriginal.
1999-149-F2.primary_subject: A mining company rebranding as a dot-com sex retailer
1999-149-F2.synopsis: Describes an Australian mining company abandoning mining to rebrand as "Adultshop.com" purely to capture dot-com stock market enthusiasm.
1999-149-F2.article_context: Introduces the column's skeptical counterpoint — connectivity's double edge — before the more celebratory Australian case studies that follow.
1999-149-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because it's a concrete, almost absurdist example of companies exploiting ".com" branding purely for stock value — a real-world instance of the same dynamic satirized fictionally in 1999-034's dot-com parodies.

1999-149-F3.quotation: Australians will often tell you that theirs has been a ''derivative country.'' They would wait for things to be invented in the U.S. or U.K. and then adapt them. That may change, said Matthew Symons, director of Schoolsnet Australia. ''The Internet got adopted here for education very early because we have all these far-flung schools where you had, say, one art teacher, working in total isolation -- so there was a real need to wire them all in. Once they were wired together, though, they started forming communities, and instead of looking for some American solution to their problems, they started sharing with one another and coming up with organic Australian solutions. It is a fascinating study in network effects.''
1999-149-F3.primary_subject: The Internet enabling Australia to move beyond a "derivative" culture
1999-149-F3.synopsis: Quotes an education official arguing that networked Australian schools began generating original local solutions rather than importing American ones, once wired together.
1999-149-F3.article_context: Provides the essay's first sublime case study — the Internet as a source of newfound cultural self-sufficiency.
1999-149-F3.analytical_significance: Selected because "network effects" here describes a cultural and political outcome (national self-confidence), not a market outcome — a distinctive application of a term usually reserved for business strategy.

1999-149-F4.quotation: Three years ago, Pauline Hanson, a xenophobic, anti-globalization politician, gained popularity here. One way the Australian Government sought to combat her influence was by wiring the whole country. ''Hanson gained popularity because rural Australia felt it was being left behind -- banks were closing, telephone boxes were being removed. Rural communities felt there was unequal access to the new economy,'' said Education Minister David Kemp. ''So the Government decided in 1998 to include access to Internet technology in the basic service package offered to everyone by the state phone company. She was taking our supporters and this was one way for us to win them back.''
1999-149-F4.primary_subject: Wiring rural Australia as a political response to anti-globalization sentiment
1999-149-F4.synopsis: Describes the Australian government deliberately expanding Internet access to rural areas as a direct political strategy to counter an anti-globalization politician's rising popularity.
1999-149-F4.article_context: Introduces a specifically political case study of connectivity being deployed to counter globalization backlash.
1999-149-F4.analytical_significance: Selected because it's a rare example in the corpus of connectivity expansion framed explicitly as a counter-populist political tool, not just an economic or cultural good.

1999-149-F5.quotation:
The Internet has been adopted here with such zeal for a simple reason: Australia is a million miles from everywhere, and sparsely populated across a vast continent. The Internet can shrink that distance between Australia and the world, and between Aussies and Aussies, for almost no cost.
“''For years we have been praying for faster airplanes -- we thought that would be our salvation,'' says Annie Hayes, an Australian conference organizer. ''With the Internet, we can be so much more in touch with the world now, without actually leaving here.''”
“Paul Gilding, the former head of Greenpeace, has an environmental consulting firm in Sydney: ''Two years ago we thought we were going to have to leave Australia because you just couldn't operate a global business from here,'' he said. ''Clients would say, 'We'd love to have you as advisers, but you can't service us from Australia.' Now we're not only advising DuPont [in Delaware], but we're able to attract experts to come live in Sydney from all over the world because they feel they can have the best of our life style and be connected.''”
“Jim Bacon, the Premier of Tasmania, the remote island off Australia's south coast, has reached for the Web with gusto. And no wonder. Tasmania has long been known as either ''the beginning of the end of the world'' or ''the gateway to Antarctica.'' Says Mr. Bacon: ''Suddenly we are connected. We have a little resort on the coast of Tasmania called Killynaught Cottages. The owners were telling me the other day they are getting all sorts of bookings now over the Internet, and just got one from Saudi Arabia.''
1999-149-F5.primary_subject: Geographic isolation as the root cause of Australia's Internet enthusiasm
1999-149-F5.synopsis: Explains Australia's outsized enthusiasm for the Internet as a direct response to its extreme geographic isolation, illustrated by a remote Tasmanian resort now booking guests from Saudi Arabia.
1999-149-F5.article_context: Delivers the column's core explanatory thesis, closing with concrete testimonials from business owners in Sydney and Tasmania.
1999-149-F5.analytical_significance: Selected because it's the column's title thesis stated directly ("shrink that distance") — the clearest single passage explaining why an unusually isolated country became an unusually enthusiastic early adopter.

1999-156-F1.quotation: Richard, a consultant, now lives in Dubai and his letter said the following: ''I found your address on a People Search site on the Internet. I was amazed that for a mere $59 I could order a complete background search on you that included, among other things, a complete listing of your assets. I kept my $59, but it made me wonder what all of this is really coming to. Your daughters and my sons can check each other out in ways that you and I never dreamed were possible.''
1999-156-F1.primary_subject: A reader's unsettling experience with a People Search site
1999-156-F1.synopsis: Recounts a reader's letter describing how a $59 online background check could reveal a complete asset listing on virtually anyone.
1999-156-F1.article_context: Opens the column with a concrete, personal anecdote illustrating the surveillance capability the column goes on to analyze.
1999-156-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because a reader's letter, not the columnist's own research, supplies the opening evidence — grounding an abstract privacy argument in an unsolicited real-world anecdote.

1999-156-F2.quotation: And it's just the beginning. Rule No. 1 of the Internet is this: We are all connected, but nobody's in charge. That is, the Internet is Orwellian in its reach, but there's no Big Brother. Instead of Big Brother, there are a lot of Little Brothers. Beware of the Little Brothers. They are going to be the problem. The Internet super-empowers individuals, Web sites, corporations and even hotels -- the Little Brothers -- so they can amass huge amounts of information outside of any government supervision. Some of these Little Brothers will use that personal data responsibly; others won't.
1999-156-F2.synopsis: Argues that instead of one centralized "Big Brother," the Internet has created countless unaccountable "Little Brothers" — companies and individuals — able to amass personal data without government oversight.
1999-156-F2.article_context: States the column's central coinage and thesis, reframing surveillance anxiety away from government toward decentralized private actors.
1999-156-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because "Little Brothers" is a distinctive, quotable reframing of Orwellian surveillance anxiety toward decentralized private power rather than the state — worth tracking as a coinage that recurs in later platform-power discourse.

1999-156-F3a.quotation:
How we deal with the Little Brothers should be a campaign issue. There are lots of ideas. One of the most thoughtful comes from Harvard Law professor Lawrence Lessig, in his upcoming book, ''Code, and Other Laws of Cyberspace.'' Mr. Lessig argues that people suffer from the illusion that however cyberspace is right now is how it must always be. It can't be changed. It's a place to be discovered, not shaped. But cyberspace was not handed down by God. Its architecture is shaped by people with certain interests, who are, as we speak, ''designing the hardware of cyberspace in ways that are determining the freedom and privacy that you and I will have there,'' says Mr. Lessig.
“The architecture of cyberspace is highly influenced by commerce and government, ''both of which have an interest in knowing as much as they can about what people are doing and where,'' says Mr. Lessig. ''So it's not an accident that the emerging Internet architecture makes it easier to track people and collect private data, because tracking people is what governments like and collecting private data is what commerce likes.''”
“Government, argues Mr. Lessig, can't legislate privacy on the Internet, but it can create incentives for people to build privacy filters and other safeguards into the Internet. ''Let's say the government says that data about you is your property and the only way that someone can take it away is by negotiating with you,'' he said. ''That would create an incentive for Web designers to make it easier for each of us to negotiate about our personal data -- what we want to give up for free, what we want to be paid for and what we don't want to give up at all.''
