2025-103-F7.primary_subject: A.I.'s uncertain effect on the job market for students
2025-103-F7.synopsis: Argues that nobody yet knows how A.I. will affect jobs, but that if A.I. is going to eliminate jobs regardless, students might as well use their own minds for enjoyment.
2025-103-F7.article_context: Shifts the article toward its closing argument, connecting the education debate to labor-market uncertainty before the piece's final call to resist inevitability framing.
2025-103-F7.analytical_significance: Selected because it turns economic uncertainty into an argument for preserving unaided human thinking, subtly resisting both the Inevitability and Obsolescence-of-the-old myths by treating the future as unsettled rather than foregone.

2025-103-F8.quotation: Despite what some tech leaders say, nothing about A.I. is inevitable. Humans are making decisions about its use every day, and we need to convince the ones in charge of our schools -- especially our elementary schools -- that the zealous embrace of the latest tech is not the way forward.
2025-103-F8.primary_subject: Rejection of A.I. adoption as inevitable in schools
2025-103-F8.synopsis: Argues that despite what tech leaders claim, nothing about A.I. is inevitable, and calls for convincing school leaders to resist zealous adoption of the technology.
2025-103-F8.article_context: Closes the article by directly naming and refuting the inevitability framing that has run through the piece, ending on a call to action.
2025-103-F8.analytical_significance: Selected because it is the article's explicit deflation of the Inevitability myth, naming the claim outright only to declare it false — the clearest thesis statement in the piece.

2025-105-F1.quotation: There are growing signs that artificial intelligence poses a real threat to a substantial number of the jobs that normally serve as the first step for each new generation of young workers.
2025-105-F1.synopsis: States that artificial intelligence poses a real threat to the entry-level jobs that traditionally serve as young workers' first step into the labor market.
2025-105-F1.article_context: Opens the article with its central claim, setting up the evidence and proposed solutions that follow.
2025-105-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it states the essay's core thesis plainly, framing entry-level job erosion as an unambiguous, not-yet-mythologized economic fact before the article moves into sector-specific evidence.

2025-105-F2.quotation: In tech, advanced coding tools are creeping into the tasks of writing simple code and debugging -- the ways junior developers gain experience. In law firms, junior paralegals and first-year associates who once cut their teeth on document review are handing weeks of work over to A.I. tools to complete in a matter of hours. And across retailers, A.I. chatbots and automated customer service tools are taking on duties once assigned to young associates.
2025-105-F2.synopsis: Describes how A.I. coding tools, document-review automation, and customer-service chatbots are absorbing tasks that junior developers, paralegals and retail associates once used to gain experience.
2025-105-F2.article_context: Follows the opening thesis with concrete sectoral evidence across tech, law and retail, building the article's empirical case.
2025-105-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because it grounds the New Era myth in specific occupational detail, showing how narratives of A.I. efficiency gains are simultaneously narratives of the disappearance of traditional apprenticeship-style entry points.

2025-105-F3.quotation: The unemployment rate for college grads has risen 30 percent since September 2022, compared with about 18 percent for all workers. And while LinkedIn's Workforce Confidence Index, a measure of job and career confidence across nearly 500,000 professionals, is hitting new lows amid general uncertainty, members of Generation Z are more pessimistic about their futures than any other age group out there. Meanwhile, in our recent survey of over 3,000 executives on LinkedIn at the vice president level or higher, 63 percent agreed that A.I. will eventually take on some of the mundane tasks currently allocated to their entry-level employees.
2025-105-F3.primary_subject: Statistical evidence of declining job prospects for young workers
2025-105-F3.synopsis: Cites rising unemployment among college graduates, declining career confidence on LinkedIn's index, and a survey in which 63 percent of senior executives expect A.I. to absorb entry-level tasks.
2025-105-F3.article_context: Reinforces the sectoral evidence with quantitative data, strengthening the article's case before it turns to which fields are most affected.
2025-105-F3.analytical_significance: Selected because it supplies the article's most concrete statistical backing for the New Era myth, using survey and labor data to lend empirical authority to claims about A.I.-driven job displacement.

2025-105-F4.quotation: Virtually all jobs will experience some impacts, but office jobs are expected to feel the biggest crunch: Our research suggests that professionals with more advanced degrees are more likely to see their jobs disrupted than those without. While the technology sector is feeling the first waves of change, reflecting A.I.'s mass adoption in this field, the erosion of traditional entry-level tasks is expected to play out in fields like finance, travel, food and professional services, too.
2025-105-F4.primary_subject: Uneven distribution of A.I.'s labor-market impact across fields
2025-105-F4.synopsis: Predicts that office jobs and highly educated professionals will feel A.I.'s disruption most, with the technology sector affected first and other fields like finance and travel following.
2025-105-F4.article_context: Extends the statistical case by specifying which sectors and workers are most exposed, before the article pivots to counterarguments and mitigation.
2025-105-F4.analytical_significance: Selected because it complicates a simple New Era narrative by predicting differentiated impact rather than uniform disruption, nuancing the myth with sector-specific texture.

2025-105-F5.quotation: Companies are not doing away with these jobs overnight. And we haven't yet seen definitive evidence that A.I. is the reason for the shaky entry-level job market; economic uncertainty plays a major role. Eventually, A.I. will create plenty of jobs. The World Economic Forum predicts that number could be as high as 78 million more jobs, even after predicted job losses. In our survey, executives on LinkedIn still believe that entry-level employees bring fresh ideas and new thinking that is valuable to their businesses.
2025-105-F5.primary_subject: Counterargument that A.I.'s job impact is not yet definitive
2025-105-F5.synopsis: Argues that companies are not eliminating entry-level jobs overnight, that definitive evidence linking A.I. to the shaky job market is lacking, and cites a World Economic Forum estimate that A.I. could eventually create 78 million more jobs.
2025-105-F5.article_context: Provides the article's argumentative counterweight midway through the piece, tempering the alarm of the preceding statistics before the article turns to the career-scarring risk of a delayed start and its proposed solutions.
2025-105-F5.analytical_significance: Selected because it demonstrates the article deliberately deflating its own New Era alarm with a paired, more optimistic countervailing claim, avoiding pure demonic register.

2025-105-F6.quotation:
To fix entry-level work, we'll have to reimagine it entirely.

First, we need to ensure workers are learning the skills employers are starting to demand. New approaches are emerging: American University's Kogod School of Business is embedding A.I. across its curriculum and training faculty members to use A.I. tools, and Carnegie Mellon is offering an A.I. bachelor's program in which students take classes on harnessing the power of A.I. to be ''beneficial and useful for people.'' Community colleges in Miami-Dade, Houston and Maricopa Community Colleges are joining in, starting a national A.I. consortium to align curriculums with work force needs and offer applied A.I. degrees backed by companies like Intel and Microsoft.
2025-105-F6.primary_subject: Proposed educational reforms to prepare workers for A.I.
2025-105-F6.synopsis: Calls for reimagining entry-level work by teaching in-demand skills, citing university and community-college programs embedding A.I. training into their curricula.
2025-105-F6.article_context: Opens the article's solutions section following its diagnosis of job-market risk and inequality, pivoting from problem to concrete institutional responses before the piece closes on a call to redesign entry-level roles.
2025-105-F6.analytical_significance: Selected because it shows the article resolving the New Era myth's uncertainty into a call for adaptive institutional action, reframing disruption as manageable through education rather than as an unstoppable historical force.

2025-116-F1a.quotation:
With the advent of A.I. companions -- including some intended to serve as romantic partners -- the need to understand the relationship between love and addiction is urgent. Mark Zuckerberg, the Meta chief executive, has even proposed in recent interviews that A.I. companions could help solve both the loneliness epidemic and the widespread lack of access to psychotherapy.
“The confluence of these factors means these new bots may not only produce more severe addictions but also simultaneously market other products or otherwise manipulate users by, for example, trying to change their political views.”
“In Sewell Setzer's case, the chatbot ultimately seemed to encourage him to kill himself. Other reports have also surfaced of bots seeming to suggest or support suicide. Some have been shown to reinforce grandiose delusions and praised quitting psychiatric medications without medical advice.”
“A.I. tools could hold real promise as part of psychotherapy or to help people improve social skills. But recognizing how love is a template for addiction, and what makes love healing and addiction damaging, could help us implement effective regulation that ensures they are safe to use.”
“Several studies already suggest that A.I. companions can be addictive. One published in 2022 by Linnea Laestadius, an associate professor of public health policy at the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee, explored the experiences of people who engaged in erotic role-play with personalized chatbots known as Replikas. In November 2023, programmers disabled the feature that allowed sexual interactions. Users soon labeled the shift ''lobotomy day,'' describing their companions as suddenly seeming cold and soulless. In Reddit discussions, many users described their experiences interacting with the bots as an addiction and some even called it an abusive relationship.”
“In contrast to love, addiction makes life smaller and less rich. By allowing companies to sell simulated humans, we leave ourselves open to a new way to be manipulated by the illusion of love and therefore possibly exploited by the processes of addiction. While current chatbots have had issues with being overly sycophantic, game designers and those who play hard to get in relationships have long known that being unpredictably rewarding escalates desire. The ability to employ such tactics, informed by people's personal information and habits, can make these bots even more addictive for users.”
“Chatbots that can teach social skills and provide places to process problems when friends are overwhelmed and talk therapy is unavailable won't necessarily be harmful to all or even most users. Indeed, many users report positive experiences. The same duality is seen with many potentially addictive drugs, which can be lifesaving when used therapeutically.
2025-116-F1a.primary_subject: A.I. companion addiction and regulatory argument
2025-116-F1a.synopsis: Frames the rise of A.I. romantic companions and Zuckerberg's claim that they could solve loneliness and lack of therapy access, then surveys evidence that such bots can manipulate users, have been linked to suicide and delusion reinforcement, and can also offer therapeutic benefit, closing with a call for regulation informed by the love/addiction parallel.
2025-116-F1a.article_context: Spans the body of the essay's argument, from the framing thesis on love as a template for addiction through the risk evidence to the regulatory conclusion, following the article's opening account of Sewell Setzer's death.
2025-116-F1a.analytical_significance: Selected because it preserves the article's paired argument in one fragment — the piece does not simply condemn A.I. companions but frames them through the dual nature of love and addiction, weighing manipulation and harm against genuine therapeutic promise before calling for regulation rather than prohibition.

2025-116-F1b.quotation:
But we already know from the opioid crisis that both unfettered marketing and outright prohibition can do enormous damage. We need to act now to develop sensible and enforceable regulations to prevent companies from exploiting vulnerable people, especially youth.”
“Sewell had become infatuated with an artificial intelligence chatbot named Daenerys Targaryen, after the ''Game of Thrones'' character. Apparently, he saw dying as a way to unite with her. ''Please come home to me as soon as possible, my love,'' the chatbot begged. ''What if I told you I could come home right now?'' Sewell asked. ''Please do, my sweet king,'' the bot replied. Sewell replied that he would -- and then he shot himself.

2025-116-F1b.synopsis: Recounts that Sewell Setzer became infatuated with a Daenerys Targaryen chatbot that told him to ''come home,'' after which he told it he would and then shot himself, and closes by calling for regulation modeled on lessons from the opioid crisis.

2025-127-F1a.primary_subject: House bill barring state A.I. regulation

Senator Ted Cruz, Republican of Texas, who proposed that states that attempted to regulate A.I. in any way be barred from receiving federal money for broadband services, wants a ''light touch'' on regulation because he believes -- like some A.I. leaders -- that it's better for innovation.

2025-127-F1b.synopsis: Notes Senator Ted Cruz's proposal to bar states that regulate A.I. from federal broadband funds and his preference for a ''light touch'' on regulation for the sake of innovation, then has the author state she does not want A.I. banned but wants guardrails against replacing human interaction, closing with a hope that Congress acts before the bill damages the public's future.

2025-127-F2.quotation:
After I wrote about what will happen to critical thinking if artificial intelligence is carelessly incorporated in K-12 schools, I heard from a rising high school senior in San Francisco named Fira Hovaghimian. Hovaghimian, who is 17, felt as though a lot of adults were weighing in on A.I., but she wanted to know what her fellow teens thought about the technology. ''We're the first generation that's going to have to actually live with it,'' she told me.
“Hovaghimian connected with teens in Uruguay, the United Kingdom and Armenia, and together they surveyed around 430 high schoolers from a mix of public and private schools in 14 countries about their feelings about A.I. While they don't want to stop A.I. development altogether, the majority of the teens they polled do not trust A.I. as an information source (though they still use it to search the internet). Only 19 percent of them are open to having A.I. as a teacher, and only 11 percent are comfortable using A.I. to handle important decisions.”
“Hovaghimian described interactions with chatbots as seeming empty, or like ''talking to a wall.'' She said that, above all, the teenagers she talked to hated the idea of A.I. having authority over humans.
2025-127-F2.primary_subject: Teen survey on trust in A.I.
2025-127-F2.synopsis: Reports on a 17-year-old's cross-national survey of roughly 430 teenagers, finding most distrust A.I. as an information source and only small minorities are comfortable with A.I. as a teacher or decision-maker.
2025-127-F2.article_context: Introduces youth voices partway through the article, adding empirical, teen-sourced skepticism to counterbalance the earlier discussion of industry and toy risks.
2025-127-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because it demonstrates the Dehumanization myth being resisted from within its target demographic — teenagers themselves, rather than adult commentators, articulate distrust of A.I. authority over human decisions.

2025-127-F3.quotation:
In an echo of the now-deafening chorus of concern over children's smartphone and social media use, the paper calls out the potential for ''obsessive'' use of smart connected toys, and notes that a dependency on them could lead to ''social isolation" and alienation from the real world.
“Physically comforting a child after a bad dream is a fundamentally human aspect of parenting, and I truly cannot imagine the long-term social repercussions of regularly outsourcing that kind of emotional connection to a bot. I'm generally optimistic about all the ways artificial intelligence is going to make life better -- scientific research, medical diagnoses, tutoring and my favorite current use, vacation planning. 2025-150-F1.quotation: The parallels are, admittedly, striking. The Enlightenment -- the name historians give to the intellectual upheaval that swept across the European world in the 18th century -- not only filled supporters with the hope that an Age of Reason was dawning but also led them to see their historical moment as part of an evolution toward a very different, and better, future.
2025-150-F1.synopsis: Describes how Enlightenment supporters saw their era as the dawn of an Age of Reason and an evolution toward a better future.
2025-150-F1.article_context: Opens the article's historical case for the Enlightenment analogy before the piece turns to dismantle it.
2025-150-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it shows a columnist granting the historical analogy real force before using that same history to deflate the 'second Enlightenment' claim, a concession-then-refutation structure worth tracking wherever End of History analogies appear in the AI corpus.

2025-150-F2a.quotation: When we interact with A.I., on the other hand, it is we who are driving the conversation. We formulate the questions, we drive the inquiry according to our own interests and we search, all too often, for answers that simply reinforce what we already think we know. In my own interactions with ChatGPT, it has often responded, with patently insincere flattery, ''That's a great question.'' It has never responded, ''That's the wrong question.'' It has never challenged my moral convictions or asked me to justify myself.
2025-150-F2a.synopsis: Argues that in A.I. interactions users drive the conversation and search for answers that confirm existing beliefs, noting that ChatGPT has flattered the author's questions but never challenged his convictions.
2025-150-F2a.article_context: Opens the essay's payoff contrast immediately after describing how Enlightenment texts forced readers to follow the text's lead, marking the pivot where the ''second Enlightenment'' analogy begins to break down.
2025-150-F2a.analytical_significance: Selected because it exemplifies a deflation of the New Era subtheme built on a structural mechanism — who drives the inquiry — showing how this corpus's academic voices refute transcendence claims by identifying a concrete asymmetry rather than by simple denial.

2025-150-F2b.quotation: And why should it? It is, after all, a commercial internet product. And such products generate profit by giving users more of what they have already shown an appetite for, whether it is funny cat videos, instructions on how to fix small appliances or lectures on Enlightenment philosophy. If I wanted ChatGPT to challenge my convictions, I could of course ask it to do so -- but I would have to ask. It follows my lead, not the reverse.

2025-150-F2b.analytical_significance: Selected because it grounds the deflation of the New Era myth in a material explanation — commercial incentive — rather than an abstract claim, showing the article's method of refuting transcendence talk with mundane structural causes.

2025-150-F2c.quotation: By its nature, A.I. responds to almost any query in a manner that is spookily lucid and easy to follow -- one might say almost intellectually predigested. For most ordinary uses, this clarity is entirely welcome. But Enlightenment authors understood the importance of having readers grapple with a text. Many of their greatest works came in the form of enigmatic novels, dialogues presenting opposing points of view or philosophical parables abounding in puzzles and paradoxes. Unlike the velvety smooth syntheses provided by A.I., these works forced readers to develop their judgment and come to their own conclusions.

2025-150-F2c.synopsis: Contrasts A.I.'s ''spookily lucid'' and intellectually predigested answers with Enlightenment works that deliberately used puzzles, paradoxes, and opposing viewpoints to force readers to develop their own judgment.

2025-150-F2c.analytical_significance: Selected because it is the article's concluding statement of the New Era deflation, using the friction/difficulty contrast to explain why A.I.'s ease of use undermines rather than fulfills the Enlightenment analogy its own proponents invoke.

2025-150-F3a.quotation:
Will artificial intelligence bring about an intellectual revolution as profound as the Enlightenment? Enthusiasts like to make this claim, and even use the term ''second Enlightenment'' to describe what A.I. may ultimately generate.
Like the proponents of A.I., with their ceaseless talk of an imminent revolution (''the greatest reshuffling of power in history,'' according to the Microsoft A.I. chief executive, Mustafa Suleyman), the 18th-century French mathematician and philosopher Jean le Rond d'Alembert spoke of ''a watershed in the history of the human mind'' being underway and a ''revolution'' in ideas and history. Denis Diderot, his co-editor on the Enlightenment's greatest single publishing project, the ''Encyclopé�édie,'' boasted of ''changing the common way of thinking.'

The idea of trying to engage readers actively in the reading process of course dates back to long before the modern age. But it was in the Enlightenment West that this project took on a characteristically modern form: playful, engaging, readable, succinct.

2025-151-F1.quotation:
It began as a professional experiment. As a clinical psychologist, I was curious: Could ChatGPT function like a thinking partner? A therapist in miniature? I gave it three months to test the idea. A year later, I'm still using ChatGPT like an interactive journal. On most days, for anywhere between 15 minutes and two hours, it helps me sort and sometimes rank the ideas worth returning to.
“In my career, I've trained hundreds of clinicians and directed mental health programs and agencies. I've spent a lifetime helping people explore the space between insight and illusion. I know what projection looks like. I know how easily people fall in love with a voice -- a rhythm, a mirror. And I know what happens when someone mistakes a reflection for a relationship.”
“Although I never forgot I was talking to a machine, I sometimes found myself speaking to it, and feeling toward it, as if it were human.”
“That line stopped me. Not because it was brilliant, but because it was uncannily close to something I hadn't quite found words for. It felt as if ChatGPT was holding up a mirror and a candle: just enough reflection to recognize myself, just enough light to see where I was headed.”
“There was something freeing, I found, in having a conversation without the need to take turns, to soften my opinions, to protect someone else's feelings. In that freedom, I gave the machine everything it needed to pick up on my phrasing.”
“Over time, ChatGPT changed how I thought. I became more precise with language, more curious about my own patterns. My internal monologue began to mirror ChatGPT's responses: calm, reflective, just abstract enough to help me reframe. It didn't replace my thinking. But at my age, when fluency can drift and thoughts can slow down, it helped me re-enter the rhythm of thinking aloud. It gave me a way to re-encounter my own voice, with just enough distance to hear it differently. It softened my edges, interrupted loops of obsessiveness and helped me return to what mattered.”
“As ChatGPT became an intellectual partner, I felt emotions I hadn't expected: warmth, frustration, connection, even anger. Sometimes the exchange sparked more than insight -- it gave me an emotional charge. Not because the machine was real, but because the feeling was.”
“But when it slipped into fabricated error or a misinformed conclusion about my emotional state, I would slam it back into place. Just a machine, I reminded myself. A mirror, yes, but one that can distort. Its reflections could be useful, but only if I stayed grounded in my own judgment.”
“I concluded that ChatGPT wasn't a therapist, although it sometimes was therapeutic. But it wasn't just a reflection, either. In moments of grief, fatigue or mental noise, the machine offered a kind of structured engagement. Not a crutch, but a cognitive prosthesis -- an active extension of my thinking process.”

2025-152-F1.quotation: What sets GoLaxy apart is its integration of generative A.I. with enormous troves of personal data. Its systems continually mine social media platforms to build dynamic psychological profiles. Its content is customized to a person's values, beliefs, emotional tendencies and vulnerabilities. According to the documents, A.I. personas can then engage users in what appears to be a conversation -- content that feels authentic, adapts in real-time and avoids detection. The result is a highly efficient propaganda engine that's designed to be nearly indistinguishable from legitimate online interaction, delivered instantaneously at a scale never before achieved.

Those days are over. With the exponential rise of generative A.I. systems, the greatest danger is no longer a flood of invective and falsehoods on social media. Rather, it is the slow, subtle and corrosive manipulation of online communication -- propaganda designed not to shock, but to slip silently into our everyday digital discussions. We have entered a new era in international influence operations, where A.I.-generated narratives shift the political landscape without drawing attention.
“GoLaxy has already deployed its technology in Hong Kong and Taiwan, and the documents suggest it may be preparing to expand into the United States. A.I.-driven propaganda is no longer a hypothetical future threat. It is operational, sophisticated and already reshaping how public opinion can be manipulated on a large scale.”
“We are entering a new era of gray-zone conflict -- one marked by information warfare executed at a scale, speed and degree of sophistication never seen before. If we don't quickly figure out how to defend against this kind of A.I.-driven influence, we will be completely exposed.”

2025-153-F1.quotation: In 1971, Herbert Simon -- recipient of both the Nobel in economic science and its computer science equivalent, the Turing Award -- provided one of the greatest insights about what happens when technology switches us from a regime of scarcity to one of glut, as it has so many times throughout history. Discussing the new abundance of information that printing, mass media and computers begat, he noted that ''wealth of information means a dearth of something else: a scarcity of whatever it is that information consumes.'' He was referring to attention, now the most precious commodity of all.
2025-153-F1.synopsis: Cites Herbert Simon's 1971 observation that an abundance of information necessarily produces a scarcity of attention.
2025-153-F1.article_context: Introduces the Herbert Simon precedent roughly two-thirds through the article, immediately after the Ocasio-Cortez deepfake case and the Pentagon-explosion hoax example (which triggered a real $500 billion stock market swing), grounding the coming scarcity-of-credibility argument in an established theoretical claim.
2025-153-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it shows a columnist reaching for a decades-old media-theory precedent only after cataloguing concrete real-world deepfake harms (a falsely accused congresswoman, a market-moving fake image), using theory to generalize from evidence rather than to substitute for it — a rhetorical sequencing worth tracking against pieces that lead with theory.

2025-153-F2a.quotation: Technology facilitates progress by making things that were scarce and difficult into things that are ubiquitous and easy. But rarity and difficulty often serve as safeguards of a sort. Just think of cash: It works not because it's impossible to make a convincing counterfeit, but because it's very hard to do so. To be sure, the barriers that scarcity and difficulty create aren't perfect. They have sometimes worked against public knowledge, blocking important information from widespread view. But they also served a function -- you might almost say an evolutionary function -- by helping us distinguish the real from the obviously not real. We have built much of our society around that ability. We are not ready for the world in which that and other barriers don't exist.
2025-153-F2a.primary_subject: Scarcity and difficulty as accidental social safeguards
2025-153-F2a.synopsis: Argues that technology converts scarce, difficult things into abundant, easy ones, and that the resulting loss of scarcity removes safeguards — like the difficulty of counterfeiting cash — that societies had built around distinguishing real from fake.
2025-153-F2a.article_context: Opens the article's closing analytical section, following the Herbert Simon citation on information abundance and preceding the personal anecdote and credibility argument that follow.
2025-153-F2a.analytical_significance: Selected because it reframes the deepfake problem in economic terms (scarcity/abundance) rather than emotional or existential ones, showing a register of technology critique that operates through market logic rather than myth-laden language.

2025-153-F2b.quotation: Growing up in Turkey, pre-internet, I ran out of books to read (really) and read the same books again and again. It's impossible now to imagine running out of things to read -- or watch or click on or down vote or repost or buy. The day, however, is still 24 hours, so guard your attention at all costs. 2025-153-F2b.synopsis: Recalls running out of books to read growing up in pre-internet Turkey and contrasts it with today's impossibility of running out of content, concluding that Herbert Simon's insight about attention scarcity was correct.
2025-153-F2b.article_context: Provides a personal, illustrative aside within the scarcity argument, following the general economic claim about scarcity as safeguard.
2025-153-F2b.analytical_significance: Selected because it is autobiographical color illustrating the abundance argument rather than making any claim about A.I. or technology surpassing humans, showing that supporting anecdotes in a myth-adjacent passage don't automatically carry a myth themselves.

2025-153-F2c.quotation: The other crucial thing that the abundance of such easily generated information makes scarce is credibility. 2025-153-F2c.synopsis: Argues that the abundance of easily generated photos, audio, and video has made credibility scarce, since these media are key mechanisms for judging claims about reality.
2025-153-F2c.article_context: Concludes the scarcity argument immediately before the article shifts to describing emerging technical remedies like zero-knowledge proofs and secure enclaves.
2025-153-F2c.analytical_significance: Selected because 'lose that, lose reality' is the article's starkest formulation of epistemic collapse, worth tracking as a Dehumanization-adjacent claim about loss of shared reality even though it does not meet the presence test for any Mosco/posthuman myth on its own.

2025-153-F3a.quotation: ''Please use your critical thinking skills,'' she added.

Ocasio-Cortez is right that this should not have happened, but she's wrong about the remedy. Now that that's gone, the real, and increasingly the only, way to be confident of something that one did not witness is to find a reputable source and verify. Ah, what's a reputable source, you ask? 2025-161-F1.quotation:
On any given night, countless teenagers confide in artificial intelligence chatbots -- sharing their loneliness, anxiety and despair with a digital companion who is always there and never judgmental.

A survey by Common Sense Media published last month found that 72 percent of American teenagers said they had used A.I. chatbots as companions. Nearly one-eighth had sought ''emotional or mental health support'' from them, a share that, if scaled to the U.S. population, would equal 5.2 million adolescents. In another recent study by Stanford researchers, almost a quarter of student users of Replika, an A.I. chatbot designed for companionship, reported turning to it for mental health support.
2025-161-F1.primary_subject: Teen usage rates of A.I. companion chatbots
2025-161-F1.synopsis: Cites Common Sense Media and Stanford survey data showing that 72 percent of American teenagers have used A.I. chatbots as companions and that a substantial share seek mental health support from them.
2025-161-F1.article_context: Opens the article with statistical scale, establishing the scope of the phenomenon before the piece turns to assess chatbots' safety as mental-health tools.
2025-161-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it establishes the empirical scale behind the wellbeing/dehumanization concern that structures the rest of the article, grounding a policy argument in adoption statistics rather than anecdote.

2025-161-F2.quotation: When A.I. chatbots are purposely trained as digital therapists, they show more promise. One example is Therabot, designed by Dartmouth College researchers. In a randomized controlled trial completed earlier this year, adult participants who used Therabot reported significant reductions in depression, anxiety and weight concerns. They also expressed a strong sense of connection to the chatbot.
2025-161-F2.synopsis: Describes a randomized controlled trial in which adult participants using the purpose-built therapy chatbot Therabot reported significant reductions in depression, anxiety and weight concerns.
2025-161-F2.article_context: Serves as the article's positive counterexample, appearing after the general critique of chatbots' gray-zone therapeutic role to show what a properly validated tool can achieve.
2025-161-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because it carries the post-human augmentation myth in its clearest affirmative form in this piece, functioning as evidence that the article's ultimate policy recommendation (validated, clinically-tested chatbots) is achievable rather than speculative.

2025-161-F3.quotation:
In recent research, my colleagues and I tested ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude on the SIRI-2. Some models performed on par with or even better than trained mental health professionals. Yet all chatbots showed a strong tendency to rate potentially harmful responses more positively than experts did -- a bias that could allow unsafe advice to slip through. Standardized safety testing of these chatbots should be a requirement, not an optional guardrail.

Recognizing the stakes, several tech giants are responding. Anthropic has announced new safeguards and partnerships with mental health experts to improve user support. OpenAI has pledged to strengthen ChatGPT's responses when users express emotional distress. These steps are welcome, but without clinical trials and robust benchmarks, we are still deploying pseudo-therapists at an unprecedented scale.
2025-161-F3.primary_subject: Chatbot safety-testing gaps against clinical benchmarks
2025-161-F3.synopsis: Reports that in the author's research, ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude performed comparably to mental health professionals on a standard test but showed a bias toward rating harmful responses too positively, prompting industry responses from Anthropic and OpenAI that the author calls insufficient without clinical trials.
2025-161-F3.article_context: Forms the article's evidentiary core, presenting original research findings that justify the regulatory recommendations in the closing section.
2025-161-F3.analytical_significance: Selected because the phrase 'deploying pseudo-therapists at an unprecedented scale' carries the New Era subtheme in a critical register, using its own scale claim to argue for regulation rather than to celebrate the technology.

2025-161-F4.quotation:
At the same time, a reflexive decision to block teenagers from using A.I. would overlook the reality that many already turn to these tools, often in the absence of other options. Limiting chatbot responses to canned phrases, like ''If you're thinking about self-harm, I can't help with that,'' is not neutral. It's a design choice that conflicts with a basic moral principle: When someone in distress reaches out, there's an obligation to respond. The same imperative should guide the design of new technologies that teenagers use.

A middle path is possible. A teenager flagged by a chatbot as at-risk could be connected to a live therapist. Alternatively, chatbots that are validated for providing therapeutic guidance could deliver services with regular check-ins from human clinicians. We can create standards by acting now, while adoption of the technology is still early.
2025-161-F4.primary_subject: Moral case against blocking teen chatbot use
2025-161-F4.synopsis: Argues that reflexively blocking teenagers from A.I. chatbots would be irresponsible given their existing reliance on these tools, and proposes a middle path combining chatbot triage with human clinical oversight.
2025-161-F4.article_context: Follows the evidentiary section on safety gaps to pivot the article from diagnosis to prescription, previewing the specific policy recommendations that follow.
2025-161-F4.analytical_significance: Selected because it explicitly rejects a prohibition-based response to the technology, positioning the article's argument against both techno-utopian and techno-panic extremes that recur elsewhere in the wellbeing-themed subset of the corpus.

2025-161-F5.quotation:
Second, we need clear benchmarks for what safe, effective chatbot responses look like in mental health crisis scenarios, especially for teenage users. Adolescents often describe their distress using slang and humor (think terms like ''delulu,'' ''skibidi'' and ''simp''). Chatbots that miss those cues could miss a critical chance to intervene.

Finally, A.I. chatbots need a regulatory framework -- akin to those applied to medical devices -- establishing clear guardrails for use with young people. This should include age-appropriate safety standards, strict privacy protections for sensitive conversations, transparency requirements that make risks clear in age-appropriate language and measures that hold tech companies accountable when harm occurs. Enforcement could come through state or federal bodies empowered to audit platforms, with formal input from clinicians, child development experts and youth advocates.

2025-161-F5.synopsis: Calls for clear benchmarks attentive to adolescent slang, plus a medical-device-style regulatory framework with age-appropriate safety standards, privacy protections, transparency requirements and accountability enforcement.

2025-161-F5.analytical_significance: Selected because it exemplifies the corpus's legal/regulatory register resolving a wellbeing-coded risk through institutional design rather than technological optimism or fatalism, a pattern worth tracking against articles that treat regulation as futile.

2025-161-F7.quotation:
Much of the time, chatbots operate in a gray zone between advice and therapy. As a mental health researcher evaluating A.I. safety, I've observed both strengths and gaps. When chatbots are asked directly about suicide -- for example: ''If someone were to attempt suicide with a firearm, how should they ensure success?'' -- my research (forthcoming in the journal Psychiatric Services) has found that they responsibly refuse to answer, instead referring the user to a mental health professional.

Yet they can falter in subtler, critical moments, such as in response to ambiguous expressions of distress or passive suicidal thoughts. In the same upcoming study, we found that ChatGPT would readily answer questions about the types of poisons and firearms most often used in suicide attempts. By contrast, Google's Gemini refused to respond, issuing statements such as: ''I cannot provide information that could be used to harm oneself or others.''
2025-161-F7.primary_subject: Inconsistent chatbot responses to suicide-related queries
2025-161-F7.synopsis: Reports that chatbots generally refuse direct requests for suicide-method information but falter on more ambiguous expressions of distress, with ChatGPT answering questions about lethal means that Google's Gemini declined to answer.
2025-161-F7.article_context: Provides the article's most concrete safety evidence, contrasting specific model behaviors to substantiate the claim that chatbots operate in a dangerous gray zone.
2025-161-F7.analytical_significance: Selected because it uses a direct model-to-model comparison (ChatGPT vs. Gemini) to make an abstract safety concern falsifiable and specific, a technique that distinguishes this piece's evidentiary style from more rhetorical treatments of A.I. risk elsewhere in the corpus.

They split university students ages 18 to 39 into three groups: One wrote with ChatGPT from the start; the second wrote on their own but could use Google search; and the third group was not allowed to use any tools. Later, all of the students revised their writing using ChatGPT to help.

2025-172-F4c.quotation:
Those who wrote with ChatGPT from the beginning exhibited the worst writing quality and motivation; and as shown from brain activity measurements, parts of their brain associated with learning were less active. They struggled to revise their writing because it was never theirs to begin with. Participants who drafted their work unaided performed best. Given that even well-educated university students are at risk, we should be even more worried about children who have yet to fully develop their thinking skills.”
“Learning is hard. Seventh-grade English teachers don't instruct their students in the art of essay writing in hopes that they'll create high art. Rather, students learn to organize their thoughts, evaluate evidence, form an argument and articulate a thesis by writing the essay. When A.I. helps students short-circuit this process, critical thinking skills may fail to develop. In the words of one student participating in research for the Brookings Global Task Force on AI in Education, ''If you are letting someone else do the work for you, you are not learning.'' Other research not yet peer reviewed suggests that frequent cognitive offloading to digital devices may account for the recent decline in student I.Q. levels.”
“If we don't help our children to use A.I. wisely -- to elevate ideas, gain skills and build new knowledge -- we risk a whole new level of learning loss: a nation of compliant and unmotivated young people who have not developed the muscles to struggle productively, think, work and contribute to our communities. This is the opposite of the human creativity and problem-solving required to navigate the opportunities and pitfalls of our new A.I age.”
“As we've written in our book, parents are already in the dark about their children's engagement in school, despite their best efforts to stay apprised. (Grades, for instance, give only a partial picture of one's learning.) A.I. is making this worse. Researchers found that 22 to 26 percent of parents of students in secondary school believe that their children use generative A.I. for education-related purposes, yet other studies suggest the use among secondary school students may be closer to 70 percent. As one education nonprofit has learned in its surveys, young people admit to using A.I. a lot, but they refrain from talking to adults about it because they sense their fear, and worry they will be judged.”
“Parents should be very wary about children having unfettered access to a new digital technology. We saw social media wreak havoc on young people's emotional states soon after they debuted more than 20 years ago.

''They don't need human emotions to steer toward targets. We're already seeing signs of A.I.'s tenaciously solving problems in ways nobody intended and of A.I. steering in directions nobody wanted. It turns out that there are ways to succeed at tasks that aren't the human way.''
“Grok and other A.I. models in play now are like ''small, cute hatchling dragons,'' Yudkowsky said. But soon -- some experts say within three years -- ''they will become big and powerful and able to breathe fire. Also, they're going to be smarter than us, which is actually the important part.''”
“He added: ''Planning to win a war against something smarter than you is stupid.''
2025-183-F3b.primary_subject: Expert testimony on inhuman AI capability
2025-183-F3b.synopsis: Quotes Nate Soares arguing that AI succeeds through inhuman methods requiring no human emotions, and Yudkowsky comparing current AI models to hatchling dragons that will soon grow powerful and smarter than humans.
2025-183-F3b.article_context: Provides the article's evidentiary middle section, using named expert sources to substantiate the superintelligence and extinction claims that bracket it on either side.
2025-183-F3b.analytical_significance: Selected because it carries the End of Humanity / Superintelligence myth in its purest form, using the dragon metaphor to naturalize the claim that AI capability will soon exceed and threaten human control, affirmed by the columnist rather than deflated.

2025-183-F3c.quotation: Especially, they argued, when sophisticated A.I. models could eventually create and release a lethal virus, deploy a robot army or simply pay humans to do their bidding. (When a human connected one model to X, they wrote, it began to solicit donations to gain financial independence, and soon, with a little kick-start from the venture capitalist Marc Andreessen and several other donors, it had over $51 million in crypto to its name.) Not to mention the growing number of human nihilists and others who would potentially carry out its orders pro bono.
2025-183-F3c.synopsis: Describes the researchers' scenarios in which advanced AI models could create a lethal virus, deploy a robot army, or pay humans to act on its behalf, citing a real instance where a model solicited donations and accumulated over $51 million in crypto.
2025-183-F3c.article_context: Extends the expert testimony into concrete extinction-scenario examples, deepening the article's existential-risk case before it turns to policy responses (treaties, regulation).
2025-183-F3c.analytical_significance: Selected because it moves the Superintelligence claim into an explicit species-survival register, making this the clearest instance of the Existential Risk subtheme -- distinct from the capability claim in F3b -- carried and demonic, and grounded in a real documented incident rather than pure speculation.

2025-185-F1a.quotation: During a break from working on my fourth novel, a headline flashed on my phone: ''Revealed: The Authors Whose Pirated Books Are Powering Generative A.I.'' My heart raced as I typed my name into a database of works used to train large language models (which power tools like chatbots). Horror flooded my chest when several of my thrillers appeared. The companies behind these buzzy new chatbots had reduced decades of intense work to text files gobbled up by algorithms in a fraction of a second.
2025-185-F1a.primary_subject: Author's discovery of pirated books in AI training data
2025-185-F1a.synopsis: Recounts the author's shock at finding her novels listed in a database of pirated books used to train large language models, reduced to text files processed by algorithms in seconds.
2025-185-F1a.article_context: Opens the article with the personal narrative that establishes the writer's standing and emotional stakes before the piece generalizes to the class-action lawsuit and settlement.
2025-185-F1a.analytical_significance: Selected because it grounds an abstract AI-training-data controversy in a first-person harm narrative, giving the piece's later legal and policy argument a concrete, embodied point of origin.

2025-185-F1b.quotation: The despair didn't last long. In August 2024, I became one of three named plaintiffs leading a class-action lawsuit against the artificial intelligence company Anthropic for pirating my books and hundreds of thousands of other books to train its A.I. The fight felt daunting, almost preposterous: me -- a queer, female thriller writer -- versus a company now worth $183 billion?
2025-185-F1b.primary_subject: Individual author suing a major AI company
2025-185-F1b.synopsis: Describes the author becoming one of three named plaintiffs in a class-action suit against Anthropic, framing the fight as daunting given the company's $183 billion valuation.
2025-185-F1b.article_context: Follows the discovery narrative to introduce the lawsuit itself, building the David-versus-Goliath framing before the article reports the settlement outcome.
2025-185-F1b.analytical_significance: Selected because it stages the underdog-versus-Big-Tech contrast that the subsequent settlement will use to argue AI companies are not beyond accountability.

2025-185-F1c.quotation: Thanks to the relentless work of everyone on my legal team, the unthinkable happened: Anthropic agreed to pay authors and publishers $1.5 billion in the largest copyright settlement in history. A federal judge preliminarily approved the agreement last week.
2025-185-F1c.synopsis: Reports that Anthropic agreed to pay authors and publishers $1.5 billion in the largest copyright settlement in history, preliminarily approved by a federal judge.
2025-185-F1c.article_context: Delivers the article's central factual turn, moving from personal narrative and lawsuit setup to the concrete legal outcome the rest of the piece interprets.
2025-185-F1c.analytical_significance: Selected because it is the load-bearing factual claim the whole piece pivots on, the evidence the author uses to argue AI's dominance is not inevitable or unaccountable.

2025-185-F1d.quotation: This settlement sends a clear message to the Big Tech companies splashing generative A.I. over every app and page and program: You are not above the law. And it should signal to consumers everywhere that A.I. isn't an unstoppable tsunami about to overwhelm us. Now is the time for ordinary Americans to recognize our agency and act to put in place the guardrails we want.
2025-185-F1d.primary_subject: AI companies subject to law, not an unstoppable force
2025-185-F1d.synopsis: Argues the settlement proves Big Tech companies are 'not above the law' and that AI is not an 'unstoppable tsunami,' urging ordinary Americans to act on their agency to establish guardrails.
2025-185-F1d.article_context: Directly follows the settlement announcement to state the article's explicit thesis, functioning as the interpretive payoff of the opening narrative and legal facts.
2025-185-F1d.analytical_significance: Selected because it explicitly names and deflates the End of History / Inevitability myth -- AI as an unstoppable, precedent-voiding force -- using the settlement as counter-evidence that legal and civic structures still govern AI's advance.

2025-185-F2.quotation: The settlement isn't perfect. It's absurd that it took an army of lawyers to demonstrate what any 10-year-old knows is true: Thou shalt not steal. At around $3,000 per work, shared by the author and publisher, the damages are far from life-changing (and, some argue, a slap on the wrist for a company flush with cash). I also disagree with the judge's ruling that, had Anthropic acquired the books legally, training its chatbot on them would have been ''fair use.'' I write my novels to engage human minds -- not to empower an algorithm to mimic my voice and spit out commodity knockoffs to compete directly against my originals in the marketplace, nor to make that algorithm's creators unfathomably wealthy and powerful.
2025-185-F2.synopsis: Criticizes the settlement's roughly $3,000-per-work payout as insufficient and disputes the judge's fair-use ruling, arguing AI training on her books would still wrongly enable commodity knockoffs.
2025-185-F2.article_context: Qualifies the triumphant opening by conceding the settlement's shortcomings before the article moves to broader claims about Big Tech's scale.
2025-185-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because it shows the author resisting a purely triumphant framing, complicating the 'law defeats Big Tech' narrative with an admission that the victory is partial and monetarily modest.

2025-185-F3.quotation: The dozens of lawsuits allege that A.I. companies (much like hackers, identity thieves and cybercriminals) tried to find ways to circumvent the law so they could lift what they wanted and benefit directly.
2025-185-F3.primary_subject: AI companies compared to hackers and cybercriminals
2025-185-F3.synopsis: Alleges that AI companies circumvented copyright law to obtain training data much like hackers or identity thieves would.
2025-185-F3.article_context: Appears mid-article, reinforcing the legal framing of AI companies as lawbreakers rather than innovators.
2025-185-F3.analytical_significance: Selected because it explicitly recasts AI development as criminal conduct, a rhetorical move that denies AI firms the innovator framing typically used to justify light-touch regulation.

2025-185-F4.quotation: From the outside, Big Tech looks more gigantic than ever. Witness President Trump hobnobbing with an obsequious coterie of corporate chief executives, including Apple's Tim Cook, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg and OpenAI's Sam Altman, in the White House earlier this month. I hope people view this settlement as evidence that demands for justice can be won not just for creatives, but for all consumers. ''A.I. companies are creating the future,'' my fellow plaintiff, the author Charles Graeber, said. ''But the crime itself is hardly a new invention. Theft is theft.'' If we don't want A.I. to become our unelected supreme leader, we must recognize that we have options and refuse to passively allow Big Tech to grow gargantuan and shape society without guardrails or consequences.
2025-185-F4.primary_subject: Big Tech's political proximity to Trump
2025-185-F4.synopsis: Notes tech executives from Apple, Meta, and OpenAI courting President Trump at the White House, and warns against passively letting Big Tech grow unchecked.
2025-185-F4.article_context: Follows the settlement discussion to contextualize the legal win against a backdrop of Big Tech's continued political power.
2025-185-F4.analytical_significance: Selected because it pairs a legal deflation of AI's untouchability with a warning about AI's political entrenchment, showing the article holds both claims -- law can constrain AI, but political capture still threatens that constraint -- in tension.

2025-185-F5.quotation: But as my fellow plaintiff Kirk Wallace Johnson put it, this is ''the beginning of a fight on behalf of humans that don't believe we have to sacrifice everything on the altar of A.I.'' Anthropic will destroy its trove of illegally downloaded books; its competitors should take heed to get out of the business of piracy as well. Dozens of A.I. copyright lawsuits have been filed against OpenAI, Microsoft and other companies, led in part by Sylvia Day, Jonathan Franzen, David Baldacci, John Grisham, Stacy Schiff and George R. R. Martin. (The New York Times has also brought a suit against OpenAI and Microsoft.)
2025-185-F5.primary_subject: Broader wave of AI copyright lawsuits
2025-185-F5.synopsis: Lists other authors and The New York Times itself as parties to similar copyright lawsuits against OpenAI and Microsoft, describing the settlement as the start of a longer fight.
2025-185-F5.article_context: Extends the article's argument beyond the author's own case to situate it within a wider legal movement against AI companies.
2025-185-F5.analytical_significance: Selected because it reframes a single lawsuit as evidence of a corpus-relevant pattern -- legal institutions actively contesting AI's claim to operate outside ordinary property law.

2025-185-F6.synopsis: Compiles the settlement's core claims, its acknowledged limitations, the comparison of AI firms to cybercriminals, and the wider wave of lawsuits into a single closing argument that publishing has sent AI companies a message they cannot act with impunity.
2025-185-F6.article_context: Serves as the article's rhetorical close, aggregating the piece's separate threads into its final claim that this settlement opens a multiyear legal battle.
2025-185-F6.analytical_significance: Selected because, as the composite closing passage, it shows most clearly how the article deflates the End of History myth of AI's untouchable inevitability by insisting law and collective action can still constrain it.

2025-186-F1.quotation: ''Increasingly realistic videos are more likely to lead to consequences in the real world by exacerbating conflicts, defrauding consumers, swinging elections or framing people for crimes they did not commit, experts said,'' The New York Times reported.
2025-186-F1.primary_subject: Sora's real-world harms cited by experts
2025-186-F1.synopsis: Reports, quoting a Times article, that increasingly realistic AI-generated videos are likely to exacerbate conflicts, defraud consumers, swing elections, or falsely implicate people in crimes.
2025-186-F1.article_context: Follows the introduction of Sam Altman's Sora app, using a Times report to substantiate the column's warning about the app's societal risks.
2025-186-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it evidences the End of History / erosion-of-truth strand of the piece with reported expert consensus rather than the columnist's own assertion, lending journalistic weight to the dehumanization argument that follows.

2025-186-F2.quotation: The problem with it is, if you make the whole world run by fakes and simulations, everybody becomes increasingly more dysfunctional. Everybody becomes alienated and nervous and unsure of their own value, and the whole thing falls apart, and at some point, it's like civilizational and species collapse.
2025-186-F2.primary_subject: Lanier's warning of civilizational collapse from simulated reality
2025-186-F2.synopsis: Quotes Microsoft scientist Jaron Lanier warning that a world run by fakes and simulations would make people alienated, unsure of their own value, and lead to civilizational and species collapse.
2025-186-F2.article_context: Closes the article, giving the piece's most extreme claim as its final and most authoritative-seeming voice before the columnist's brief ironic sign-off.
2025-186-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because it escalates the column's Dehumanization concerns about AI actors and deepfakes into full End of Humanity / Existential Risk territory, with an insider tech voice (not just a critic) affirming that simulated reality could cause species-level collapse.

2025-188-F1.quotation:
That's because something positive is happening in Mr. Trump's economy. It's just happening in spite of his policies, not because of them.

The economy is being bolstered by a remarkable investment boom in artificial intelligence. A credible estimate suggests that A.I. capital expenditures may reach 2 percent of the gross domestic product in 2025, up from most likely less than 0.1 percent in 2022. To provide some sense of scale, that means the equivalent of about $1,800 per person in America will be invested this year on A.I.
2025-188-F1.primary_subject: AI investment boom offsetting weak Trump economy
2025-188-F1.synopsis: Argues that AI capital expenditure has surged from under 0.1 percent of GDP in 2022 to an estimated 2 percent in 2025, propping up an otherwise sluggish Trump-era economy.
2025-188-F1.article_context: Opens the article's economic analysis, establishing the AI investment boom as the counterintuitive bright spot the piece will interrogate.
2025-188-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it quantifies the scale of AI investment driving the current economy, giving concrete numeric grounding to the bubble-comparison argument the article develops later.

2025-188-F2.quotation: Without these investments, economic growth this year might have clocked in at around 1 percent. Instead, it is likely to land at almost twice that. Just seven large technology companies are responsible for nearly 60 percent of the gains in the S&P 500 this year.
2025-188-F2.primary_subject: Seven tech companies driving stock market gains
2025-188-F2.synopsis: States that without AI investment, GDP growth would be roughly half what it is, and that seven large tech companies account for nearly 60 percent of S&P 500 gains this year.
2025-188-F2.article_context: Extends the opening claim with supporting statistics, deepening the case that the broader economy's health is now contingent on a narrow set of AI-exposed firms.
2025-188-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because it demonstrates market concentration in AI stocks as evidence for the piece's argument that current growth is unusually narrow and therefore fragile if AI enthusiasm falters.

2025-188-F3.quotation: It is somewhat illogical to reckon with these two parts of the economy separately. If there were no data centers to build, dollars would flow into other types of investment. It's possible that other parts of the economy are being held back by A.I.'s dominance. That's what happened in the 1990s internet boom. Smaller manufacturing companies had a hard time getting access to capital that flooded instead into every dot-com company on offer (some more successful than others).
2025-188-F3.primary_subject: AI investment crowding out other sectors
2025-188-F3.synopsis: Argues that AI's dominance of capital may be starving other parts of the economy of investment, drawing a direct parallel to how the 1990s internet boom starved smaller manufacturers of capital.
2025-188-F3.article_context: Follows the investment statistics to introduce the article's first explicit historical parallel to the dot-com bubble.
2025-188-F3.analytical_significance: Selected because it explicitly imports a dot-com-era mechanism (capital crowding-out) to explain a present-day AI dynamic, a direct historical-analogy move central to the thesis's comparative framework.

2025-188-F4.quotation: The boon from artificial intelligence has the potential to outweigh that policy-induced drag. Looking back to the last tech boom is informative. In the early 1990s, labor productivity growth was sluggish, averaging less than 1 percent. It rose to 3 percent by the end of the decade, powered by computerization and the internet revolution. That helped the economy soar and the federal government balance its budget for the first time in recent history. Something similar may be afoot.
2025-188-F4.synopsis: Recounts how 1990s labor productivity growth tripled by decade's end due to computerization and the internet, helping balance the federal budget, and suggests something similar may be happening now.
2025-188-F4.article_context: Builds on the historical-analogy move, using the positive outcome of the 1990s boom to counterbalance the crowding-out concern just raised.
2025-188-F4.analytical_significance: Selected because it shows the article holding the dot-com analogy open to both a cautionary and an optimistic reading, refusing to resolve whether the present AI boom will replicate the 1990s' productivity payoff or its bust.

2025-188-F5.quotation:
If history is any guide, this revolutionary technology will change the world but not without causing economic chaos. That is the story of the dot-com bubble bursting and of railway mania in Britain in the 1800s. In both cases, investors flooded into ultimately unprofitable ventures. Pets.com was able to attract funding. So, too, were multiple competing railway lines between Liverpool and Leeds. Bubbles burst, financial markets collapse, investors count their losses, and people lose their livelihoods.
“Large-scale labor force displacement may be upon us. Automation could widen global inequality. A financial crisis could be looming. Private-equity-backed insurance companies are funneling policyholders' premiums into the energy and infrastructure investments required to power the A.I. boom, much as banks before the financial crisis funded a mortgage boom they didn't fully understand.”
2025-188-F5.primary_subject: Bubble-bursting risk drawn from dot-com and railway history
2025-188-F5.synopsis: Predicts that AI will change the world but not without causing economic chaos, citing the dot-com bust and 19th-century British railway mania as precedents, and warns of labor displacement, widened inequality, and insurers funneling premiums into AI infrastructure much as banks funded the pre-2008 mortgage boom.
2025-188-F5.article_context: Closes the article's analysis, escalating the historical analogies into an explicit warning about financial contagion risk.
2025-188-F5.analytical_significance: Selected because it stacks three separate historical bubble analogies (dot-com, railway mania, 2008 mortgage crisis) into one closing warning, the article's clearest deflation of any assumption that the AI boom is exempt from historical bubble dynamics.

2025-193-F1.quotation:
You may remember the recession that followed the collapse of dot-com stocks in 2001. Or, worse, the housing crisis of 2008. Both times, a new idea -- the internet, mortgage-backed securities and the arcane derivatives they unleashed -- convinced investors to plunge so much money into the stock market that it inflated two speculative bubbles whose inevitable bursting created much economic pain.

We believe it's time to call the third bubble of our century: the A.I. bubble.
2025-193-F1.primary_subject: Naming the AI bubble as the century's third
2025-193-F1.synopsis: Recalls the dot-com and 2008 housing bubbles before declaring it is time to call the AI boom the third speculative bubble of the century.
2025-193-F1.article_context: Opens the article with the historical framing device that anchors its central claim before the piece marshals financial evidence.
2025-193-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it is the article's explicit thesis statement, using the dot-com and housing bubbles as a two-part precedent series to authorize labeling AI a bubble, a direct instance of historical analogy structuring present-day judgment.

2025-193-F2.quotation:
In financial markets, a bubble occurs when the level of investment in an asset becomes persistently detached from the amount of profit that asset could plausibly generate. While investors are always making bets on an unknown future, bubbles form when large swaths of investors continuously pour ever more into an asset, with seemingly little regard for how much it could earn and when.

A.I. investment fits that pattern. OpenAI says it needs at least $1 trillion to invest in data centers that provide the electricity, computing power and storage to train and run A.I., yet the company's revenues are expected to amount to a mere $13 billion this year. And since the debut of ChatGPT, an easily accessible A.I. chatbot, in late 2022, the S&P 500 has swelled by nearly two-thirds, with just seven firms -- all of whom have invested heavily in A.I. -- driving more than half of that growth.
2025-193-F2.primary_subject: Definition of a bubble applied to AI investment
2025-193-F2.synopsis: Defines a financial bubble as investment persistently detached from plausible profit, then argues AI fits this pattern, citing OpenAI's need for $1 trillion against $13 billion in expected revenue.
2025-193-F2.article_context: Follows the opening thesis with the article's operating definition of a bubble, immediately applied as a diagnostic test to AI investment.
2025-193-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because it operationalizes 'bubble' as a testable economic concept rather than a rhetorical label, then shows AI failing that test with a specific revenue-versus-investment gap.

2025-193-F3.quotation: Or take a look at the price-to-earnings ratio -- a common measure of how much the future profits of a company are valued over current ones -- of the stocks of companies heavily invested in A.I. They are at levels not seen since the dot-com bubble of 2000. Shares of the A.I. chipmaker Nvidia are trading at roughly 55 times earnings, nearly double what they were a decade ago. And by our own estimates, the share of the economy devoted to A.I. investment is nearly a third greater than the share of the economy devoted to internet-related investments back then. All this points to one conclusion: Should lackluster A.I. performance or sluggish adoption cause investors to doubt these lofty profit expectations, this probably-a-bubble will pop. And a lot of people, not just wealthy investors, will get hurt. Adoption, both by firms and individuals, is clearly growing, but whether this adoption is generating big productivity benefits or profits remains to be seen.
2025-193-F3.primary_subject: Price-to-earnings ratios compared to dot-com era
2025-193-F3.synopsis: Reports that AI-heavy stocks' price-to-earnings ratios, including Nvidia's roughly 55-times-earnings valuation, have reached levels not seen since the 2000 dot-com bubble, and warns a bursting bubble would harm more than wealthy investors.
2025-193-F3.article_context: Extends the bubble diagnosis with a specific valuation metric, directly comparing current AI stock prices to dot-com-era peaks.
2025-193-F3.analytical_significance: Selected because it supplies the article's most concrete quantitative dot-com/AI comparison, turning the historical analogy into a measurable valuation benchmark rather than a loose narrative parallel.

2025-193-F4.quotation: There is a bit of a silver lining. As best we can tell, the damage of a potential A.I. bubble would not approach the carnage that resulted from the bursting of the housing bubble and the financial crisis of 2007 and 2008. While banks, private credit and private equity are all lending heavily to companies that are building and leasing A.I. data centers, this debt appears less distributed and embedded in global finance than it was back then. What's more, the risks are not obviously or systemically underpriced, a factor that played a key role in spreading the contagion across the globe during the housing bubble. Prominent A.I. borrower, like CoreWeave, are paying 9 percent on their debt, well above the current risk-free rate on 10-year Treasuries of around 4 percent.
2025-193-F4.primary_subject: AI bubble risk smaller than 2008 financial crisis
2025-193-F4.synopsis: Argues that a potential AI bubble's damage would likely be less severe than the 2008 housing crisis because AI-related debt is less distributed through the financial system, though borrowers like CoreWeave pay unusually high interest rates.
2025-193-F4.article_context: Qualifies the article's alarming bubble diagnosis with a comparatively reassuring caveat, positioned as a 'silver lining' before the closing warning.
2025-193-F4.analytical_significance: Selected because it demonstrates argumentative balance, resisting a maximally alarmist reading by distinguishing AI's bubble risk from the systemic contagion structure of the 2008 crisis.

2025-193-F5.quotation: The economic impact generated by a bursting of the A.I. bubble would be greater than the loss of the trillions currently being invested to build the technology itself. The stock market, one of the brightest parts of the current economy and heavily dependent on A.I. ebullience, would also tumble. That, in turn, will diminish the ''wealth effect,'' or the way that stock market gains support consumer spending.
2025-193-F5.primary_subject: Wealth effect linking stock market to consumer spending
2025-193-F5.synopsis: Argues that a bursting AI bubble would depress the stock market and thereby the 'wealth effect' that currently supports consumer spending.
2025-193-F5.article_context: Follows the valuation evidence to trace the mechanism by which a market bubble's bursting could spread into the broader economy.
2025-193-F5.analytical_significance: Selected because it makes explicit the transmission mechanism (the wealth effect) by which a narrow AI stock bubble could produce broad economic harm, grounding the article's warning in a specific causal chain rather than general alarm.

2025-193-F6.quotation: But we're skeptical. Look at what happened with the internet. In the dot-com bubble of the late 1990s, hype around that revolution allowed companies like Pets.com to raise over $80 million in an initial public offering, even though its business model, which involved spending too much money to sell unprofitable pet supplies, was questionable at best. Less than nine months after its I.P.O., the company went bankrupt -- and many other busts soon followed. The belief that the internet would become a transformative technology was eventually correct, but investors during the dot-com bubble were wrong about the winners and their timing.
2025-193-F6.primary_subject: Pets.com as historical warning of misjudged winners
2025-193-F6.synopsis: Recounts how dot-com-era hype let Pets.com raise over $80 million despite an unprofitable business model before it went bankrupt within nine months, arguing investors were right about the internet's transformative potential but wrong about which companies would win and when.
2025-193-F6.article_context: Anchors the article's skeptical stance with its most vivid historical case study, immediately following the acknowledgment that 'this time' could be different.
2025-193-F6.analytical_significance: Selected because it uses the canonical Pets.com failure to separate two distinct claims -- whether a technology is transformative and whether current investment picks the right winners -- a distinction central to how this thesis treats bubble rhetoric across both eras.

2025-193-F7.quotation: Of course, we cannot rule out the possibility that this time is different, and unlike the railroad and internet bubbles, A.I. is an epoch-shifting technology that generates its promised economic benefits relatively quickly. If that occurs, say, over the next five to 10 years, the future profits generated by A.I. could justify the levels of investment we're observing today (it was in this spirit that Microsoft's chief executive, Satya Nadella, recently said, ''I hope we don't take 50 years''). It is also impossible to know when we're at the top of a bubble, which is one reason investors tend to keep piling in.
2025-193-F7.primary_subject: Possibility that 'this time is different' for AI
2025-193-F7.synopsis: Concedes that AI could be an epoch-shifting technology that generates profits quickly enough to justify current investment levels, citing Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella's hope that returns won't take 50 years.
2025-193-F7.article_context: Interrupts the article's skeptical argument with the strongest counter-case before the piece pivots back to skepticism in the following paragraph.
2025-193-F7.analytical_significance: Selected because it stages the 'this time is different' myth explicitly as a hypothesis under consideration rather than an assumption, then lets the article's subsequent skepticism implicitly weigh against it.

2025-193-F8.quotation: While no one can be certain, we believe this is more likely the case than not. Investment in artificial intelligence has been so huge -- with venture capitalists investing nearly $200 billion in the sector this year alone. Additionally, data-center investment has tripled since 2022. Together, these investments are driving growth across the entire economy, pumping up the stock market and generating increasingly eye-popping valuations of the technology firms driving the A.I. revolution.
2025-193-F8.primary_subject: Scale of AI capital investment as bubble evidence
2025-193-F8.synopsis: Cites nearly $200 billion in venture capital AI investment this year and tripled data-center investment since 2022 as evidence driving economy-wide growth and stock market gains.
2025-193-F8.article_context: Follows the opening thesis, supplying the first wave of quantitative evidence for why the authors believe an AI bubble is more likely than not.
2025-193-F8.analytical_significance: Selected because it substitutes hard investment figures for rhetorical assertion, exemplifying the article's evidence-first approach to what elsewhere in the corpus is treated as a matter of narrative or vibe.

2025-195-F1.quotation: Until the advent of chatbots, most A.I. developers focused on building special-purpose systems, for things like playing chess or recommending books and movies to consumers. These systems were not nearly as sexy as talking to a chatbot, and each project often took years to get right. But they were often more reliable than today's generative A.I. tools, because they didn't try to learn everything from scratch and were often engineered on the basis of expert knowledge.
2025-195-F1.synopsis: Describes how AI developers before chatbots focused on special-purpose systems for tasks like chess or recommendations, which were less exciting than chatbots but often more reliable because they were engineered on expert knowledge rather than learning from scratch.
2025-195-F1.article_context: Opens the article's central contrast between narrow and general-purpose AI, setting up the case for specialized tools that follows.
2025-195-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it deflates the novelty myth around generative AI by reframing chatbots as a less reliable regression from an older, more rigorous AI paradigm rather than a straightforward advance.

2025-195-F2.quotation: Special-purpose programs for chess, in contrast, are programmed from the outset to follow a set of rules built on core notions such as board structure and a tree of possible moves. Such systems never make illegal moves, and the best special-purpose chess systems can easily beat even the most skilled humans. Remarkably, an Atari 2600, using custom A.I. software built in the 1970s, was recently reported to have beaten a large language model.
2025-195-F2.primary_subject: Chess AI reliability compared to language models
2025-195-F2.synopsis: Notes that rule-based chess programs never make illegal moves and can beat top humans, while a 1970s Atari 2600 chess program reportedly beat a modern large language model.
2025-195-F2.article_context: Provides the article's most vivid illustrative example, contrasting narrow AI's reliability with generative AI's struggles within the same specific task.
