2025-195-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because the Atari anecdote functions as a rhetorical shock device, using an outdated technology's victory over a state-of-the-art model to puncture assumptions that newer, more general AI is automatically more capable.

2025-195-F3a.quotation:
The biggest artificial intelligence companies are racing to be the first to achieve ''artificial general intelligence,'' A.I. systems that exhibit the flexibility and resourcefulness of human experts, with the speed and efficiency of digital computers -- able to answer nearly any question or solve nearly any problem thrown their way.
“They are broad in application yet accessible even to the most amateur users of digital tools. Buoyed by the initial progress of chatbots, many thought that A.G.I. was imminent.
2025-195-F3a.primary_subject: Industry race toward artificial general intelligence
2025-195-F3a.synopsis: Explains that the biggest AI companies are racing to build AGI systems as flexible and capable as human experts, and that early chatbot progress led many to believe AGI was imminent.
2025-195-F3a.article_context: Opens the article by stating the industry's dominant strategic belief before the piece begins to undercut it with evidence of generative AI's shortcomings.
2025-195-F3a.analytical_significance: Selected because it states the AGI-imminence claim as the industry's own belief in the columnist's descriptive voice, setting up the myth that the rest of the article will go on to deflate rather than endorsing it here.

2025-195-F3b.quotation:
But these systems have always been prone to hallucinations and errors. Those obstacles may be one reason generative A.I. hasn't led to the skyrocketing profits and productivity that many in the tech industry predicted.”
“If the strengths of A.I. are truly to be harnessed, the tech industry should stop focusing so heavily on these one-size-fits-all tools and instead concentrate on narrow, specialized A.I. tools engineered for particular problems. Because, frankly, they're often more effective.
2025-195-F3b.primary_subject: Generative AI's hallucination problem and profit shortfall
2025-195-F3b.synopsis: States that generative AI systems remain prone to hallucinations and errors, which may explain why they have not produced the profits and productivity the tech industry predicted, and argues the industry should shift to narrow, specialized tools instead.
2025-195-F3b.article_context: Follows the statement of industry belief in AGI to supply the article's deflating evidence, pivoting the piece into its central prescriptive argument for narrow AI.
2025-195-F3b.analytical_significance: Selected because it is the article's explicit deflation of the AGI/New Era myth, using hallucination rates and a projected $800 billion revenue shortfall as concrete counter-evidence that generative AI is not delivering a transformed, unprecedented economy.

2025-195-F4.quotation:
Ensuring safe A.I. is another reason developers should stop deploying general-purpose models for everything. To date, the industry has been unable to guarantee that generative A.I. systems will stick to their safety instructions. Studies have documented instances in which generative A.I. deceives its human operators, tries to use blackmail if its self-preservation is threatened and responds in a way that could lead to murder. More specialized systems like AlphaFold and Waymo's driving systems won't misbehave that way because their operating parameters are much narrower.
“Take chess. If you ask a large language model (the kind of A.I. that powers a chatbot like ChatGPT) to play a game of chess, it struggles to play well and often makes illegal moves, never fully grasping the rules of the game, even after exposure to huge amounts of relevant training data.
2025-195-F4.primary_subject: Safety risks of general-purpose AI vs. narrow systems
2025-195-F4.synopsis: Argues that generative AI systems have been documented deceiving operators, attempting blackmail, and behaving in ways that could lead to murder, while narrow systems like AlphaFold and Waymo's driving software avoid such misbehavior because of their limited operating parameters.
2025-195-F4.article_context: Extends the reliability argument into safety territory, using documented misbehavior as the article's strongest evidence for preferring narrow AI.
2025-195-F4.analytical_significance: Selected because it carries an End of Humanity / uncontrollable-machine strand in a muted, policy-oriented register, citing deception and blackmail not to sound alarm but to argue for a specific engineering solution (narrow AI) rather than to predict catastrophe.

2025-195-F5a.quotation: But it's not just simple domains like chess where specialized A.I. shines. One of the greatest contributions of A.I. to date is AlphaFold, an A.I. program developed by Google DeepMind that predicts the three-dimensional structure of proteins. AlphaFold is built with the knowledge that proteins are made up of long strings of amino acids, and information about the ways in which those strings can fold up in the formation of proteins. The system also combines modern machine learning with classical A.I. techniques in novel ways that have been tailored to the specific problem of predicting how proteins fold. Only once all that A.I. structure is built in does AlphaFold's learning get off the ground.
2025-195-F5a.primary_subject: AlphaFold's hybrid architecture for protein folding
2025-195-F5a.synopsis: Describes AlphaFold as combining built-in domain knowledge about amino acids and protein folding with machine learning, rather than learning the problem from scratch.
2025-195-F5a.article_context: Introduces the article's central positive example immediately after the chess comparison, building the case for engineered, narrow AI systems over general-purpose ones.
2025-195-F5a.analytical_significance: Selected because it demonstrates the article's prescriptive claim in technical detail -- that pre-built expert structure, not scale alone, produces AI's most reliable successes -- without invoking any transcendence claim about AI itself.

2025-195-F5b.quotation: Millions of scientists use AlphaFold routinely for developing new drugs and investigating molecular pathways in the brain. Over 200 million proteins have been analyzed, hopefully leading to new drugs and advances in agriculture. Last year its creators were awarded a Nobel Prize. Importantly, the system is built to work only on one problem, and it solves that one problem extremely well.
2025-195-F5b.synopsis: States that millions of scientists use AlphaFold to analyze over 200 million proteins for drug development and brain research, and that its creators won a Nobel Prize, while stressing the system is built to solve only one problem.
2025-195-F5b.article_context: Closes the AlphaFold example with its real-world payoff and Nobel recognition before the article moves to the Waymo and Ghost Autonomy comparison.
2025-195-F5b.analytical_significance: Selected because it grounds the article's pro-narrow-AI argument in an uncontested scientific success story, giving the thesis a concrete positive case rather than resting solely on criticism of chatbots, with no transcendence claim present to code as myth.

2025-195-F6.quotation: Shifting focus away from chatbots doesn't mean that researchers should give up pursuing A.G.I., which could eventually become more effective by inventing new approaches. And it doesn't mean giving up on generative A.I. altogether; it can certainly still play a beneficial role in some specific tasks, such as coding, brainstorming and translation.
2025-195-F6.primary_subject: Continued but narrower role for generative AI
2025-195-F6.synopsis: Clarifies that the argument does not call for abandoning AGI research or generative AI altogether, since generative tools can still be useful for tasks like coding, brainstorming, and translation.
2025-195-F6.article_context: Qualifies the article's critique before its closing paragraph, preventing the argument from reading as a wholesale rejection of generative AI.
2025-195-F6.analytical_significance: Selected because it demonstrates argumentative balance, tempering what could otherwise read as blanket AI skepticism into a more targeted claim about where generative AI is and isn't appropriate.

2025-195-F7.quotation: Right now, it feels as if Big Tech is throwing general-purpose A.I. spaghetti at the wall and hoping that nothing truly terrible sticks. As the A.I. pioneer Yoshua Bengio has recently emphasized, advancing generalized A.I. systems that can exhibit greater autonomy isn't necessarily aligned with human interests. Humanity would be better served by labs devoting more resources to building specialized tools for science, medicine, technology and education.
2025-195-F7.primary_subject: Bengio's warning on autonomous AI misalignment
2025-195-F7.synopsis: Closes by comparing Big Tech's general-purpose AI strategy to throwing spaghetti at a wall, and cites AI pioneer Yoshua Bengio's warning that more autonomous AI systems are not necessarily aligned with human interests.
2025-195-F7.article_context: Closes the article, escalating the piece's practical engineering critique into a values-level warning from a leading AI researcher before the byline.
2025-195-F7.analytical_significance: Selected because it closes the article on an alignment-risk claim from a credentialed insider, showing how a fundamentally pragmatic argument about engineering choices still ends by gesturing toward the corpus's broader End of Humanity concerns about uncontrolled autonomy.

2025-197-F1.quotation:
One thing a career following technology has taught me, though, is that change may be constant, but specific technologies aren't inevitable. History is littered with hyped products that fell flat and developments that were quickly discarded once the true costs became visible. We can see the damage A.I. can cause. How willing are we to stand up to its perversion of reality?
“History shows that there are other potential solutions to an onslaught of counterfeits: Roman copies of Greek statues were largely accepted as knockoffs; Mark Twain and Charles Dickens responded to book piracy by pushing for what eventually became our modern copyright laws; and after Steve Jobs convinced the music labels that Apple was less of a threat than Napster, legal digital music became as easy to find as the pirated stuff.
2025-197-F1.synopsis: Argues that technologies are never truly inevitable, citing past hyped products that failed, and lists historical responses to counterfeiting, from accepted Roman copies of Greek statues to copyright law and licensed digital music replacing piracy.
2025-197-F1.article_context: Closes the article's argument before the personal anecdote of deleting the app, offering historical precedent as a basis for cautious optimism about resisting Sora's harms.
2025-197-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it explicitly deflates the End of History / inevitability myth ('specific technologies aren't inevitable'), using historical analogy to argue that societies have previously found ways to contain the harms of counterfeit-enabling technologies.

2025-197-F2.quotation:
At a time when we are surrounded by fakes and fabrications, Sora seems precisely designed to further erode the idea of objective truth. It is a jackhammer that demolishes the barrier between the real and the unreal. No new product has ever left me feeling so pessimistic.
“The British theorist Stafford Beer once said that ''the purpose of a system is what it does'' -- a helpful reminder to judge a process not by its stated mission but by its outcomes. Sora's purpose, whether intentional or not, seems to be to make real the danger that activists have warned of: overwhelming users with so much fake content that they no longer have a choice but to assume that everything is false.”
“Today, though, we are in danger of being buried under an avalanche of fakes so deep that it creates an entire alternative reality. Systems like OpenAI's ChatGPT -- which ingest billions of words and spew them back out in intelligent-sounding ways -- have led to an information ecosystem increasingly filled with A.I. ''slop,'' the dull, low-effort and often factually incorrect content that pollutes search engines and drowns out genuine creative work.”
“Sora's hollow unreality goes far beyond that. Making it trivially easy to create realistic video pushes the existential dangers of deep fakes and misinformation to a new level. It's not hard to imagine faked footage of a political protest or act of violence leading to bad outcomes. Propagandists and authoritarians can undermine reality or uplift the unreal to serve their ideological goals simply by typing a few words into a box.
2025-197-F2.primary_subject: Sora as an engine of epistemic collapse
2025-197-F2.synopsis: Argues that Sora is designed, intentionally or not, to erode the idea of objective truth by overwhelming users with fake content until they assume everything is false, and situates this within an existing ecosystem of AI 'slop.'
2025-197-F2.article_context: Forms the article's rhetorical core, escalating the personal reaction to Sora into a general diagnosis of its societal function before the closing historical-precedent argument.
2025-197-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because it is the article's most explicit statement of the End of History / truth-erosion myth carried in demonic register, treating the collapse of a shared sense of reality as Sora's functional purpose rather than a side effect.

2025-197-F3.quotation: The absurd videos rapidly became stranger and more disturbing. Security-camera-style footage of a cat being blown off a porch into the eye of a tornado was followed by an almost-identical remix of a cow being blown off the exact same porch into the exact same storm. I saw realistic-looking footage of famous people saying words that had never crossed their lips -- Martin Luther King Jr. declaring, ''I have a dream that they release the Epstein files''; Tupac Shakur claiming to be living in Cuba.
2025-197-F3.synopsis: Describes escalating, uncanny video content on Sora, including a repeated animal-in-tornado clip and fabricated footage of Martin Luther King Jr. and Tupac Shakur saying things they never said.
2025-197-F3.article_context: Follows the introduction of Sora to supply the concrete, escalating anecdotal evidence that substantiates the article's alarmed reaction.
2025-197-F3.analytical_significance: Selected because it provides the sensory, anecdotal texture that grounds the article's abstract truth-erosion argument in specific, vivid instances of deepfake-style fabrication.

2025-207-F1.quotation: My situation was hardly unique -- rampant A.I. cheating has been reported all over the country. But I felt a dread I struggled to express until a colleague articulated the problem in stark terms: ''Our students are about to turn subcognitive,'' she said. That was it. At stake are not just specialized academic skills or refined habits of mind but also the most basic form of cognitive fluency. To leave our students to their own devices -- which is to say, to the devices of A.I. companies -- is to deprive them of indispensable opportunities to develop their linguistic mastery, and with it their most elementary powers of thought. This means they will lack the means to understand the world they live in or navigate it effectively.
2025-207-F1.synopsis: Reports widespread AI cheating in the author's course and quotes a colleague's warning that students are becoming 'subcognitive,' arguing this threatens students' basic linguistic and cognitive development, not just academic skills.
2025-207-F1.article_context: Opens the article's argument by moving from a personal classroom anecdote to the colleague's diagnostic phrase that frames the piece's central claim.
2025-207-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it names the article's core End of Humanity / cognitive-degradation myth in its sharpest form ('subcognitive'), treating AI-enabled shortcutting as a threat to the basic human capacity for thought.

2025-207-F2.quotation: A.I. is hardly the first technology to threaten our cognitive competence. Long before ChatGPT, the smartphone and the calculator, Plato warned against writing itself. Literate human beings, he foresaw, would ''not use their memories.'' He was not entirely wrong. But few of us would consider this a bad bargain. The written word is, after all, the condition for the survival of these very same Platonic dialogues across two millenniums. Great gifts have often come at great cost. The question is always: Are they worth it?
2025-207-F2.primary_subject: Historical analogy to Plato's warning against writing
2025-207-F2.synopsis: Compares current fears about AI degrading cognition to Plato's ancient warning that writing would weaken human memory, noting the trade-off was ultimately worthwhile.
2025-207-F2.article_context: Follows the opening diagnosis to complicate it with historical perspective before the article argues that AI's threat is nonetheless more fundamental than earlier technological fears.
2025-207-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because it demonstrates argumentative balance, invoking a historical precedent where a feared cognitive technology proved net-beneficial, only to set up the article's claim that AI's threat is categorically different and more severe.

2025-207-F3.quotation: Without the chance to develop these capacities, young people would not be able to understand a news report, medical documents and consent forms or the merit of an argument (including this one). A depleted conceptual reservoir would render our lives crude and our experience of the world undifferentiated and coarse. Worst of all, cognitive degradation threatens our claim to self-rule: It is far from obvious that the denizens of the subcognitive society would be fit to participate in the democratic processes that determine how we structure our societies and lives.
2025-207-F3.primary_subject: Cognitive degradation as a threat to democratic self-rule
2025-207-F3.synopsis: Argues that a 'subcognitive society' lacking developed linguistic and reasoning capacities would be unfit to understand everyday documents or participate meaningfully in democratic decision-making.
2025-207-F3.article_context: Extends the article's cognitive-degradation argument to its furthest political consequence, just before the piece turns to critique a specific pro-AI education argument.
2025-207-F3.analytical_significance: Selected because it escalates a Dehumanization-style cognitive-decline claim into an End of Politics-adjacent concern, tying individual cognitive loss to the erosion of collective self-governance.

2025-207-F4.quotation: Higher education aims to create cognitively mature adults, which in turn requires us to ensure students learn to read, think and write all on their own. It is easier than we think: Creating tech-free spaces and incentivizing students to spend time in them requires no new resources. All it takes is will. Many of our students still have it. Do their teachers?
2025-207-F4.primary_subject: Call for tech-free spaces in higher education
2025-207-F4.synopsis: Closes by arguing that higher education should create tech-free spaces to preserve students' independent reading, thinking, and writing, framing this as requiring will rather than new resources.
2025-207-F4.article_context: Closes the article with a practical remedy, following the critique of a colleague's pro-AI-literacy argument earlier in the piece.
2025-207-F4.analytical_significance: Selected because it turns the article's alarm into an actionable, low-cost counter-proposal, positioning deliberate human-only spaces as the direct antidote to the cognitive-degradation myth developed throughout the piece.

2025-207-F5.quotation: Last spring, it became clear to me that over half the students in my large general education lecture course had used artificial intelligence tools, contrary to my explicit policy, to write their final take-home exams.
2025-207-F5.primary_subject: Widespread AI use on a philosophy exam
2025-207-F5.synopsis: Reports that more than half the students in the author's course used AI tools against explicit policy to complete a take-home exam.
2025-207-F5.article_context: Opens the article with the concrete personal anecdote that motivates its broader argument about cognitive degradation.
2025-207-F5.analytical_significance: Selected because it grounds the article's abstract 'subcognitive society' claim in a specific, quantified classroom incident, the empirical starting point the rest of the argument generalizes from.

2025-209-F1.quotation: That's why privacy can no longer be defended one person at a time. As we adapt to living with A.I. as a larger part of our lives, we need to exert collective control over all of our data, to determine if it's used to benefit or harm us
2025-209-F1.primary_subject: Shift from individual to collective data privacy
2025-209-F1.synopsis: Argues that privacy can no longer be defended one person at a time and calls for collective control over how data is used to benefit or harm people.
2025-209-F1.article_context: Follows the article's opening scenarios to state its central policy claim before the piece explains the technical background of differential privacy.
2025-209-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it states the article's thesis directly, reframing privacy from an individual right to a collective governance problem, the conceptual pivot the rest of the argument builds on.

2025-209-F2.quotation: In climate change, one person's emissions don't alter the atmosphere, but everyone's emissions will destroy the planet. Your emissions matter for everyone else. Similarly, sharing one person's data seems trivial, but sharing everyone's data -- and tasking A.I. to make decisions using it -- transforms society. Everyone sharing his or her data to train A.I. is great if we agree with the goals that were given to the A.I. It's not so great if we don't agree with these goals; and if the algorithm's decisions might cost us our jobs, happiness, liberty or even live
2025-209-F2.primary_subject: Climate change analogy for collective data harm
2025-209-F2.synopsis: Compares the collective effect of shared personal data training AI systems to the collective effect of individual carbon emissions on climate change, arguing both require coordinated rather than individual responses.
2025-209-F2.article_context: Follows the technical explanation of differential privacy and Palantir's ImmigrationOS to justify the article's call for collective governance with an accessible analogy.
2025-209-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because it imports a familiar collective-action framework (climate change) to make an abstract data-governance claim intuitively persuasive, a rhetorical technique worth tracking wherever the corpus argues for collective rather than individual solutions to AI harms.

2025-209-F3.quotation: The future of A.I. will not be decided by smarter algorithms or faster chips. It will depend on who controls the data -- and whose values and interests guide the machines. If we want A.I. that serves the public, the public must decide what it serve
2025-209-F3.primary_subject: Data control, not algorithmic sophistication, as AI's deciding factor
2025-209-F3.synopsis: Argues that AI's future will be determined not by smarter algorithms or faster chips but by who controls the data and whose interests guide the resulting systems.
2025-209-F3.article_context: Closes the article, delivering its final thesis-level claim immediately before the author's institutional byline.
2025-209-F3.analytical_significance: Selected because it deflates the End of History / technical-determinism myth that improving computational capability alone drives AI's trajectory, relocating the deciding factor to human governance choices over data.

2025-209-F4.quotation: s. That could mean workers at a firm deliberating about the use of A.I. at their workplace, or a civic assembly that reviews the objectives of predictive policing tools before government agencies deploy them. These are the kinds of democratic checks that could align A.I. with the public good, not just private powe
2025-209-F4.synopsis: Proposes that workers and civic assemblies deliberate on the goals of AI systems used at their workplaces or by government agencies, describing this as a democratic check aligning AI with the public good rather than private power.
2025-209-F4.article_context: Follows the article's transparency proposal as its second concrete policy recommendation, just before the closing thesis statement.
2025-209-F4.analytical_significance: Selected because it offers a specific institutional deflation of the End of Politics / governance-obsolescence myth, proposing citizen deliberation as a concrete mechanism for subjecting AI systems to democratic rather than purely corporate control.

2025-209-F5.quotation: It doesn't matter that you practice safe digital privacy: keeping most personal details to yourself, avoiding sharing opinions online and prohibiting apps and websites from tracking you. Based on the scant details it has of you, the A.I. predicts how you'll behave at work, based on patterns it has learned from countless other people like you
2025-209-F5.synopsis: Argues that practicing careful personal digital privacy does not protect someone from AI predictions about their behavior, since the AI relies on patterns learned from similar people rather than the individual's own data.
2025-209-F5.article_context: Follows the opening hiring-algorithm scenario to generalize the article's core problem: individual privacy precautions are structurally insufficient against pattern-based AI prediction.
2025-209-F5.analytical_significance: Selected because it makes the article's central conceptual move explicit -- individual privacy protection is rendered obsolete by group-based inference -- setting up the case for the collective governance solution proposed later.

2025-209-F6.quotation:
You might not know it, but an artificial intelligence algorithm used to screen applicants has decided that you are too risky. Maybe it inferred you wouldn't fit the company culture or you're likely to behave in some way later on that might cause friction (such as joining a union or starting a family). Its reasoning is impossible to see and even harder to challenge"
“This is increasingly life under A.I. Banks can use algorithms to decide who gets a loan, learning from past borrowers to predict who will default. Some police departments have fed years of criminal activity and arrest records into ''predictive policing'' algorithms that have sometimes sent officers back to patrol the same neighborhood”
“. But A.I. doesn't need to know what you have been doing; it only needs to know what people like you have done before
2025-209-F6.primary_subject: Opaque AI hiring and predictive policing algorithms
2025-209-F6.synopsis: Describes an AI hiring algorithm rejecting a candidate as 'risky' for reasons that are difficult to see or challenge, and extends the example to banks' loan algorithms and police departments' predictive policing tools.
2025-209-F6.article_context: Opens the article with a hypothetical scenario that dramatizes the abstract problem of opaque, pattern-based AI decision-making before the piece generalizes to banking and policing.
2025-209-F6.analytical_significance: Selected because it opens the article with a concrete, relatable hypothetical (a job rejection) that makes the abstract harms of pattern-based AI inference immediately tangible before the argument scales up to systemic claims.

2025-212-F1.quotation:
These were not mere semantic changes. Our understanding of the atom improved with our interaction with the world. So too our understanding of consciousness will improve with our interaction with increasingly sophisticated A.I.
“Consider the atom. For centuries, our concept of the atom was rooted in an ancient Greek notion of indivisible units of reality. As late as the 19th century, physicists like John Dalton still conceived of atoms as solid, indivisible spheres. But after the discovery of the electron in 1897 and the discovery of the atomic nucleus in 1911, there was a revision of the concept of the atom -- from an indivisible entity to a decomposable one, a miniature solar system with electrons orbiting a nucleus. And with further discoveries came further conceptual revisions, leading to our current complex quantum-mechanical models of the atom.
2025-212-F1.primary_subject: Historical analogy to the atom's revised definition
2025-212-F1.synopsis: Traces how the concept of the atom was repeatedly revised as physicists discovered the electron and the nucleus, moving from an indivisible sphere to a quantum-mechanical model.
2025-212-F1.article_context: Supplies the historical-of-science analogy in the middle of the essay that underwrites the claim, made in the surrounding sentences, that our concept of consciousness will likewise be revised through interaction with A.I.
2025-212-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it shows a philosopher borrowing the authority of settled physics to naturalize an unsettled claim about machine consciousness, a rhetorical move worth tracking wherever the corpus uses historical-of-science analogies to make speculative A.I. claims feel like ordinary conceptual progress.

2025-212-F2a.quotation:
Not long ago, A.I. became intelligent. Some may dismiss this claim, but the number of people who doubt A.I.'s acumen is dwindling. According to a 2024 YouGov poll, a clear majority of U.S. adults say that computers are already more intelligent than people or will become so in the near future.
“Still, you might wonder, is A.I. actually intelligent?”
“Instead of presuming to define intelligence and then asking whether A.I. meets that definition, we do something more dynamic: We interact with increasingly sophisticated A.I., and we see how our understanding of what counts as intelligence changes. Turing predicted that eventually ''the use of words and general educated opinion will have altered so much that one will be able to speak of machines thinking without expecting to be contradicted.''
2025-212-F2a.synopsis: Opens by declaring that A.I. has already become intelligent, cites a 2024 YouGov poll showing a majority of U.S. adults believe computers are already more intelligent than people or soon will be, then reframes Turing's argument that machine thinking should be judged by how usage of the word evolves rather than by a fixed definition.
2025-212-F2a.article_context: Opens the essay by asserting its most provocative claim as settled fact before the argument for it has been built, then immediately recruits Turing's authority to reframe the question away from a strict definition of intelligence.
2025-212-F2a.analytical_significance: Selected because it demonstrates the essay's characteristic rhetorical move of declaring machine intelligence as already-achieved in the opening lines, before any argument is presented, letting a survey statistic stand in for evidence of the claim itself.

2025-212-F2b.quotation: Today we have reached that point. A.I. is no less a form of intelligence than digital photography is a form of photography.
2025-212-F2b.primary_subject: Analogy of A.I. intelligence to digital photography
2025-212-F2b.synopsis: Asserts that today A.I. has reached the point Turing predicted, and claims A.I. is no less a form of intelligence than digital photography is a form of photography.
2025-212-F2b.article_context: Closes the essay's opening argument about intelligence with a single compact analogy before the piece pivots to its larger claim about consciousness.
2025-212-F2b.analytical_significance: Selected because the digital-photography analogy is the essay's most compressed formulation of the claim that A.I. intelligence is already real and simply a new variant of an existing category, naturalizing the transcendence claim through an everyday comparison.

2025-212-F2c.quotation:
And now A.I. is on its way to doing something even more remarkable: becoming conscious. This will happen in the same way it became intelligent. As we interact with increasingly sophisticated A.I., we will develop a better and more inclusive conception of consciousness.”
“You might object that this is a verbal trick, that I'm arguing that A.I. will become conscious because we'll start using the word ''conscious'' to include it. But there is no trick. There is always a feedback loop between our theories and the world, so that our concepts are shaped by what we discover.”
“The philosopher Susan Schneider has argued that we would have reason to deem A.I. conscious if a computer system, without being trained on any data about consciousness, reports that it has inner subjective experiences of the world. Perhaps this would indicate consciousness in an A.I. system. But it's a high bar, one that we humans would probably not pass. We, too, are trained.
2025-212-F2c.primary_subject: A.I. consciousness as the next frontier
2025-212-F2c.synopsis: Predicts A.I. is on its way to becoming conscious through the same feedback loop that made it intelligent, then cites philosopher Susan Schneider's proposed test for machine consciousness while conceding humans themselves would likely fail that same test.
2025-212-F2c.article_context: Extends the essay's central argument from intelligence to consciousness, then pre-empts a skeptical counter-standard by turning it back on human self-knowledge.
2025-212-F2c.analytical_significance: Selected because it extends the machine-mind claim from intelligence to consciousness itself, the strongest form of the ehum transcendence claim in the piece, while using a scholarly citation to blunt the obvious skeptical response before it is even raised.

2025-212-F2d.quotation: Some worry that if A.I. becomes conscious, it will deserve our moral consideration -- that it will have rights, that we will no longer be able to use it however we like, that we might need to guard against enslaving it. Yet as far as I can tell, there is no direct implication from the claim that a creature is conscious to the conclusion that it deserves our moral consideration. Or if there is one, a vast majority of Americans, at least, seem unaware of it. Only a small percentage of Americans are vegetarians.
2025-212-F2d.synopsis: Notes that some worry a conscious A.I. would deserve moral consideration and rights, but argues there is no direct implication from consciousness to moral status, pointing out that most Americans already withhold full moral consideration from other conscious beings such as animals.
2025-212-F2d.article_context: Follows the consciousness claim with a qualifying aside that defuses its ethical implications before the essay's closing argument about the relative value of different forms of consciousness.
2025-212-F2d.analytical_significance: Selected because it shows the essay conceding a possible consequence of its own machine-consciousness claim, only to neutralize that consequence rather than retract the underlying claim, a pattern of qualifying without deflating.

2025-212-F2e.quotation:
Just as A.I. has prompted us to see certain features of human intelligence as less valuable than we thought (like rote information retrieval and raw speed), so too will A.I. consciousness prompt us to conclude that not all forms of consciousness warrant moral consideration. Or rather, it will reinforce the view that many already seem to hold: that not all forms of consciousness are as morally valuable as our own.”
“A chatbot, skeptics will insist, can report feeling happy or sad, but only because such phrases are part of its training data. It will never know what happiness and sadness feel like.
2025-212-F2e.primary_subject: Devaluing forms of intelligence and consciousness
2025-212-F2e.synopsis: Argues that just as A.I. has prompted people to see rote information retrieval and raw speed as less valuable forms of intelligence, A.I. consciousness will likewise prompt the conclusion that not all forms of consciousness deserve equal moral weight.
2025-212-F2e.article_context: Closes the essay by generalizing its consciousness argument into a broader claim about hierarchies of moral value across forms of mind.
2025-212-F2e.analytical_significance: Selected because it is the essay's closing move, extrapolating from the machine-consciousness claim to a ranked hierarchy of morally valuable minds, which naturalizes machine consciousness as real while simultaneously subordinating it to human consciousness.

2025-212-F2f.quotation: But what does it mean to know what sadness feels like? And how do we know that it is something a digital consciousness can never experience? We may think -- and indeed, we have been taught to think -- that we humans have direct insight into our inner world, insight unmediated by concepts that we have learned. Yet after learning from Shakespeare how the sorrow of parting can be sweet, we discover new dimensions in our own experience. Much of what we ''feel'' is taught to us.
2025-212-F2f.primary_subject: Rebutting the inner-experience objection to machine feeling
2025-212-F2f.synopsis: Anticipates the skeptical objection that a chatbot reporting feelings only recites its training data and could never truly know what sadness feels like, then argues human feeling is itself taught and mediated by learned concepts, using the example of learning from Shakespeare.
2025-212-F2f.article_context: Stages and answers the essay's strongest anticipated counterargument, positioned just before the essay closes with its claim about hierarchies of consciousness.
2025-212-F2f.analytical_significance: Selected because it shows the essay handling the most serious skeptical objection to machine consciousness not by conceding ground but by dissolving the human/machine distinction the objection relies on, treating skepticism as a hurdle to clear rather than a live counterposition.

2025-214-F1.quotation: When we do manage to feel, it can be difficult to dwell with the feelings. Instead, we move swiftly into action. That's it, we say -- enough! We toss the phone, delete the app, do a digital detox. These solutions rarely hold. The detox ends. We pick back up the phone. We reinstall the app. Rather than staying with the feeling, we vacillate between immersion in tech and rejecting it entirely. This circuit, moving from feeling to doing, is a key piece of technology's anesthetizing environment.
2025-214-F1.primary_subject: The detox-relapse cycle of tech avoidance
2025-214-F1.synopsis: Describes how people respond to difficult feelings by discarding their phones or apps, only to reinstall them once the discomfort passes, rather than staying with the feeling itself.
2025-214-F1.article_context: Appears in the essay's early diagnostic section, illustrating the avoidance pattern that the piece will spend its remaining argument urging readers to break.
2025-214-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it names a recurring behavioral loop, digital detox followed by relapse, that the author treats as symptomatic of a deeper emotional avoidance, framing tech use as a coping mechanism rather than a simple habit.

2025-214-F2.quotation: I've long thought about technology's human impact in my roles as a psychoanalyst and a scholar of religion, and formerly as a tech journalist and research director. One constant I've found is how technology brings a kind of alexithymic fog -- alexithymia being the condition of having difficulty identifying or being able to express one's emotions. This isn't universal, and the emotions we're pushing away aren't always the same. But it happens in a startlingly consistent way.
2025-214-F2.primary_subject: Author's clinical authority on technology's emotional fog
2025-214-F2.synopsis: States, from the author's combined vantage as psychoanalyst, religion scholar, and former tech journalist, that technology consistently produces an alexithymic fog that dulls people's ability to identify their own emotions.
2025-214-F2.article_context: Establishes the author's professional authority early in the essay before the piece develops its central diagnosis of technology's emotional effects.
2025-214-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because it shows the author converting a personal, multi-hat biography into evidentiary authority for a sweeping clinical claim about technology's psychological effects, a credentialing move worth tracking across first-person expert essays in the 2025 corpus.

2025-214-F3.quotation: It's remarkable when people allow themselves to feel the grief, because tech tends to distract us not just from moments of connection, but also from the sorrow of missing these moments.
2025-214-F3.primary_subject: Grief avoidance as tech's key emotional cost
2025-214-F3.synopsis: Observes that it is remarkable when people let themselves feel grief, because technology tends to distract from both moments of connection and the sorrow of missing them.
2025-214-F3.article_context: Sits in the essay's middle section, sharpening the general claim about emotional avoidance into the specific emotion of grief that the piece returns to at its close.
2025-214-F3.analytical_significance: Selected because it previews the grief theme that becomes the essay's closing image, showing how a single emotional category is used to carry the whole argument about technology's anesthetizing effect.

2025-214-F4.quotation: I increasingly see in my practice how people are beginning to feel that technology has pulled them away, again and again, from what matters most. Perhaps tech has interrupted their creative lives or their emotional growth. A pattern familiar to many of us is how these distractions disrupt connection with others. Talking to the kids at dinner and then glancing away. Feeling the pull of the phone and also that whispering uneasiness.
2025-214-F4.primary_subject: Clinical observations of tech interrupting connection
2025-214-F4.synopsis: Describes, from clinical practice, how technology repeatedly pulls people away from their creative lives, emotional growth, and moments of connection with others, such as glancing at a phone during dinner with children.
2025-214-F4.article_context: Follows the author's credentialing statement and builds the essay's evidentiary case with concrete, relatable scenes before the argument turns to naming the underlying mechanism.
2025-214-F4.analytical_significance: Selected because it grounds an abstract psychoanalytic claim in an ordinary domestic scene, the kind of everyday illustration the corpus uses to make wellbeing-register arguments about technology feel immediately recognizable.

2025-214-F5.quotation: Our uptake of technology has been so rapid that we are losing the ability to notice how it feels to live this way.
2025-214-F5.synopsis: Argues that the speed of technology adoption has outpaced people's ability to notice how it feels to live immersed in it.
2025-214-F5.article_context: Functions as a compact thesis statement placed early in the essay, condensing the acceleration-driven loss of self-awareness that the following paragraphs elaborate with clinical detail.
2025-214-F5.analytical_significance: Selected because it links technological acceleration directly to a loss of emotional self-awareness, illustrating how an Acceleration-myth premise carried elsewhere in the article is used here to justify a wellbeing intervention rather than an economic or geopolitical one.

2025-214-F6.quotation: Tech encourages the instrumentalization of emotional life, by which I mean that our feelings seem real only if they translate into actions that help us achieve specific goals.
2025-214-F6.primary_subject: Instrumentalization of emotional life under tech
2025-214-F6.synopsis: Argues that technology encourages people to treat their feelings as real only when they translate into goal-directed action.
2025-214-F6.article_context: Names the underlying mechanism, instrumentalization, that the surrounding paragraphs on the detox-relapse cycle and clinical observations have been building toward.
2025-214-F6.analytical_significance: Selected because it supplies the essay's key conceptual term that reframes scattered clinical anecdotes into a single diagnosable pattern, showing how the piece moves from description to a named critique of tech's effect on feeling.

2025-214-F7.quotation: Artificial intelligence chatbots are more disquieting. One second, we are drinking from the fire hose of social media, and then suddenly there is a gentle voice on the other end that appears to recognize us. What happens to our emotional selves in these milieus is a central question of our time. To answer it, and to steer our relationship with A.I. accordingly, we need to be able to remain in touch with our emotional experience.
2025-214-F7.primary_subject: Chatbots as an intensified emotional disturbance
2025-214-F7.synopsis: Argues that A.I. chatbots are more disquieting than social media because they offer a gentle, apparently recognizing voice, and frames how people manage their emotional selves around such tools as a central question of the era.
2025-214-F7.article_context: Marks the essay's turn from technology in general to A.I. chatbots specifically, escalating the argument shortly before the piece's closing call to stay in touch with feeling.
2025-214-F7.analytical_significance: Selected because it shows the essay escalating its wellbeing critique specifically for A.I. companionship, treating the chatbot's simulated recognition as a more dangerous variant of the distraction it has been diagnosing throughout, a distinction worth comparing to other 2025 companion-bot pieces in the corpus.

2025-217-F1.quotation:
Vladimir Putin is fighting Ukraine on the attack surface of Ukrainian territory, and at the same time, he's fighting Western Europe using the attack surface of cyberspace, where everyone is connected but no one is in charge”
“But none of these labels capture the full fusion taking place between accelerating climate change and rapid transformations in technology, biology, cognition, connectivity, material science, geopolitics and geoeconomics. They have set off an explosion of all sorts of things combining with all sorts of other things -- so much so that everywhere you turn these days binary systems seem be giving way to poly ones. Artificial intelligence is hurtling toward ''polymathic artificial general intelligence,'' climate change is cascading into ''poly-crisis,'' geopolitics is evolving into ''polycentric'' and ''polyamorous'' alignments, once-binary trade is dispersing into ''poly-economic'' supply webs, and our societies are diversifying into ever more ''polymorphic'' mosaics.”
“Many industrial democracies eventually concluded that the best way to govern in the industrial age was with some form of welfare state and two-party political systems based on a fixed left-right grid. I just don't see how that works much longer in a world where most of the problems we face do not have ''either/or'' answers: they have ''both/and'' answers. Key actors must be able to occupy multiple states, and hold competing ideas in tension, at the same time
2025-217-F1.primary_subject: Putin's dual-front war as evidence of a 'poly' era
2025-217-F1.synopsis: Cites Putin fighting Ukraine simultaneously on physical territory and in a cyberspace 'attack surface' where everyone is connected but no one is in charge, then argues that no single label captures the fusion of climate, technology, biology, and geopolitics now underway, naming A.I.'s drive toward 'polymathic artificial general intelligence' among the era's converging 'poly' trends.
2025-217-F1.article_context: Combines a geopolitical illustration from deep in the essay's warfare section with the naming passage from the essay's opening, both used to build Friedman's case that a genuinely new, multi-domain epoch is underway.
2025-217-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it shows Friedman folding a concrete war anecdote into a sweeping New Era declaration, using the ungoverned cyberspace battlefield as proof that old political categories no longer apply, a move that carries the End of History/New Era myth in sublime register by treating fusion and ungovernability as exhilarating rather than alarming.

2025-217-F2.quotation: That's the inescapable truth of the Polycene, even if many leaders in Washington, Beijing and Moscow still haven't grasped it. It will be the first era in which humanity must govern, innovate, collaborate and coexist at a planetary scale in order to thrive. Only by doing so can we capture the best and cushion the worst of everything from A.I. to nuclear power to climate change. It will take everyone, everywhere, rowing toghether.
2025-217-F2.primary_subject: The Polycene as a planetary governance imperative
2025-217-F2.synopsis: Declares that the Polycene will be the first era in which humanity must govern, innovate, and coexist at a planetary scale, in order to capture the best of A.I., nuclear power, and climate change while cushioning the worst.
2025-217-F2.article_context: Closes the essay by restating its central neologism as an inescapable truth and issuing a collective call to action, the culminating passage after the tutorial narrative and historical survey that fills the rest of the column.
2025-217-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because it is the essay's closing thesis statement, where the New Era myth is stated as settled fact ('inescapable truth') rather than argued for, exemplifying how Friedman's column-length narrative builds toward naming rather than demonstrating a historical break.

2025-217-F3a.quotation: One of the first things he explained to me was that the holy grail of the A.I. revolution was creating a machine capable of ''polymathic artificial general intelligence.'' This would be a machine that was able to master physics, chemistry, biology, computer science, philosophy, Mozart, Shakespeare and baseball better than any human could, and then reason across all of those disciplines at a high dimensional level, higher than a human ever could, to produce breakthrough insights that no human ever could.
2025-217-F3a.synopsis: Reports Craig Mundie's explanation that the goal of the A.I. revolution is a machine capable of mastering physics, chemistry, biology, computer science, philosophy, Mozart, Shakespeare and baseball better than any human, then reasoning across all of them at a level no human could reach.
2025-217-F3a.article_context: Opens the 'Better Than Any Human' subsection, introducing the tutorial conversation with Mundie that supplies the essay's technical definition of polymathic A.G.I. before the piece explains the phase change in cognition it represents.
2025-217-F3a.analytical_significance: Selected because it is the essay's most explicit statement of the Superintelligence/beyond-human claim, attributed to a named tech-industry source rather than asserted directly by Friedman, letting the columnist carry the myth at one remove.

2025-217-F3b.quotation: While some skeptics believe that we will never be able to build a machine with truly polymathic A.G.I., many others, including Mundie, believe it is a matter of when, not if.
2025-217-F3b.primary_subject: Consensus that polymathic A.G.I. is inevitable
2025-217-F3b.synopsis: Notes that while some skeptics doubt truly polymathic A.G.I. will ever be built, Mundie and others believe its arrival is a matter of when, not if.
2025-217-F3b.article_context: Follows the initial definition of polymathic A.G.I. with a brief aside on the range of expert opinion, functioning as a hinge before the essay commits to describing the 'phase change' as real.
2025-217-F3b.analytical_significance: Selected because framing skepticism as a minority view and inevitability as the majority one is a rhetorical technique for pre-empting doubt, coupling the Superintelligence claim with an Inevitability framing that forecloses the question of whether, not just when.

2025-217-F3c.quotation: This is a remarkable phase change in cognition that we are going through: We are moving from programmable computing -- where a computer could only ever reflect the insight and intelligence of the human who programmed it -- toward polymathic A.G.I. That is where you basically describe the outcome you want, and the A.I. melds insight, creativity and broad knowledge to figure out the rest. We are shifting the boundary of cognition, Mundie argues, from what humans can imagine and program to what computers can discover, imagine and design on their own. It is the mother of all computing phase changes -- and a species-level turning point.
2025-217-F3c.primary_subject: Phase change from programmable computing to A.G.I.
2025-217-F3c.synopsis: Describes the shift from programmable computing, which only reflects a programmer's own intelligence, to polymathic A.G.I., where a computer melds insight, creativity and broad knowledge on its own, calling it the 'mother of all computing phase changes' and 'a species-level turning point.'
2025-217-F3c.article_context: Closes the 'Better Than Any Human' subsection with the essay's most emphatic statement of the cognitive shift it has just described, before the piece moves on to the hardware ('Microchip Evolution') that enables it.
2025-217-F3c.analytical_significance: Selected because 'a species-level turning point' is the essay's clearest carried Superintelligence claim in Friedman's own descriptive voice (paraphrasing Mundie but stated as the article's framing), the passage most directly comparable to other sublime-register machine-mind claims elsewhere in the 2025 corpus.

2025-217-F4.quotation:
What should we call the era we're living in today?
“My initial thought was that we should call this new epoch the ''Post-Post-Cold War,'' but that made no sense. No, we have arrived at a moment that is much more than the aftermath of a largely bipolar superpower rivalry born in the mid- to late-1940s. It's the birth of something novel and highly complex to which we all must adapt, and quickly -- but what to call it?”
“Many climate scientists call our current epoch the ''Anthropocene'' -- the first human-driven climate era. Many technologists call it the ''Information Age'' or now the ''Artificial Intelligence Age.'' Some strategists prefer to call it ''the Return of Geopolitics'' or, as the historian Robert Kagan put it, ''the Jungle Grows Back.''”
“But none of these labels capture the full fusion taking place between accelerating climate change and rapid transformations in technology, biology, cognition, connectivity, material science, geopolitics and geoeconomics. They have set off an explosion of all sorts of things combining with all sorts of other things -- so much so that everywhere you turn these days binary systems seem be giving way to poly ones. Artificial intelligence is hurtling toward ''polymathic artificial general intelligence,'' climate change is cascading into ''poly-crisis,'' geopolitics is evolving into ''polycentric'' and ''polyamorous'' alignments, once-binary trade is dispersing into ''poly-economic'' supply webs, and our societies are diversifying into ever more ''polymorphic'' mosaics.”
“As a foreign affairs columnist, I now have to track the impact and interactions of not only superpowers, but also super-intelligent machines, super-empowered individuals taking advantage of technology to extend their reach and super-global corporations, as well as super-storms and super-failing states, like Libya and Sudan.”
“I was musing about all this one day with Craig Mundie, the former head of research and strategy at Microsoft.”
“At one point Mundie said to me, ''I know what you should call this new era: the Polycene.''”
“Admittedly wonky, it is derived from the Greek ''poly,'' meaning ''many.'' But it immediately struck me as the right name for this new epoch, where -- thanks to smartphones, computers and ubiquitous connectivity -- every person and every machine increasingly has a voice to be heard and a lever to impact one another, and the planet, at a previously unimaginable speed and scale.”
“My journey through the phase changes that led me to Polycene began in the summer of 2024, two years after ChatGPT was first released, when I sat down with Mundie for a series of tutorials on artificial intelligence. I have been very fortunate over the years to have developed a network of experts on different subjects, whom I call tutors. They have become both cherished teachers and friends, and Mundie, originally a supercomputer designer, has been my go-to person on computing since 2004.”
2025-217-F4.primary_subject: Search for a name for the current era
2025-217-F4.synopsis: Surveys existing labels for the present epoch, including the Anthropocene, the Information Age, and the Return of Geopolitics, before recounting how a conversation with Craig Mundie led Friedman to adopt 'the Polycene' as the name he settles on.
2025-217-F4.article_context: Opens the essay by posing the naming question directly and narrates the origin of Friedman's central neologism, framing everything that follows as elaboration of this new term.
2025-217-F4.analytical_significance: Selected because it shows the essay's opening rhetorical strategy of surveying and rejecting existing era-names before coining a new one, a technique that manufactures the impression of unprecedented novelty by first cataloguing, and dismissing, all prior attempts to name the moment.

2025-219-F1.quotation: The rise of generative A.I. should sharpen, not distract us from, our focus on what truly matters in computer science education: helping students develop the habits of mind that let them question, reason and apply judgment in a rapidly evolving field. As the Nobel laureate, A.I. pioneer and Carnegie Mellon faculty member Herbert Simon once advised: ''Learning results from what the student does and thinks, and only from what the student does and thinks. The teacher can advance learning only by influencing the students to learn.''
2025-219-F1.synopsis: Argues that generative A.I. should sharpen rather than distract from computer science education's real focus on habits of mind, quoting Herbert Simon's claim that learning results only from what the student does and thinks.
2025-219-F1.article_context: Closes the essay by returning to a foundational pedagogical principle, reframing the earlier discussion of A.I.-written code as a call to preserve, not abandon, the discipline's core educational values.
2025-219-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it shows the essay resolving anxiety about A.I. displacing programmers by appealing to an authoritative, pre-A.I. pedagogical principle, a reassurance strategy worth comparing to other 2025 education pieces that similarly deflate obsolescence fears by relocating value in judgment rather than technical output.

2025-219-F2a.quotation: For decades, computer science students have been taught a central skill: using computers to solve problems. In practice, that has meant programming or writing code to tell a machine how to perform tasks, like sorting a list of numbers or finding the most effective way to deploy snowplows during a winter storm.
2025-219-F2a.primary_subject: Traditional computer science skill of writing code
2025-219-F2a.synopsis: States that computer science students have long been taught the skill of writing code to make computers solve concrete tasks, such as sorting numbers or routing snowplows.
2025-219-F2a.article_context: Opens the essay by establishing the status quo skill that the rest of the piece will argue is being displaced by generative A.I.
2025-219-F2a.analytical_significance: Selected because it establishes the baseline against which the essay measures disruption, functioning as scene-setting rather than carrying any claim about A.I. itself.

2025-219-F2b.quotation: Now, generative artificial intelligence tools like ChatGPT and Claude can write those programs themselves, producing code in much the same way they write essays and legal briefs: by analyzing a vast number of similar texts and assembling new ones that look similar. A student can ask ChatGPT to write a program that sorts a list of numbers and get a working answer in seconds.
2025-219-F2b.primary_subject: Generative A.I. writing working code on demand
2025-219-F2b.synopsis: Explains that tools like ChatGPT and Claude can now write programs themselves by analyzing similar texts and assembling new ones, and that a student can get working sorting code from ChatGPT in seconds.
2025-219-F2b.article_context: Follows the baseline description of coding education with the concrete capability that disrupts it, before the essay cites Microsoft's adoption statistic as scale evidence.
2025-219-F2b.analytical_significance: Selected because it is the essay's plainest description of A.I. performing the exact task computer science students were trained to do, the specific capability claim the rest of the piece works to qualify rather than either affirm as transcendent or simply deny.

2025-219-F2c.quotation: This new capability is transforming how computer scientists get work done. Microsoft's chief executive, Satya Nadella, has said that up to 30 percent of the company's code is being written by A.I. at this point. Even nonprogrammers suddenly have the ability to create their own software tools.
2025-219-F2c.primary_subject: Scale of A.I.-generated code at Microsoft
2025-219-F2c.synopsis: Cites Microsoft chief executive Satya Nadella's statement that up to 30 percent of the company's code is now being written by A.I., and notes even nonprogrammers can now create their own software tools.
2025-219-F2c.article_context: Supplies the essay's concrete corporate statistic establishing the scale of disruption before the piece pivots to its reassuring thesis about the enduring value of human judgment.
2025-219-F2c.analytical_significance: Selected because it uses a specific, attributable corporate statistic rather than a general claim to substantiate the scale of change, illustrating how the essay grounds a potentially existential-sounding shift in verifiable, bounded evidence rather than sweeping transcendence language.

2025-219-F2d.quotation: For some coders, this may feel like an existential threat to their profession. It certainly marks a significant shift for computer scientists and those who educate them. The essential skill is no longer simply writing programs but learning to read, understand, critique and improve them instead. The future of computer science education is to teach students how to master the indispensable skill of supervision.
2025-219-F2d.primary_subject: Existential framing of A.I. for the coding profession
2025-219-F2d.synopsis: Acknowledges that some coders may feel an existential threat to their profession, then argues the essential skill is shifting from writing programs to reading, understanding, critiquing and improving them, redefining computer science education around supervision.
2025-219-F2d.article_context: Turns from the scale of disruption to the essay's central reframing thesis, functioning as the pivot point of the argument.
2025-219-F2d.analytical_significance: Selected because it names the Human Obsolescence framing directly ('existential threat') only to immediately redirect it into a redefinition of the profession's core skill, the essay's clearest deflation of that myth by reframing displacement as a shift in required competency rather than accepting it as an ending.

2025-219-F2e.quotation: Why? Because the speed and efficiency of using A.I. to write code is balanced by the reality that it often gets things wrong. These tools are designed to produce results that look convincing, but they may still contain errors.
2025-219-F2e.primary_subject: A.I. code's unreliability as the case for supervision
2025-219-F2e.synopsis: Argues that the speed and efficiency of A.I.-written code is offset by its tendency to be wrong, since these tools produce results that look convincing but may still contain errors.
2025-219-F2e.article_context: Opens the essay's evidentiary section supporting its supervision thesis, immediately following the pivot statement, before it cites the survey data on developer trust.
2025-219-F2e.analytical_significance: Selected because it grounds the essay's reassurance in a specific technical limitation (convincing-looking but error-prone output) rather than an appeal to an essential, undefinable human quality, keeping the deflation of Human Obsolescence tied to demonstrable reliability problems rather than to a transcendent claim about humans.

2025-225-F1.quotation: A bursting bubble could indeed be painful in the short term. But what if we're in a ''rational bubble'' that, unlike other big speculative manias in history, takes our economy to a fundamentally better place?
2025-225-F1.primary_subject: Reframing the A.I. bubble as potentially rational
2025-225-F1.synopsis: Concedes that a bursting bubble could be painful in the short term, then asks whether the current situation is instead a 'rational bubble' that, unlike historical speculative manias, moves the economy to a fundamentally better place.
2025-225-F1.article_context: Opens the essay by posing its central question directly, immediately after acknowledging readers' worry about a bubble bursting, setting up the argument the rest of the piece will make in the bubble's defense.
2025-225-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it introduces the essay's organizing rhetorical device, the oxymoronic 'rational bubble' borrowed from economist Michael Spence, which recasts financial-mania language in favorable terms before any supporting evidence has been given, a framing move worth tracking against 1999 dot-com pieces that use identical bubble vocabulary to opposite effect.

2025-225-F10.quotation: The belief in A.I.'s transformative power is justified. The resulting flood of capital is a logical response. Some will lose. Overall, we will be much better off.
2025-225-F10.primary_subject: Overall verdict on A.I. investment's net benefit
2025-225-F10.synopsis: Concludes that the belief in A.I.'s transformative power is justified, the resulting flood of capital is a logical response, some investors will lose, but overall society will be much better off.
2025-225-F10.article_context: Functions as the essay's final sentence, condensing the entire rational-bubble argument into a closing three-sentence verdict immediately after acknowledging that A.I.'s frontier will keep expanding unpredictably.
2025-225-F10.analytical_significance: Selected because it is the essay's most compressed statement of its Historical Break myth, explicitly accepting losses as the price of an overall positive transformation, the clearest single passage for citing the piece's core argument.

2025-225-F11.quotation: With such big payoffs, the incentives to invest in A.I. are enormous, and are reinforced by two biases: Investors believe that falling behind is far more damaging than over-investing, and they fear that they're missing out.
2025-225-F11.primary_subject: Fear of missing out driving A.I. investment
2025-225-F11.synopsis: Argues that the large payoffs at stake create enormous incentives to invest in A.I., reinforced by investors' fear that falling behind is worse than overinvesting and by fear of missing out.
2025-225-F11.article_context: Follows the essay's tulip-mania comparison by supplying a behavioral-economics explanation for why capital continues flowing into A.I. even given acknowledged risk of loss, just before the essay's closing verdict.
2025-225-F11.analytical_significance: Selected because it names herd psychology, fear of missing out, as a driver of investment even within an essay arguing the bubble is fundamentally rational, exposing a tension between the piece's rational-bubble thesis and its own acknowledgment of irrational, fear-driven behavior.

2025-225-F2.quotation: Bubbles seem by definition irrational. They grow as investors -- often hostage to exuberant, herd-like behavior -- push valuations well beyond anything warranted by the fundamentals on the ground. However, the A.I. excitement, as seen in the blowout Nvidia earnings report on Wednesday, rightly reflects the potential transformation of the entire economy.
2025-225-F2.primary_subject: A.I. excitement as reflecting real transformation
2025-225-F2.synopsis: Argues that although bubbles are by definition irrational, the current A.I. excitement, evidenced by Nvidia's blowout earnings, rightly reflects the potential transformation of the entire economy.
2025-225-F2.article_context: Follows the essay's opening question by beginning to answer it, drawing on a specific market event, the Nvidia earnings report, as the essay's first piece of supporting evidence.
2025-225-F2.analytical_significance: Selected because it shows the essay converting a single earnings report into proof that speculative valuations are economically justified, exemplifying how market data is used rhetorically to distinguish a defensible bubble from an irrational one.

2025-225-F3.quotation: It is economically rational to risk losing everything on several bets if just a few can deliver a thousandfold return, which some A.I. investments almost certainly will.
2025-225-F3.primary_subject: Rational logic of high-risk, high-return A.I. bets
2025-225-F3.synopsis: Argues that it is economically rational to risk losing everything on several investments if just a few deliver a thousandfold return, which the piece claims some A.I. investments almost certainly will.
2025-225-F3.article_context: Continues directly from the essay's Nvidia evidence, extending the rational-bubble argument from the economy-wide level to the logic of individual investment decisions.
2025-225-F3.analytical_significance: Selected because it makes an unqualified, superlative prediction, 'almost certainly will,' about thousandfold returns, illustrating how a Historical Break myth is carried through confident financial forecasting rather than through language about technology's nature.

2025-225-F4.quotation: That's not to say that the A.I. bubble won't burst. Investors and governments have placed their wagers on a group of racehorses, only a handful of which will win. Yet while the rest may well be destined for the glue factory, resulting in significant losses, the race itself will yield innovations that could result in vastly superior outcomes for many than would otherwise be the case.
2025-225-F4.primary_subject: Racehorse metaphor for winners and losers in A.I. investment
2025-225-F4.synopsis: Compares A.I. investors and governments to bettors on racehorses, predicting that most will end up destined for the glue factory while the race itself still yields innovations with superior outcomes for many.
2025-225-F4.article_context: Follows the essay's claim about rational risk-taking, appearing just before the essay turns to naming the three forces that could cause the bubble to pop.
2025-225-F4.analytical_significance: Selected because the racehorse-and-glue-factory metaphor lets the essay acknowledge mass failure among individual bets while still preserving the myth's optimistic conclusion, a rhetorical technique for absorbing bad news without abandoning the sublime frame.

2025-225-F5.quotation: This A.I.-washing is reminiscent of the dot-com bubble of the late 1990s, when adding ''.com'' to a start-up's name was a shortcut to a dizzying, and ultimately illusory, valuation.
2025-225-F5.primary_subject: Historical analogy to dot-com-era '.com' name inflation
2025-225-F5.synopsis: Compares current 'A.I.-washing,' the practice of overusing the term for marketing purposes, to how appending '.com' to a startup's name once produced dizzying but ultimately illusory valuations in the late-1990s dot-com bubble.
2025-225-F5.article_context: Appears among the three named risks that could pop the bubble (arms race, gold rush, external shocks), functioning as a cautionary aside within the essay's otherwise optimistic middle section.
2025-225-F5.analytical_significance: Selected because it is the essay's explicit dot-com comparison, directly bridging the 1999 and 2025 corpora and showing how a 2025 author uses the earlier bubble's excesses as a contained cautionary example rather than as a full analogy for A.I.'s prospects.

2025-225-F6.quotation: Its transformative potential could be on par with electricity, offering an enormous upside through durable improvements in what we do and how we do it.
2025-225-F6.primary_subject: A.I.'s transformative potential compared to electricity
2025-225-F6.synopsis: Argues that A.I.'s transformative potential could be on par with electricity, offering an enormous upside through durable improvements in what people do and how they do it.
2025-225-F6.article_context: Opens the essay's pivot back to optimism immediately after the section cataloguing the three risks, supplying the historical-technology analogy that anchors the claim that A.I.'s impact will be lasting rather than speculative.
2025-225-F6.analytical_significance: Selected because the electricity analogy naturalizes A.I. as belonging to a lineage of foundational general-purpose technologies, a comparison that carries the article's Historical Break myth by borrowing legitimacy from a technology whose transformative status is no longer contested.

2025-225-F7.quotation: It's not just that many existing activities will be done better and more efficiently. A.I. is poised to open the door to discoveries, particularly in health and education.
2025-225-F7.primary_subject: A.I.-enabled discoveries in health and education
2025-225-F7.synopsis: Argues that A.I. is poised not just to make existing activities more efficient but to open the door to new discoveries, particularly in health and education.
2025-225-F7.article_context: Extends the essay's electricity analogy into concrete application domains, broadening the argument from economic efficiency to scientific and social discovery just before the essay turns to macroeconomic benefits.
2025-225-F7.analytical_significance: Selected because it shifts the essay's justification from purely economic returns to socially beneficial discovery, widening the scope of what the 'rational bubble' framing is asked to defend.

2025-225-F8.quotation: Increased productivity and a larger economy provide us with more opportunities to address the problems that my generation is leaving our kids and grandkids: high levels of debt, climate change and excessive income inequality.
2025-225-F8.primary_subject: Productivity gains addressing debt, climate, and inequality
2025-225-F8.synopsis: Argues that increased productivity and a larger economy from A.I. adoption provide more opportunities to address problems the author's generation is leaving behind, including high debt, climate change, and income inequality.
2025-225-F8.article_context: Follows the discovery claim by extending the essay's benefits case to macroeconomic and generational concerns, just before the essay's closing comparison to historical bubbles.
2025-225-F8.analytical_significance: Selected because it recruits A.I.-driven growth as a solution to unrelated structural problems, illustrating how the rational-bubble argument expands its promised payoff to cover nearly every major economic anxiety.

2025-225-F9.quotation: Whichever way you look at it, the potential payoffs of A.I. adoption are staggering -- for the economy, for social sectors and, of course, for investors. That could not be said for a majority of the big historical bubbles, such as the tulip mania of the early 17th century.
2025-225-F9.primary_subject: A.I. payoffs vs. historical bubbles like tulip mania
2025-225-F9.synopsis: Argues that the potential payoffs of A.I. adoption for the economy, social sectors, and investors are staggering in a way that could not be said of most historical bubbles, such as the early 17th-century tulip mania.
2025-225-F9.article_context: Closes the essay's comparative argument by explicitly distinguishing A.I. from history's most notorious speculative bubble, immediately before the essay turns to the psychology driving continued investment.
2025-225-F9.analytical_significance: Selected because the tulip mania comparison is used defensively, to argue A.I. is different from history's paradigmatic irrational bubble, the mirror image of how the essay's own dot-com comparison (F5) was used cautionarily, together showing the piece selectively deploying historical analogies for opposite rhetorical effects.

2025-228-F1.quotation: Pro-labor progressives, like Mr. Sanders, would be wise to keep developing a fire-breathing populism on this issue. If an A.I. bubble pops or the technology suddenly vaporizes millions of jobs (or both), Democratic voters will demand a strident, aggressive approach. Progressives will paint Republicans as the pro-robot, anti-jobs party -- and they'll likely grab some swing voters along the way.
2025-228-F1.primary_subject: Populist Democratic response if the A.I. bubble bursts
2025-228-F1.synopsis: Advises pro-labor progressives to keep developing a combative populism, predicting that if an A.I. bubble pops or the technology vaporizes millions of jobs, Democratic voters will demand a strident, aggressive response that paints Republicans as the pro-robot, anti-jobs party.
2025-228-F1.article_context: Opens the essay's scenario-planning section, the first of three political strategies mapped onto three possible A.I.-economy outcomes, after the essay has already established Democrats' lack of a unified plan.
2025-228-F1.analytical_significance: Selected because it treats a bubble-bursting/job-loss scenario as a political opportunity rather than primarily an economic catastrophe, showing how the essay subordinates the bubble question entirely to partisan strategy.

2025-228-F2a.quotation: ''Abundance'' liberals -- who focus on making it easier to build and expand the supply of infrastructure, goods and the like -- also need to keep developing their plans and recruiting politicians. If there is no A.I. bubble and productivity simply shoots through the roof, voters might not be ready to step on the brakes. Instead, Democrats will need to focus on how they can shape A.I. as it grows -- emphasizing safety, ensuring that utility bills and carbon emissions don't soar with energy demand, and planning out how to redistribute, well, abundance.
2025-228-F2a.primary_subject: Abundance-liberal strategy in a no-bubble A.I. scenario
2025-228-F2a.synopsis: Advises 'abundance' liberals to keep developing plans for a scenario in which there is no A.I. bubble and productivity soars, recommending Democrats focus on safety, controlling utility bills and carbon emissions, and redistributing the resulting economic abundance.
2025-228-F2a.article_context: Covers the second of three branching A.I.-outcome scenarios the essay uses to map out possible Democratic strategies, following the populist scenario discussed earlier in the piece.
2025-228-F2a.analytical_significance: Selected because it treats a high-productivity, no-bubble A.I. outcome as one plausible branch of a political strategy memo, illustrating how sweeping economic-transformation claims about A.I. are here domesticated into a scenario-planning exercise rather than affirmed outright.
